# Logic library — reasoning failures and how they were caught

> *Kit edition. Each entry keeps the mod's name, what the issue was, how it was fixed, what got in the way and the reasoning lesson. Direct evidence is removed by the build's stated rule (offsets, byte patterns, disassembly, record IDs, asset paths, code from other authors) and shows as `[... removed]`. Other documents' references to an entry by number predate this edition: search by heading.*

*Doc v1.5.5, revised 2026-10-14 - page layout gate, 2026-10-14*




































<!-- VERSIONING-RULES -->
> **Versioning rules (CLAUDE.md rules 6 and 48 - identical for mods and documents):**
> * `X.Y.Z`. A change increments the THIRD number. At `.9` the MINOR rolls: `1.0.9 -> 1.1.0`;
>   `1.0.10` never exists.
> * The next number is **LAST WORKING + 1**. A failed, scratch or untested test build does NOT
>   consume its number - the next attempt at the same step REUSES it.
> * Numbers are never typed. ONE tool, `.MD\scripts\version-gate.ps1`, holds every version rule
>   and is a GATE that fails: `bump` issues the next number and writes every location, `record`
>   proves it working (evidence + the binary's hash), `gate` refuses packaging or finalizing
>   anything it did not issue. Documents go through `docs-pipeline.ps1 -Action bump` and the rules
>   through `rules-version.ps1 -Action bump`, both of which take their arithmetic from that same
>   tool. A number typed by hand is wrong until the tool agrees.








**What this file is for.** the owner, 2026-08-27: *"every time something goes wrong and you find the
answer, you can document it and reference it as needed in the future and learn from your mistakes."*

**This is not a rules file and not a changelog.** `CLAUDE.md` holds his standing rules.
`PROGRESS.md` holds the state of each mod. Bug reports hold individual defects. **This holds the
reasoning** — the class of mistake, why the wrong answer looked convincing at the time, and the check
that would have caught it sooner.

**Read the entries for an area BEFORE acting in it, not only when diagnosing** (the owner,
2026-09-12). Grep the index block below for the topics of the work about to start and read what it
points to, at the moment work enters that area. Symptom lookup after a failure is the second use; a
library consulted only after a failure has already let the logged mistake repeat once, and a library
only ever written to is a diary. Entries are titled by **symptom** and indexed by **topic**, so they
can be found both ways.

**Written to without being asked**, at the moment an answer is found — not batched up later, once the
reasoning that produced the mistake has faded.

> **Index of the past-mistakes library - read this, then open only the entries you need.** Each line is an entry's heading
> (which in this library is the lesson itself), the line it starts on, and its topics. Jump
> straight to a line, or grep this block for a topic. Regenerate with
> `python .MD\scripts\logic-index.py`; `optimize-project.ps1` fails section 6 when it is stale.
>
> The library is deliberately NOT split into parts the way the rules are. The rules are looked
> up by pipeline stage, which you know before you open them; this file is looked up by SYMPTOM,
> and its entries earn their place by applying to a problem in some OTHER domain. Splitting it
> by domain would make you guess where the answer lives before you know what it is.

---

## 1. A stack trace names the plugin that DIED, not the one that broke it

**Symptom:** a crash log whose call stack contains only third-party code.

**What I concluded:** that our mods were uninvolved, because none of our DLLs appeared anywhere in
the stack.

**Why that looked right:** it is normally true. A crash inside `ActorValueGenerator.dll`, called from
`LexiconSKSE.dll`, with no frame of ours anywhere, reads unambiguously as someone else's bug.

**What was actually true:** a control run with all fourteen of our mods disabled did not crash.
One of ours was corrupting state that a plugin *later in the load order* then tripped over.

**The check:** SKSE dispatches messages in load order — case-insensitive alphabetical by DLL
filename. When something dies during message dispatch, the culprit is as likely to be a plugin that
already ran as the one holding the stack. **Bisect; do not read attribution off a stack.**

---

## 2. Correlation is not mechanism — and five of them in a row means the model is wrong

**Symptom:** "X changed and then it broke", repeatedly, with each new theory replacing the last.

**What went wrong:** four consecutive confident diagnoses on one crash, each individually plausible,
each wrong — a co-save theory, a mod-toggle confound, a suspected DevBench hook, and a build that
turned out byte-identical to its predecessor.

**The pattern:** each wrong answer was reasoning from *what changed* rather than from *how it could
possibly cause this*. When a proposed mechanism cannot be stated — "a per-frame HUD guard kills
another plugin at `kDataLoaded`, somehow" — that is a signal the model is wrong, not that the
mechanism is merely unknown.

**The check:** state the mechanism before believing the correlation. If it cannot be stated, keep
bisecting rather than fixing. **CLAUDE.md rule 49 now enforces the stopping point at five.**

---

## 3. Hold every other variable fixed — including the ones you did not choose to change

**Symptom:** a bisect where two things differ between runs.

**What went wrong:** a DEM version change and a Compass Navigation Overhaul toggle moved together
across runs, so neither could be attributed. I noticed only after drawing a conclusion from it.

**The check:** before comparing two runs, **enumerate what differed** rather than assuming it was
only the thing you edited. Profile state, mod enable flags and plugin lists all drift during a
session — sometimes because the user changed them.

---

## 4. A disabled mod's DLL may still be loaded, because another mod ships it

**Symptom:** a plugin's log appears in a run where you disabled that plugin's mod.

**What was true:** three separate mods in the list contained `CompassNavigationOverhaul.dll` — the
upstream mod, our SMF conversion, and a third-party *patch* that quietly ships its own modified
copy. Disabling ours changed nothing about whether CNO was in the process.

**The check:** to establish whether a DLL is loaded, **search every enabled mod folder for that
filename**, rather than reading the enable state of the mod you associate it with.

---

## 5. Inline no-op stubs compile away — a "feature removed" build can be byte-identical

**Symptom:** two builds that should differ come out the same size.

**What went wrong:** to test whether a subsystem caused a crash, I replaced its header with inline
no-ops and removed its implementation. The next build then deleted all 24 call sites by hand — and
produced a binary the same size, because the no-ops had already compiled to nothing. The second test
would have burned a launch to learn nothing.

**The check:** after producing an isolation build, **verify it actually differs** — compare size and
hash against the build it is meant to differ from. And note the corollary: arguments to a no-op
function are still evaluated, so stubbing a function does **not** remove work done in computing its
arguments. That has to be deleted outright.

---

## 6. Verify the premise before acting on it — timestamps are cheap

**Symptom:** a theory that implies destroying something (deleting saves, reverting work).

**What went wrong:** I reasoned that a plugin added and then removed had left dangling references in
a save's co-save data, and was about to endorse deleting saves. One command disproved it: the newest
save predated the plugin's installation by 22 minutes, and reading the co-save confirmed the plugin's
name was absent.

**The check:** when a theory implies a destructive action, **spend the one command that tests the
premise first**. File timestamps, a hash, a grep — all cheaper than the mistake.

---

## 7. Never reason about a timeline from a truncated log

**Symptom:** a conclusion drawn from `tail -n` output.

**What went wrong:** a `tail -40` hid an INI reload that reset a keybind, which led to a confident
and wrong claim about what a keypress had been bound to at the time.

**The check:** when timing matters, read the whole relevant span, or grep for the specific events and
read their timestamps. Never infer "X did not happen" from a window that might not contain it.

---

## 8. Commit before letting an agent edit the working tree

**Symptom:** wanting to rebuild a known-good version and finding its source no longer exists.

**What went wrong:** builds 1.5.4 through 1.5.6 were made from uncommitted working-tree state. A
sub-agent then edited the same files. When 1.5.6 turned out to be the last working build, its exact
source could not be recovered — only its DLL — and it had to be reconstructed by stripping edits back
out.

**The check:** **commit before delegating work that touches a repo**, and commit a build you have
just confirmed working. A tag costs nothing; recovering a lost source state is expensive and lossy.

---

## 9. A logged failure in one subsystem means the whole subsystem is suspect

**Symptom:** a startup log reporting a resolution or initialisation failure, dismissed as narrow.

**What went wrong:** `Failed to resolve signature for lookupFormByID` was read as affecting only the
perk-requirement feature. It actually meant that plugin's *address resolution in general* was
unreliable — and a different unresolved address in the same plugin crashed the game an hour later.

**The check:** in a signature-scanning or address-resolving plugin, **one failed resolution invalidates
confidence in all of them** until proven otherwise. Treat it as load-bearing, not cosmetic.

---

## 10. Null checks do not defend against a bad code address

**Symptom:** an access violation that says "tried to EXECUTE memory", not "tried to read".

**What was true:** the guards were all present and correct — [code removed] sat on the very
next line — but the crash happened *inside the call that was supposed to produce* the value. Control
never returned, so the guard never ran.

**The check:** distinguish **bad data** (guardable by null checks) from **a bad code address**
(not guardable at all — you either avoid depending on the address or validate it before calling
through it). The exception text tells you which: *execute* versus *read*.

---

## 11. ROUTINE — when rebuilding or re-versioning a mod, set every location in one operation

**Symptom:** a version that is right in one file and stale in another, discovered much later.

**What went wrong:** across one evening a single mod ended up with `CMakeLists.txt` at 1.5.11,
`vcpkg.json` still at **0.1.1** (never updated once, across eight bumps), the package README at
1.5.10 and the folder name at 1.5.11. Each bump was a hand edit of whichever file was in front of
me, and nothing checked the rest.

**The mistaken design decision underneath it:** the first version checker was deliberately built to
*refuse* on drift rather than harmonise it, reasoning that silently rewriting files hides which
value was intended. That is right for a check run against an unknown state — but it left every real
bump as a manual multi-file edit, which is precisely how the drift begins. The owner's correction:
*"make sure they all line up automatically, because that has cost us a lot of time tonight."*

### The routine

**Never hand-edit a version.** State it once:

[code example removed; the text around it says what it showed]

Three tools, three distinct jobs, and the split is the point: **set** is automatic but explicitly
intentional; **check** still refuses rather than fixing, because drift found by a check means
something was edited by hand and a human should see it; **ledger** records whether the build
actually ran, which no file in the repo can tell you.

### The trap this routine exists to catch

**Do not assume every build system records a version the same way.** Writing this script surfaced
one immediately: Wait Your Turn Redux does **not** put the literal in `set_version("x.y.z")` — it
assigns `local version = "1.0.4"` and passes the variable. A patcher targeting `set_version` would
have matched nothing and reported success, which is the same silent failure in a new coat.

**So a "nothing to change" result is a finding, not a pass.** If a bump reports no changes,
establish whether the file was genuinely already correct or whether the pattern simply missed. The
script says so explicitly for that reason.

### Locations per build system, found by scanning rather than memory

| Build system | Mods | Where the version lives |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CMake + vcpkg | 9 | `CMakeLists.txt` `VERSION`, `vcpkg.json` `version-string`, `cmake\version.rc.in` |
| raw MSBuild | RememberLockpickAngle | `include\RLA_Version.hpp` (`_MAJOR`/`_MINOR`/`_PATCH`), `.vcxproj` |
| xmake | Wait Your Turn Redux | `xmake.lua` — **`local version = "..."`**, not the `set_version` call |
| all | all | package `README.txt`, package folder name, and the DLL's generated `FileVersion` |

The DLL's `FileVersion` is deliberately **not** written by the setter — it is generated at compile
time, so if it disagrees after a build, the build did not pick the change up. That is a real
finding worth surfacing, not something to paper over.

---

## 12. Inventory before deleting — "it's a temp folder" is not an inspection

**Symptom:** deleting something on the strength of *where it lives* rather than *what it contains*.

**What went wrong:** clearing old Claude session scratch folders from `%TEMP%`, I listed their names,
sizes and ages and deleted them. I never looked inside. The owner asked afterwards whether I had read the
contents, and the honest answer was no. The deletion used `Directory.Delete`, which bypasses the
Recycle Bin, so nothing was recoverable.

**Why it looked right:** the folder is designated for temporary files, the storage analysis had rated
it safe, and the user had authorised trimming exactly the items rated safe. Every individual step was
defensible.

**What made it wrong anyway:** two filenames leaked out in error messages during the delete —
`scratchpad\cat\dllscan\FLICK_NG_181603_1.3.` and a git `pack-*.idx`. So those folders held a DLL
scan of a specific mod and a cloned repository. Possibly disposable; possibly hours of someone's
analysis. **I could not say which, because I had not looked**, and by the time the question was
asked the answer was unrecoverable.

The point is sharpened by what the *current* session's scratchpad held at that moment: Spriggit
plugin round-trip output, downloaded Nexus archives, and the DLL copies hashed for VirusTotal
submissions. These folders demonstrably accumulate real working material.

### The checks

**Inventory first.** Before deleting a directory, list what is in it — file types, notable names, the
few largest items. It costs one command and it is the difference between "I deleted scratch files"
and "I deleted something I cannot describe".

**Prefer recoverable deletion when the contents have not been examined.** `Directory.Delete` and
`Remove-Item` are permanent. The Recycle Bin exists precisely for the case where confidence is high
but not total, and on a machine with 180 GB free there is no reason to skip it.

**A category-level safety rating is not per-item verification.** "Temp folders are safe to clear" is
a statement about the category. It says nothing about the specific thing in front of you, in the same
way that "this mod is disabled" said nothing about whether its DLL was loaded (entry 4).

**Note the contrast with what was done correctly in the same operation:** the 16 GB crash dump was
deleted only after SHA-256 hashing both copies to prove the archive was byte-identical. That was the
right standard. It was applied to the item that looked risky and not to the items that looked
routine — which is backwards, because the routine-looking ones are where the unexamined assumptions
hide.

---

## 13. ROUTINE — in analysis mode, instrument a WORKING mod before re-reading your own

**Symptom:** five failed fixes, and each new theory about your own code is as wrong as the last.

**The instruction** (the owner, 2026-08-27): *"part of the analysis is always to compare to working
versions of other similar mods as a primary troubleshooting mechanism first, then go from there"* —
and, more pointedly: *"add in the DevBench hooks to alternate mods when troubleshooting under the
analysis fallback, so that you can see what's actually happening. And you're not adding any
functions, you're just pulling what's happening in this already completely functional mod."*

### Why reading is not enough

Reading someone else's source tells you what its author **intended**. Instrumenting a running build
tells you what actually **happens** — and after five wrong theories, the gap between those two is
precisely where the answer is hiding. It also yields a genuine *comparison*: the same measurement,
taken from a working mod and a broken one, on the same machine, in the same session, rather than one
reading held against a memory of the other.

### The routine

1. **Identify at least three references.** The source material the mod derives from; a comparable mod
   by a different author; peers under the same constraint. In this project they are usually already
   installed in the modlist — the answer is on disk before anything is downloaded.
2. **Add read-only DevBench status hooks to the working reference**, where its source is available.
   Report the state that matters to the problem at hand.
3. **Run both and compare the same fields**, rather than reasoning about the difference.
4. **Then, and only then**, return to your own source.

### The hard constraint

**Add no functionality to a reference mod.** Hooks observe; they never change behaviour. A reference
that has been modified is no longer a reference, because its entire value is that it *works* — and a
change that alters whether it works destroys the only property being measured.

### Why this belongs at the front of analysis, not the middle

An existence proof beats a theory. A mod that solves the same problem and does not crash establishes
that the problem is solvable, bounds the solution space, and often reveals that the approach being
patched was the wrong shape from the start — which no amount of re-reading the broken code will
show, because the broken code embodies the wrong assumption.

---

## 14. The answer was already filed — search the reference folders BEFORE investigating

**Symptom:** a long investigation that rediscovers something already written down in the project.

**What went wrong:** an hour of comparative analysis established that the peer minimap solves the
HUD-visibility problem by shipping its own Scaleform menu rather than living in `HudElements`.
`RESOURCES.md` already said so, verbatim, and had done for some time:

> *"Relationship to Dragon's Eye Minimap: none — different author, different era, different
> architecture: this one ships its own Scaleform `MiniMapMenu.swf` and an INI, whereas DEM has no ESP
> and no menu SWF and renders through Infinity UI and Local Map Upgrade."*

The archive itself was sitting in `2. Mod Types\Framework or Utility` — **the folder rule 24 exists
to make you search** — and a Nordic UI variant of the same mod was in `3. analyze mods`.

**Why it happened:** the problem presented as novel ("why does our minimap flicker"), so it felt like
something to investigate rather than something to look up. Rule 24 says to search for an existing
solution *before* inventing a fix; I went straight to inventing.

### The check

**Before investigating, search the project's own references — in this order:**

1. `.MD\RESOURCES.md` — grep it for the mod, the subsystem, and the symptom. It is a catalogue
   written precisely so this question has an answer.
2. `2. Mod Types\Framework or Utility` — the archives themselves.
3. `3. analyze mods` and `3. analyze mods\completed` — prior analyses and variants.
4. The mod's own `PORT-NOTES.md` — what changed from upstream and why.
5. `PROGRESS.md` — grep by symptom, not by mod name. The Tween-menu churn in this same
   investigation had been root-caused there **two days earlier** (duplicate Tween Menu reskin
   installs) and was rediscovered from scratch.

This costs minutes. The investigation it replaces cost hours and produced two confident wrong
answers on the way.

### A real structural gap, separate from the above

`5. current project mod` holds only the **active** project's reference copy, so a finished mod's
upstream rotates out when its work concludes. For Dragon's Eye Minimap the upstream survives only as
`[NoDelete] 0373 Dragon's Eye Minimap` **inside the MO2 modlist** — which no rule points at.

**So for a mod whose port finished long ago, the reference is in the modlist, not the pipeline.**
Add `<MO2>\Apostasy\mods\` to the search above when the subject is an older mod. That is also
where every peer implementation lives, already installed and runnable — which is what makes
instrumenting them (entry 13) practical at all.

---

## 15. ROUTINE — a check for an invisible failure has to run on a schedule, not on noticing

**What went wrong:** Nine structural folders — the six `2. Mod Types` triage categories, both
research sub-folders under `3. analyze mods`, and `8. confirm compatibility\checked archives` —
had no custom icon for weeks. Rule 37's tooling generated and applied icons perfectly well, but
only for folders already listed in its spec. Nothing ever asked *"is anything missing from the
list?"*, so a folder added after the spec was written simply never entered it.

**Why it went unnoticed for so long:** a folder missing a custom icon is indistinguishable from a
folder that is supposed to look default. There is no error, no warning, nothing that draws the eye.
The owner found it by browsing, which is the only way it could have been found.

**The general lesson, which is bigger than icons:** when a failure produces *no signal* — no
exception, no log line, no visible difference from the correct state — then "we'll notice it" is not
a plan. It has to be actively checked on a schedule, by something that walks the whole space and
reports gaps. The same shape has already bitten this project twice: version numbers drifting between
five files (entry 11), and a build failing to earn its number (`version-ledger.ps1`). Both were
solved the same way — a tool that walks everything and refuses.

**The routine now in place:** `set-folder-icons.ps1 -Audit` reports folders with no icon and folders
whose icon was never applied. It runs at the end of every `watcher\reconcile.ps1` pass, logs, and
**queues** a failure so it surfaces where work is picked up.

**The design point worth reusing:** the audit reports, it does not decide. It cannot know whether a
new folder is a *distinction* (earns a glyph) or an *instance* (one of a hundred mod folders; must
stay plain), so it does not try — instance-holding stages are declared in `$ContentStages`, and
everything else is raised for a decision. **Erring toward a false report is correct here**, because a
wrong flag costs one line of output while a silent skip costs weeks. When building this kind of
sweeper, make it noisy at the boundary and let the declaration list absorb the noise over time.

---

## 16. Verify a capability against the binary, not against documentation for an older release

**What went wrong:** `health-gate.ps1` read temperatures from the `root/LibreHardwareMonitor` WMI
namespace. LibreHardwareMonitor **0.9.6 removed WMI publishing entirely**, so the query could never
succeed on this machine. The gate therefore ran *permanently temperature-blind* — while printing a
confident, plausible-sounding `LibreHardwareMonitor is INSTALLED but NOT RUNNING`.

**Why it survived so long:** the failure mode was indistinguishable from the expected one. "Not
running" is a perfectly normal state for that tool, so the message never looked like a bug. It was
only caught by running the tool, watching it appear in Task Manager, and *still* getting "not
running" — a contradiction the message itself could not produce on its own.

**Why the wrong belief was reasonable and still wrong:** WMI publishing existed in LHM for years,
and most guidance online still describes it. The documentation was not wrong, it was *stale*. A
string scan of the two shipped binaries settled it in seconds: no provider, no namespace, nothing
but the PawnIO driver and a web server.

**The lesson:** when code depends on a specific mechanism of a third-party tool — a namespace, an
endpoint, a registry key, an export — confirm it exists **in the binary actually installed**. Search
the file. Version-specific capabilities are exactly where inherited knowledge goes stale, and a
stale mechanism fails *quietly*, by taking a legitimate-looking "not available" branch.

**Corollary, learned in the same hour:** a diagnostic message must distinguish *"the thing is
absent"* from *"I could not reach the thing."* The old branch collapsed both into "not running,"
which is what let a false explanation stand for weeks. The rewritten version checks for the process
first and says **"RUNNING but the web server is not answering"** when both are true — a message that
can contradict itself is a message that can be caught being wrong.

### Second finding, same session: never gate on "the hottest sensor"

At genuine idle (1.4% CPU) this board's Nuvoton NCT6687D reports **`PCIe x1` at 81 °C** and
**`M2 #1` at 0.0 °C** — both unconnected headers. A health gate taking the maximum temperature would
have read 81 °C on an idle machine and refused to build **forever**, and the refusal would have
looked principled. Gate on the sensors belonging to the parts that actually throttle (CPU die, GPU
core), and exclude the mainboard's aggregate readings. Verify the idle baseline of any new sensor
before trusting it in a threshold.

---

## 17. ROUTINE — form a hypothesis, then try to kill it, before building anything (rule 56)

**The failure this replaces:** the Dragon's Eye Minimap crash was chased through five consecutive
hypotheses, each of which got a fix or a test build before being disproved — MGEF archetype lookup,
stale co-save state, a CNO confound, the DevBench hook, and a 1.5.10 build that turned out
byte-identical to 1.5.9. Every one plausible, every one wrong, two of them burning a version number
on a dysfunctional build.

They all share one shape: **the hypothesis was tested by fixing it.** That is the most expensive
test available and also the least informative — when the problem persists you have learned only
that this idea was wrong, not anything about what is right.

**The routine.** Analyse → state the hypothesis → **write down what result would prove it wrong,
before running anything** → list rival explanations → run the *cheapest test whose outcome differs
depending on whether the hypothesis is true* → only then build. `falsification-log.ps1 -Action open`
refuses to record a hypothesis with no killing condition, which is the part that makes it real
rather than advisory.

**Why writing the falsifier first is load-bearing.** A criterion chosen after seeing the result is
not a test; it is a rationalisation, and it feels identical from the inside. Committing to it in
advance is what makes the difference detectable.

**Why "cheapest discriminating" is two requirements, not one.** *Discriminating*: if the test comes
out the same whether the hypothesis is true or false, it has told you nothing, however convincing
it felt. *Cheapest*: a string scan, a byte comparison, a log grep, disabling one mod — all beat a
build-test cycle. Two of this project's most decisive findings cost seconds each: a `strings` scan
proving LibreHardwareMonitor 0.9.6 has no WMI provider, and noticing an 81 °C sensor reading on a
machine idling at 1.4% CPU described the *sensor*, not the machine.

**Keep score, and keep it honest.** `-Action stats` separates the pre-mode baseline (33%, 3 of 9)
from episodes under the method, warns below a 60% hit rate, treats a kill rate under ~15% as
evidence the attacks are too gentle rather than as excellence, and refuses to conclude anything
from fewer than five fixes. A scorecard that only flatters its method is measuring its own
marketing.

**The realistic risk is theatre, not omission.** Writing a paragraph of scepticism on the way to
doing exactly what was planned anyway. Three checkable tells: the killing condition was written
after the test; the test was a build; nothing ever dies.

---

## 18. A test that never ran returns "no result" — which reads exactly like a negative result

**What happened:** searching LibreHardwareMonitor's binaries for tray-related settings, I ran
`strings <exe> 2>/dev/null | grep -i tray`, got no output, and reported that no tray strings
existed. In fact **`strings` is not installed on this machine.** The command failed instantly, and
`2>/dev/null` discarded the "command not found" that would have said so. The empty output was not
evidence of absence — it was evidence of nothing at all. A proper scan (a short Python script
reading ASCII and UTF-16LE strings) found `minTrayMenuItem` and the label `Minimize To Tray`
immediately.

**Why this is dangerous rather than merely annoying:** a negative result and a non-result are
*indistinguishable at the point of use*. Both are an empty screen. One means "I looked and it is not
there," the other means "I never looked." Everything downstream treats them identically, and a
confident wrong conclusion gets built on the second one.

**What makes it worse:** `2>/dev/null` was added out of habit, to suppress permission-denied noise
while scanning binaries. Suppressing stderr is exactly what converts a *loud* failure into a
*silent* one. The habit that tidies output is the same habit that hides the error.

**The rule:**
* **Never suppress stderr on a command whose EMPTY output you intend to reason from.** Noise is
  cheaper than a false negative.
* **Confirm the tool ran at all** before believing its silence — check the exit code, or make the
  first run of any new tool one you know should produce output.
* **A search that finds nothing should be sanity-checked with a term you know is present.** Here,
  searching for `MenuItem` would have returned dozens of hits and proved the scan worked; instead
  the first real search was also the first search, so it had nothing to be compared against.

**The connection to rules 56 and 57:** this is the failure mode those rules exist to catch, in its
purest form. "No tray strings found" was a *conclusion* drawn from an experiment that never
executed. A sceptic track asked "what would we expect to see if this scan were working, and did we
see it?" kills it in one question.


---

## 19. A licence declared in a build manifest is not evidence — only the LICENSE file is

Found 2026-08-27, twice in one research pass, in opposite directions, while surveying SKSE/ImGui
repos for material a permissively-licensed framework could safely learn from. Getting this wrong is
expensive in both directions: discard a usable reference, or unknowingly build on copyleft code.

**Case 1 — under-claiming.** `Patchu1i/ModExplorerMenu`'s `vcpkg.json` declares
`"license": "GPL-3.0"`. Its actual `LICENSE.txt` is **MIT**. The manifest is still named
`"sampleplugin"` — the field is an untouched leftover from the CommonLibSSE plugin template.
Trusting it would have discarded the single best permissive reference found in the whole survey.

**Case 2 — over-claiming.** `powerof3/PhotoMode`'s `vcpkg.json` declares `"license": "MIT"`. Its
actual `LICENSE` file is the **GNU GPL v3** text. Trusting *that* one would have meant reading and
borrowing from copyleft code while believing it was permissive — the far worse failure of the two.

Same ecosystem, same template lineage, errors pointing in opposite directions. **There is no safe
direction in which to trust the field.**

**The rule: verify a licence from the repository's LICENSE file, or from host metadata that is
computed from it. Never from a `license:` field in `vcpkg.json`, `package.json`, `Cargo.toml`, a
README badge, or a Nexus page.** Those are author-typed strings that nothing validates and nothing
keeps in sync with the file that actually governs.

### The corollary that nearly caused a false negative

Fetching `raw.githubusercontent.com/Patchu1i/ModExplorerMenu/master/LICENSE` returned **404**. That
is not evidence the repo is unlicensed — it is evidence the *path* was wrong. The file is
`LICENSE.txt`. Listing the root tree found it immediately.

This is §18 wearing different clothes: **"I could not reach the artifact" reads exactly like "the
artifact says no."** A 404, an empty grep, and a genuine absence are three different results, and
must be told apart before anything is concluded from any of them. The cheap discriminator is to
widen one step — list the directory instead of guessing a filename, or confirm the fetch succeeded
before reading meaning into an empty match.

The same pass produced the well-behaved version. A grep for "dll" across Dear ImGui's
`docs/FAQ.md` returned nothing. Rather than concluding "ImGui documents no DLL guidance", the fetch
was re-run with `-w "HTTP:%{http_code}"` and a byte count: HTTP 200, 60,544 bytes, zero matches.
*Then* it was a true negative and safe to record as one. **Confirm the tool ran before believing
what it did not say.**

**Third case, 2026-08-27 (Wheeler Refined, c0kadam/Wheeler-Refined):** the GitHub repo-metadata
API (the GitHub API) reported `license.spdx_id: "NOASSERTION"` — i.e. GitHub's own
detector declined to classify it — while the repo's actual `LICENSE` file opened with an
unambiguous plain-English statement ("Wheeler Refined is licensed under the GNU General Public
License version 3 only (GPL-3.0-only)") followed by the full GPL-3 text. A third failure shape
alongside the original two: this time the metadata wasn't wrong, it was simply *silent* — which
still would have produced a false "unlicensed" conclusion if the LICENSE file itself hadn't been
fetched and read. Same rule, same fix: the LICENSE file is the only source that counts; host
metadata is, at best, a hint that still has to be checked.

## 20. MO2's `modlist.txt`: a separator's members are the mods listed ABOVE it, and file-bottom wins conflicts

Found 2026-08-27, researching Apostasy's controller/gamepad mods for the Wheeler Refined
integration analysis. Two facts about `<profile>\modlist.txt`, neither obvious from the file's own
formatting, and getting either wrong silently misattributes a mod to the wrong section or predicts
the wrong VFS winner:

**Grouping direction.** A line like `-Keybinds and Gamepad_separator` is a collapsible header in
MO2's UI, but in the file its own line comes *after* the mods it groups, not before. The mods
between one separator line and the next belong to the **lower** (later-in-file) separator, not the
one immediately above them. Confirmed by content: mods between `Optional Gameplay Tweaks_separator`
and the next separator down were all Precision-trail/EVLS/cubemap visual-effect mods — content that
only makes sense as belonging to `Optional Visual Tweaks_separator`, the one that followed them in
the file, not the gameplay-named separator sitting above. The task brief's own pointer to "Optional
Gameplay Tweaks" turned out to be exactly this kind of misattribution — the real controller mods
were three groups later, under `Keybinds and Gamepad_separator`.

**Priority direction - CORRECTED 2026-09-17.** The paragraph that stood here said `modlist.txt`
mirrors the display top-to-bottom, so a mod written LATER in the file wins. That is backwards, and
it misled a diagnosis tonight: the owner saw no Loading Menu Overhaul swipe UI in the loading
screen, Norden UI (line 1035 of the Test profile) sits ABOVE Loading Menu Overhaul (line 1041) in
the file and ships its own `[asset path removed]`, and the game was plainly showing Norden's.
`modlist.txt` is written in REVERSE priority: the FIRST mod line is the highest priority (the
bottom of MO2's list, last-loaded, wins VFS conflicts), and a mod written EARLIER in the file
outranks one written later. Two proofs from the same file: "Norden UI DIP Patch" (a patch, which
must win over its base) is written above "Norden UI"; and the "test ..." builds that override
installed mods are the first lines of the file, right under the header comment. The grouping rule
above is unaffected (a separator's members are still the lines above it). Caught a live, unintentional conflict this way: `Apostasy -
Controller Configuration` and `Apostasy - Default Controlmap` both ship `Root\ControlMap_Custom.txt`
at the game root; the Controller Configuration mod's own `meta.ini` notes even say to disable
Default Controlmap when using it (implying the pack author meant them as alternatives) — but both
are enabled, and because Default Controlmap is written *below* Controller Configuration in the file,
Controller Configuration's copy wins for that one shared file and Default Controlmap's is silently
unused (corrected 2026-10-09, step 3.2 of the pipeline restructure: this sentence first read the
backwards direction and named Default Controlmap the winner). In `modlist.txt` the FIRST mod line is
the highest priority - top-of-file wins, the opposite of how the file reads; `install-test-build.py`
checks exactly this at install time (step 3.1).
