its config and anchors its widgets. The SkyHUD feasibility document had already settled this:
"FORBIDDEN: ... decompiling its SWF to copy its logic" and "SkyHUD's SWF cannot be decompiled".
The export was deleted unread beyond the loader, and nothing from it is used.

How it happened: the gate lives in `4. plans/skyhud-conversion/feasibility-2026-09-05.md`, and the
task arrived as a feature request rather than as "work on SkyHUD", so the plan was not re-read
before reaching for the tool that answers the question fastest.

How to avoid it: before touching ANY third-party file with an analysis tool (ffdec, a
disassembler, a decompiler), re-read that mod's licence gate in its plan document first. The
licence-clean routes for the same questions exist and are the ones to use: runtime inspection of
the live movie's public display-list properties (what every HUD mod does), the engine's own menu
lifecycle, and the mod's public documentation.

## 24. A menu that ignores synthesized input is driven through the game's own handler, found from the vanilla SWF's GameDelegate calls (2026-09-05)

Character Progression Control's attribute-gain hook could not be proven for eleven runs because
the level-up's attribute prompt never took a choice: Enter, E, arrow keys, a mouse click through
InputBench, and even a Scaleform Invoke of the button's own ActionScript function all left the
character with no attribute gain. The hook was blamed first (register clobbering, wrong entry,
a branch overwritten), then the readout, then the profile's other mods. A control run with the
hooks OFF finally showed vanilla did not grant the attribute either - the harness, not the hook.

What worked, and is the method from now on: export the VANILLA menu's scripts (Bethesda's SWF
from the Interface BSA - licence-clean, unlike a third-party replacer's), read which
[code removed] the button fires (`addHealth` / `addMagicka` /
`addStamina`), find that name's single code reference in the running game (the delegate
registration), take the handler address loaded beside it, and call what the handler calls
(`[value removed](menu, av)`). That opened the confirmation MessageBox the prompt actually goes through
("Increase Health? Ok / Cancel"), which is pressed the same way - the message box SWF's
`buttonPress` GameDelegate call, invoked through [code removed]. Both are now
`cpc.control` test ops (`levelup`, `msgbox`).

Rules of thumb: when synthesized input does nothing in a Scaleform menu, stop retrying input
variants after the second failure and look for the delegate callback instead; run the CONTROL
(hooks off) before the fifth hypothesis, not after the eleventh; and a `.text` scan for
RIP-relative references to a game setting's storage is a cheap way to enumerate every reader of
that setting - it found the only other reader of `iAVDhmsLevelUp` and showed it was NPC
auto-calc, not a menu path, in one boot.

## 25. A modlist swap that disables the old slot also disables its plugin - re-enable it in plugins.txt (2026-09-05)

Staging Potion of Clarity 1.0.7 as a new MO2 slot and turning the 1.0.5 slot off in modlist.txt
left `PotionOfClarity.esl` listed in the profile's plugins.txt WITHOUT its leading `*` - MO2 had
recorded the plugin as disabled when the mod that carried it went off, and the new slot's identical
file does not re-enable it. The joint proof run then reported "PotionOfClarity.esl is not in the load
order" and the potion could not exist. The standing memory (mo2-modlist-edits-must-sync-plugins)
already said this; it was not applied because the swap script only edits modlist.txt.

How to avoid it: every install/stage script for a mod that ships an ESP/ESM/ESL must also assert the
`*` on that plugin's line in each profile's plugins.txt (and add the line if missing) after the modlist
swap - and the proof runner's first read after boot should be the mod's own "plugin resolved" line, so
a missing plugin fails the run at once instead of three steps later.

## 26. A Nexus download that returns curl `000` on every CDN is usually a SPACE in the URI, not a network fault (2026-09-05)

Pulling 55 SMF-consumer mods through the v1 API for the AMF checklist, seven downloads failed
with `000 0` on every CDN in the `download_link.json` array while the rest went through at once -
the same symptom the earlier Casting Bar (173070) attempt had shown, which had been written off as
a flaky CDN. The link JSON explains it: uploads made recently get a UUID CDN path
(`cf-files.nexusmods.com/cdn/e9/6d/1f/e96d1fac-...`), but older uploads keep the ORIGINAL file
name in the path, spaces and all (`.../cdn/1704/175935/Dynamic Interior Fog 0.0.6-175935-...zip`).
curl rejects a URL containing a literal space before it ever connects, exits 3, and `-w
'%{http_code}'` prints `000` - identical to a dead host. Retrying the other CDNs, which the loop
did, cannot help because every URI carries the same file name.

How to avoid it: percent-encode the URI before handing it to curl (`$uri = $u.URI -replace ' ',
'%20'`; `[uri]::EscapeUriString` also works), and treat `000` as "curl never sent the request" -
check the URL for illegal characters before blaming the network or retrying. The mod's own age is
the tell: a file uploaded before roughly mid-2026 will have the spaced path.

## 27. PowerShell 5.1: `@(... | ConvertFrom-Json)` on a top-level JSON ARRAY gives a one-element array - the loop runs once with everything, and curl was handed seven URLs (2026-09-05)

The Nexus `download_link.json` endpoint returns a JSON array of CDN entries. The first download pass
wrote `$lj = @(Get-Content -Raw | ConvertFrom-Json)` and then a loop handing each item's URI to the download command. In Windows PowerShell 5.1 `ConvertFrom-Json` emits a top-level array as ONE pipeline
object (it does not unroll it), so `@()` wrapped that object in a second array: `$lj.Count` was 1
and `$u` was the whole seven-entry array. `$u.URI` therefore expanded to seven URLs on curl's
command line; `-o` bound to the first, and the other six bodies streamed to stdout - into the
`$res` variable, into the results CSV (1.5 GB for 55 rows), and finally into a
`ConvertTo-Json` OutOfMemoryException. Every archive on disk was correct, which is what made the
bug look like a logging problem rather than a download one. The tell was the `http` field reading
`Nexus CDN Amsterdam Prague Chicago ...:200 9482529PK...` - all seven short_names joined by
spaces, followed by a zip header.

How to avoid it: never `@()`-wrap `ConvertFrom-Json` output. Assign it plainly (`$lj = (... |
ConvertFrom-Json)` already yields the `Object[]`), or unroll explicitly with `@($lj | ForEach-Object
{ $_ })`; and when a native command's captured output is used as a status string, cast it
(`[string](& curl ...)`) and assert its length before storing it. The library's earlier "flatten
defensively on read" rule (entry near line 923) is the same family; this is its JSON-array face.


## 28. A test rig that SUPPLIES the thing under test proves nothing - the MO2 alias plugin made every AMF compatibility pass a false pass (2026-09-05)

Three Nexus users and a chat list reported that most SKSE Menu Framework mods showed no page in
AMF 1.5.8. Every in-game check here had passed, and the checks were honest: the pages really did
register on this machine. The difference was one file. `AMFLoadOrder.py`, the MO2 file-mapper
plugin written for the earlier module-name problem, presents AMF's DLL virtually as
`SKSE/Plugins/SKSEMenuFramework.dll` - and the stock consumer header gates registration on
[code removed] BEFORE it ever asks for the
module. On this machine the file existed; on a player's it never does. The harness had quietly
supplied the exact condition the product was supposed to create.

How to avoid it: before calling a compatibility claim proven, list what the test environment
provides that the shipped package does not, and remove it (here: rename the plugin off, relaunch -
registry dropped from 30 mods to our own 9 in one run). The rig used to reproduce a user's report
must be a user's install, not the developer's. The plugin stays off on this machine now.

## 29. A header's enum is a contract by NAME, and its structs are a contract by LAYOUT - not the numbers your library happens to use (2026-09-05)

Once consumers reached AMF, Simple Follower Framework's page crashed reading address 0: it called
`igGetStyle`, which AMF did not export, and dereferenced the stub's null. Adding the export was the
small half. The consumer header was generated against Dear ImGui 1.90 DOCKING; AMF's SE/AE line
embeds 1.90.2 without docking (two `ImGuiCol_` entries fewer in the MIDDLE of the enum, three
`ImGuiStyleVar_` fewer) and its 1.7.x line embeds 1.92.8 (reordered colours, renamed tabs,
reshuffled style vars, a different `ImGuiItemFlags_` bit layout, `ImGuiStyle` and `ImGuiViewport`
with fields inserted). Passing a consumer's index straight through was silently tinting the wrong
colour on one line and reading the wrong bytes on the other, and only the null crash made any of
it visible.

How to avoid it: every value that crosses an ABI boundary defined by someone else's header is
translated by NAME at compile time (a table indexed by the consumer's enum, filled with our own
constants under `#if IMGUI_VERSION_NUM`), and every struct handed back is a copy in THEIR layout.
Check the layout mechanically - diff the two structs' field lists - not by eye. A push that this
side cannot honour still pushes something harmless, so the consumer's matching pop stays balanced.

## 30. "Local\" is the logon SESSION's namespace - a once-only guard named that way is shared with every other game left running, including a wedged one (2026-09-05)

AMF's SKSEPlugin_Load guard created `Local\ApocryphaMenuFramework.SKSEPlugin_Load.once` and treated
ERROR_ALREADY_EXISTS as "the alias second load, do nothing". A 1.7.104 game left stuck in its exit
(one thread, no window, Stop-Process could not end it) still held that event, so the NEXT game's AMF
saw it already present at its first and only load and returned inert: SKSE logged "loaded
correctly", no log line was written, no menu, no alias. The symptom read as "the log is stale" and
"the DevBench tool is unknown" until the process list showed the remnant. A lingering
SkyrimSE.exe is ordinary on a player's PC.

How to avoid it: a per-process once-only guard must be scoped to the process - put the PID in the
kernel-object name, or use a process-local static where the module is the only thing that can call
twice. And when a fresh run's log looks unchanged, check the process table for an older instance
before reading the log as this run's.

## 31. A running Mod Organizer instance intercepts `moshortcut://` launches aimed at ANOTHER instance's executable (2026-09-05)

With the 1.7.104 test instance's MO2 still open (waiting on its wedged game), launching
`<MO2>\Apostasy\ModOrganizer.exe -p "Test Build" moshortcut://:SKSE` did not start
Apostasy at all: the already-running MO2 took the request and launched ITS `SKSE` entry, so a second
1.7.104 game appeared from the Steam folder, DevBench answered on 8920 from the wrong game, and the
"Apostasy" sweep read another instance's registry. Identify the game from the process path before
trusting anything a launch produced (rule 8's own advice), and never launch one instance while any
other MO2 is alive - close or kill the stale one first (a force-kill of MO2 is the lesser evil once
its game is a kernel remnant, after backing up the profile it may truncate).

## 32. PowerShell variable names are case-insensitive: `$I` and a loop's `$i` are the SAME variable (2026-09-05)

An install script set `$I = '<MO2>\Steam 1.7.104 Test'` and later ran `for ($i=0; ...)`.
Every path built from `$I` after that loop pointed at `C:\WINDOWS\system32\92\...` - the loop
counter - and Start-Process refused a working directory of [bytes removed]. Nothing warned. Name paths with
words (`$inst`, `$repo`), never single letters, and never reuse a letter that a counter uses.


## 33. A Steam-packed executable's in-memory import directory is the PACKER's - patching "the exe's import of X" finds nothing (2026-09-05)

The first fast-exit design walked SkyrimSE.exe's import table for ExitProcess and redirected the
thunk, the same technique that works on every SKSE plugin. In game it reported "the game
executable imports no ExitProcess by name". The headers GetModuleHandle(NULL) points at belong to
the Steam stub, whose import directory lists only what the stub itself needs; the game's real
imports are resolved by the stub into locations the visible headers do not describe. The on-disk
scanning entry (#22) is the same executable seen from the other side.

How to avoid it: for the game executable, hook the FUNCTION (kernel32!ExitProcess itself - a
five-byte jump to a page allocated within reach) rather than any import of it; reserve
import-table patching for modules whose headers are their own (plugins, runtime DLLs). And a
"not found" from an import walk on the exe is not evidence the exe never calls the function.

## 34. Skyrim SE's Quit does not pass through ExitProcess, and `qqq` is a hard quit - neither exercises an exit hook (2026-09-05)

With kernel32!ExitProcess hooked and the hook confirmed installed, SE 1.5.97 exited in under a
second from QuitToDesktop and from `qqq`, and the hook's log line never appeared: that build ends
its process by another route. The same hook on Skyrim 1.7.104 fired at once ("the game asked to
exit (code 0)") - the build that wedged in its exit earlier that day. So a test of an exit-path
change on SE proves nothing about 1.7; run it where the exit path actually runs, and treat "the
process is gone" as separate from "my code ran" - the log line is the evidence, the process count
is not.

## 35. vcpkg installs headers with the source archive's OLD timestamps, so ninja does not rebuild against a changed dependency version - link errors against symbols from the previous headers (2026-09-05)

After the imgui overlay port moved both AMF lines from 1.90.2 / 1.92.8 to 1.90.8, the first build
linked only some objects and failed on symbols like ArrowButton(const char*, int) and
ImageWithBg(ImTextureRef...) - mangled names from the OLD imgui.h. vcpkg had installed the new
headers with mtimes from the 2024 tarball, older than yesterday's .obj files, so ninja's depfile
check saw nothing newer and reused the stale objects while the library was new. Delete the .obj
and .pch files under CMakeFiles/<target>.dir (or touch the installed headers) after any
dependency version change, then build; an incremental build cannot be trusted across one.

## 36. The game keeps some of the player's permanent actor-value modifiers across a save and drops others - a co-save "applied" amount is only trustworthy after the load has been checked against it (2026-09-05)

Character Progression Control 1.0.9 applies its starting health and its carry-weight formula as
permanent modifiers (ModActorValue) and keeps the net applied amount in the co-save so switching
off can take exactly that away. On the first reload the health modifier came back (170) and the
carry-weight one did not (300 where 420 had been saved), and "off" then subtracted a phantom 120
(300 -> 180). The fix is a record that also carries the permanent value as it stood after the last
apply: the first apply after a load compares - equal means the modifier survived, equal minus the
applied amount means it was dropped and the applied amount starts from zero. Any mod that tracks
its own contribution to an actor value across saves needs that check; the standalone Carryweight
on Level Up has the drift (its applied number grows by the formula on every load) without noticing
because it never undoes anything.

## 37. `player.advlevel` takes the level directly and offers no attribute choice; a driven level-up needs real character XP, and the LevelUp Menu's confirm box swallows synthesized keys (2026-09-05)

Two runs tried to exercise the attribute-choice hook with `player.advlevel` then Skills-menu keys:
the internal level went 1 -> 2 with no LevelUp Menu ever opening, because advlevel consumes the
level without a pending level-up. What worked: earn real XP (`player.incpcs onehanded` x6 crossed
the 100-XP threshold), open the StatsMenu through DevBench's `menu open` (it brings the LevelUp
Menu up itself when a level-up is pending), drive the choice with the mod's own op, and answer the
confirm box with `cpc.control {"msgbox":0}` - while that MessageBoxMenu was open, InputBench key
presses reached nothing, which is what made the first attempts look like dead keys. Check `menu
list` for MessageBoxMenu before concluding that input is broken.

## 38. A hooked call site can rely on a register the ABI calls volatile: the skill-improve call site adds the returned xp to [operand removed], so the level-income hook must not clobber rcx - keep it a leaf, or save rcx in the stub (2026-09-06)

The level-income hook (an asm stub replacing the game's `call` to its level-experience function, then
`CPC_LevelExp_Hook`) had run for days as a leaf. Adding one logger::debug call to it crashed the game
on the first skill increase at `[offset removed] [instruction removed]` - the instruction right after
the hooked call, which adds the returned value to the experience the pointer in rcx addresses. The
original callee never touches rcx, so the compiler let the caller keep its pointer there across the
call; anything non-trivial in the hook (a logger, fmt, an allocation) clobbers it. Rule for every
call-site hook: read the instructions AFTER the call for registers used without being reloaded, and
either preserve them in the stub or keep the hook free of calls. Crash log: crash-2026-09-06-04-04-19.

**Resolved 2026-09-06 (falsification episode 15):** the same clobber also explained a symptom that had looked
unrelated - with the leaf hook attached, supplement mode "paid nothing" (xp stayed 0.0 after `incpcs`). rcx had
landed on readable memory, so the game added the income to the wrong address and the real field never moved.
The stub now saves rcx, rdx, r8-r11 and xmm1-xmm5 around the hook call (rax is provably clobbered by the original,
`[instruction removed]`), the hook logs again, and every reading matched the traced returns (0 -> 22 -> 399 -> 435 -> 715).
Lesson sharpened: a register clobber does not always crash - when it lands on a valid address it silently writes
the right value to the wrong place, which presents as "the feature does nothing". A hook that produces a
mysterious no-op is a register-contract suspect before it is a logic suspect.

## 39. Synthesized key presses do not reach every menu: InputBench's splice never reached the Lockpicking Menu or the Journal, AUO's BSInputEventQueue press reached both, and neither turns a lock (2026-09-06)

Five proof runs tried to break a lockpick by holding D in the Lockpicking Menu through `bench.input`
(InputBench splices ButtonEvents into the PollInputDevices stream): Tab could not even close the menu,
so nothing was reaching it - only DevBench's `menu close` worked. `auo.input` (a real BSInputEventQueue
press) opened the menu with E and moved the Journal, but a held-D press through it still turned nothing
and broke no pick: the lockpicking minigame reads a key that stays down across frames with a growing
heldDownSecs, which a one-shot synthesized press does not provide. Rule: when a synthesized input
produces nothing, first prove the input reaches the menu (a key with a visible effect, or `menu list`
before and after), and treat "holding" as a separate capability from "pressing" - a pick break, a
charged attack, a lock turn need the real device or a driver that repeats the down event per frame.

## 40. A console `prid` selection does not carry between DevBench console execs - use the `<ref>.command` form (2026-09-06)

`prid [id removed]` then `lock 60` in two separate DevBench console calls locked nothing: the second exec
ran without a selected reference, silently. The first proof run therefore drove every feature at an
unlocked chest and every decision path correctly did nothing, which read as "the mod is dead" until
`describe` on the reference showed no lock data at all. `<refid>.lock 60` and `<refid>.activate player`
work in one exec each. Also measured: console `lock N` maps N=0..? Novice, 25 Apprentice, 26-50 Adept,
51-75 Expert, 76-100 Master, 101+ key-required - one tier UP from the naive 0/25/50/75/100 reading.

## 41. `menu accept` with the box's own cancelIndex of -1 crashes the game inside devbench (SelectOption(-1)) (2026-09-06)

The original Lock Overhaul's activation box ("What would you like to do?" - Pick Lock / Smash Lock /
Unlock) reported cancelIndex -1, and passing that straight back as the index to dismiss it crashed
SkyrimSE in devbench.dll's MessageBoxMenu::SelectOption (crash-2026-09-06-22-49-12.log). A negative
index is "no cancel button", not a button. Pass only an index from the buttons array; to dismiss a box
without one, pick the button that means no.

## 42. Console `activate` bypasses perk activation entry points - a perk-based mod (Lock Overhaul's choice box) only shows itself on a REAL activation (2026-09-06)

With the original's quests running and its perks on the player, `<ref>.activate player` opened the
vanilla Lockpicking Menu every time; a real E press (AUO's input path, crosshair on the chest through
Better Third Person Selection) brought up its message box instead. Perk "Activate" entry points are
applied by the player's activation code, not by TESObjectREFR::ActivateRef, so a console activation
is a fair test for menu sinks and hit events but NOT for anything perk-driven. Compare against a
perk-based original only through a real activation.

### 43. "Off restores vanilla" from compiled constants is a write, and it undoes every ESP's record (2026-09-06)

**What happened.** Character Progression Control's Difficulty tab (1.1.0) and Custom Difficulty UI both
"restore vanilla" when their damage control is off - by writing twelve compiled vanilla numbers into the
GameSettings at every load. Beside Blade and Blunt (damage-by-player 1.5 / 1.25 / 1 / 1 / 0.75 / 0.5 in its
ESP) or Requiem (all twelve = 1.0 by design) that write silently reverted the overhaul's tuning on every
load, with the user's switch OFF. Measured 2026-09-06 on Test Build: Blade and Blunt's records were live at
kDataLoaded and vanilla after the save loaded. The compatibility files had said "off restores the values the
game came with" and "written only while the user's own switches are on" - both accepted from the code's
intent, never measured against an ESP that changes those records.

**The rule.** A control that is OFF writes nothing. "Vanilla" for a GameSetting is the value the game holds at
kDataLoaded (after every ESP's records), captured then - never a compiled constant. An on->off flip restores
the captured value; a fresh load with the control off does not touch the setting at all. And the rule-15
check for anything that writes GameSettings includes ONE run with an ESP that overrides those records
(any overhaul will do) with our control off - the value after load must equal the ESP's.

## 44. Killing a hung game or task: Claude runs elevated, so use the graceful-first ladder, never a reflexive force (2026-09-06)

The owner always launches Claude Code elevated: the session runs at High integrity, Administrator, with
**SeDebugPrivilege enabled**. Task Manager's "End task" is `TerminateProcess()` from exactly that
kind of process, so the Claude session already reaches everything Task Manager reaches, SYSTEM-owned
processes included - there is no privilege gap and no separate elevated helper is needed. Verified
stable across fresh tool calls 2026-09-06.

Because the reach is already there, the value is the APPROACH, not more power. A reflexive forced
kill skips a program's own cleanup (flushing files, releasing driver / virtual-filesystem handles),
which is how it leaves half-dead processes. So: ask the process to close first, wait, and only then
force. The standing utility is `.MD\scripts\prockill.ps1` - `-Id`/`-Name` -> `CloseMainWindow` ->
wait `-GraceMs` -> P/Invoke `TerminateProcess`; it enables SeDebugPrivilege in its own token and
reports which rung ended the process. Prefer it over `Stop-Process -Force`.

The one exception is `SkyrimSE.exe` (see 1328): force-killing it with ENB + usvfs is what wedges it
into an unkillable zombie, and any privilege-holding killer hits the same wedge, then reports a false
success. A hung Skyrim wants AMF's FAST EXIT (the `kernel32!ExitProcess` hook, AMF 1.6.1+) or a
graceful menu quit - never `prockill`, never any force-kill.

Building `prockill` also cost a real bug worth remembering: the `TOKEN_PRIVILEGES` struct passed to
`AdjustTokenPrivileges` needs `Pack = 4`. With default 8-byte alignment the LUID lands past the
offset the kernel reads, so the privilege silently fails to enable - and the same-user kill still
works (it needs no privilege), which masks the failure until you aim at a higher-integrity target.

Full assessment: `4. plans\process-killer\plan.md`. The always-on elevated helper was deliberately
not built - redundant while Claude is elevated, and a "kill any PID, elevated" drop file is a
privilege-escalation surface; revisit only for an un-elevated Claude, and then via an ACL'd named
pipe, never a drop file.

---

## 45. A PowerShell function that prints a line before `return $false` returns a TRUTHY array - and `if (Fn)` takes the branch it was written to skip (2026-09-07)

[code removed] does not
return `$false`. Everything a function emits is pipeline output, so the caller receives
`@("!! not found", $false)` - a two-element array, which is truthy. In the language proof rig this
meant a page that was NOT registered was "selected", its tool was queried (404), and five captures of
the framework's own Settings page were filed as the mod's, while the log line that would have
revealed it went into the array instead of the console.

The tell: a diagnostic string that never appears in the output but a branch that behaves as if the
condition held. Fix: `Write-Host` (or `Write-Warning`) for diagnostics inside anything whose
return value is tested, and never emit bare strings on the path to a boolean `return`. Same family as
the [code removed] enumeration copy (rule 35's watcher) and the single-element array
unwrap - PowerShell's pipeline-as-return is the mechanism behind all three.

Second thing the same run taught, already in the gotchas but worth the cross-check: a rig that
reports "0 translation files" through `Get-ChildItem "$slot\..."` on a `[NoDelete]` slot reports
nothing about the slot - the brackets are a wildcard class. `.NET` file APIs or `-LiteralPath` for
every path that can carry brackets, including `Copy-Item`'s DESTINATION (the slot was never created and
the "rig" line said so in a way that read like a counting bug).

And the third, which cost the rerun: **PowerShell variable names are case-insensitive.** `$mods =
'<MO2>\Apostasy\mods'` followed by `$Mods = @(@{...})` leaves ONE variable holding the array;
`Join-Path $mods "..."` then stringifies it and the "slot" was created at
`C:\WINDOWS\system32\System.Collections.Hashtable\[NoDelete] 0747 SkyHUD Settings Menu 1.0.4` - every
file copy succeeded, the rig line counted eleven files, and the game never saw the mod. Name a
collection and its folder differently in more than case.


## 46. Routing a page's literals through a string table: three ways the tooling passes while strings stay English (2026-09-07)

Learned across the four Opus-patched mods of the language rollout (Lock Interaction Overhaul, Custom
Difficulty UI, Dragon's Eye Minimap, Character Progression Control). None of the three failed loudly;
each would have shipped a page with some text permanently English while every check said OK.

1. **A helper whose signature hides the key from the regex loses translations silently.** The first
   `ComboTR(keyLiteral, englishLiteral, ...)` shape meant the label never appeared as
   `TR("KEY", "text")`, so neither the generator nor `translations-check.py` saw it - the check passed
   with those labels English forever. Rule: a helper takes an ALREADY-TR'd string, so every key stays
   visible at the call site in the exact shape the tooling greps for. Diff the extracted key list
   against the page by eye once per mod.
2. **A patch anchor with the wrong line ending matches nothing, and a repo mixes endings per file -
   and sometimes WITHIN a file.** The vendored `SKSEMenuFramework.h` is CRLF while `source\*.cpp` are
   LF; and Dragon's Eye Minimap's `UI.cpp` is LF with six stray CRLF lines, so `"\r\n" in text` said
   CRLF and every multi-line anchor missed. Decide the ending per file by COUNTED MAJORITY
   (`\r\n` count against `\n` count) and rewrite each anchor to it before matching. Must-match
   anchors (found exactly once or raise) are what turned this into a loud failure instead of a
   half-patched file - keep them in every patch script.
3. **The specifier check reads English, not printf.** `"1% of ..."` parses as a `% o` specifier and a
   translated `investment%s` plural cannot move its argument; both were rewritten in the English
   ("one percent", a translated plural word) rather than special-cased in the check. A translated
   format with our own `snprintf` arguments (the tier help line, two `%s`) is guarded only by the
   check's specifier-order comparison - MSVC has no positional arguments, so a language that needs
   the arguments reversed cannot be expressed; none of the ten did.

Also from the same batch, for the SWF-sharing case (Character Progression Control): when one
translation file feeds two consumers (the game's Scaleform translator for a menu SWF and our page),
list the keys the MOVIE actually references (decompress the SWF, grep `$Name`) before renaming or
dropping any "odd" key in an existing language file - the two Russian keys renamed and two dropped
in 1.1.3 were confirmed unreferenced by `levelupmenu.swf` first.

## 47. Writing into an engine container the game sized for itself: it never grows, and CommonLibSSE will grow it anyway (2026-09-08)

Character Progression Control 1.1.3 crashed a user's game 85 seconds into loading, inside its own
`MenuStrings::Install()`, adding the level-up menu's labels to the game's Scaleform translation
table.

**The mechanism.** That table is a `tHashSet` the game allocates once at a fixed size. SKSE's own
insert refuses when it is full - `kInsert_OutOfSpace` in `skse64\GameTypes.h`, `tHashSet::Insert` -
and never resizes it. CommonLibSSE's `BSTScatterTable::emplace()` does the opposite: at `_free == 0`
it calls `reserve()`, which `malloc()`s a replacement entry array **from the calling DLL's heap**,
repoints the game's live table at it, rebuilds every chain into it, and `free()`s the array the
**game** allocated. Nothing fails at that moment. The damage shows up later, in whoever next walks a
chain and follows a link that is neither an entry nor the table's end-of-list sentinel.

**The general lesson: a container reached through CommonLibSSE is not yours to grow.** The library
models the game's structures faithfully for reading, and its insert paths match the game's byte for
byte - except the growth path, which has no counterpart in the engine at all. So the rule for any
`BSTHashMap`/`BSTArray` that the GAME created: you may read it, and you may add to it only while you
can prove there is room. Growth is the one operation the engine never performs and the one the
library performs silently.

**Why the change that exposed it looked harmless.** The language rollout merged the settings page's
310 keys into the same translation file the menu uses. No code changed - `MenuStrings.cpp` had not
been touched since 1.0.4 - but the file grew from 5,072 to 54,304 bytes and the insert count went
from 43 to 353. A data file's size is a code path's input; growing one by 8x is a behavioural change
even when the diff shows no source edit. The keys also did not belong there: a page that reads its
own strings should not also push them into an engine namespace shared with the vanilla menus.

**Why our testing could not have caught it.** The proof ran on the minimal Test Build profile, whose
table has 2048 slots with 898 free, so all 353 fitted and the log cheerfully said
`353 of 354 entries added`. Capacity-dependent bugs are invisible on a small load order **by
construction** - the minimal profile that makes UI testing tractable is the same property that hides
them. When a change increases pressure on a shared engine resource, the test has to run somewhere
that resource is scarce.

**Ask the container whether it is still the game's.** Reproducing on a 945-mod list showed the table
was already wrecked before our mod read it: capacity 631 (not a power of two, which the mask
`hash & (capacity - 1)` requires), free count 6460 larger than the capacity, and the end-of-list
sentinel at a heap address instead of inside SkyrimSE.exe where the game's static lives. Another
plugin had already run `reserve()` on it. **A healthy game container's sentinel points into the game's
image; a heap sentinel means someone has replaced it.** That check is cheap, and it is now the gate:
identify the structure before writing to it, and log what you saw when you refuse.

This is entry 1 again from the other side - a stack trace names the plugin that died, not the one
that broke it - and here both were true at once: our mod supplied the pressure, and on big lists
somebody else had already done the damage.

**The failed first fix, recorded because the reasoning was the instructive part.** The first 1.1.4
attempt only cut the insert count from 353 to 43 and guarded on the free-slot counter. It crashed
again immediately, in `find()`, before inserting anything - because on that list the *counters
themselves* were garbage, so a guard that reads them proves nothing. **A guard computed from fields
you have not first established are valid is not a guard.** Validate the structure, then trust its
numbers; never the reverse.

## 48. A before/after screenshot proves nothing unless the thing you changed was on screen (2026-09-08)

Stage 1 of the three-perk-trees mod asks one question: does Skyrim's skill menu draw perk trees from
the position fields on `BGSSkillPerkTreeNode`? The code side was proven in minutes - all eighteen
trees read, 198 nodes, per-skill counts matching vanilla exactly, positions written and restored
byte-for-byte. Then **four consecutive visual experiments were run and all four were invalid**, and
the fourth nearly produced a wrong verdict on the whole design.

1. **Changed the data while the menu was already open.** Scaleform menus build their display when
   they open. Nothing redrew, which says nothing about whether the fields are read.
2. **Nudged a skill that was not on screen.** Destruction was moved; the camera was parked on Sneak,
   with Destruction's constellation off-screen entirely. Two screenshots of an untouched skill were
   compared and found identical - which was guaranteed regardless of the answer.
3. **Let the game state drift between captures.** Opening and closing the level-up menu consumed
   pending level-ups, so the character went from level 1 to 2 to 4 between "before" and "after".
   Even a real difference would not have been attributable.
4. **Repeated (2) with a different skill**, again off-screen, with the level-up panel covering the
   middle of the view.

**The near-miss.** After (2) the conclusion drawn was "the noise floor is larger than the signal,
therefore the dome does not use these fields" - from a pixel diff. The diff was measuring the
animated nebula. The owner said *"check screenshots"*; the screenshots showed both captures were of
Sneak, a skill never touched. **A numeric diff over a screenshot is not a substitute for looking at
it** - it cannot tell you that you photographed the wrong thing.

**The checks that would have caught all four**, and which belong on any visual A/B in a game menu:

* **Name the pixel you expect to move, before running it.** If you cannot point at what should look
  different, the experiment is not designed yet.
* **Confirm the changed object is in frame** - screenshot first, identify the subject, then change
  the subject that is actually visible.
* **Change everything, when you cannot control the camera.** Moving all eighteen trees removes the
  "wrong skill" failure mode entirely; whatever is on screen must respond.
* **Hold the rest still** (entry 3's rule again): a menu that consumes game state on open is not a
  passive observer.
* **Prefer a shape change to a translation.** A uniform shift can be hidden by a camera that
  re-centres on its subject; a spread cannot.

**Also recorded, unresolved:** applying a spread at `kDataLoaded` was followed by a crash inside
SkyrimSE.exe with no frames of ours, while the control run with the experiment switched off loaded
cleanly. One trial each, so this is a suspicion and not a finding - but writing perk-tree positions
that early is the prime suspect and needs isolating before the design is trusted.

## 49. The menu framework's header calls GetProcAddress results WITHOUT null-checking, so any ImGui call the loaded framework lacks is a jump to address zero (2026-09-08)

The first build of the Item Explorer crashed the game the instant its page drew. The crash log was
useless at first glance - `EXCEPTION_ACCESS_VIOLATION at [value removed]`, "tried to EXECUTE memory
at 0", and a stack containing nothing but CrashLogger's own handler. The one clue was a register:
`RCX` held `"Re-read"`, a button label from our own page.

**The mechanism.** Every wrapper in `SKSEMenuFramework.h` looks like this:

[code example removed; the text around it says what it showed]

`GetMenuFrameworkFunction` returns `nullptr` when the loaded framework does not export that symbol,
and the wrapper calls it anyway. **"Execute at [value removed]" with one of your own string literals in RCX is
the signature of this, and it means the framework you are running is older than the call you made.**

**What was actually missing.** The profile loaded Apocrypha Menu Framework 1.4.9, which exports 50
functions. The page used eight it does not have: the entire table API (`igBeginTable`, `igEndTable`,
`igTableNextRow`, `igTableNextColumn`, `igTableSetupColumn`, `igTableHeadersRow`), plus
`igSmallButton` and `igInputTextWithHint`. Rewritten against 1.4.9's own export list - `Button`
instead of `SmallButton`, `InputText` instead of `InputTextWithHint`, plain rows with
`PushID`/`PopID` instead of a table - the page draws correctly on every version.

**The guard has to fail CLOSED, and mine failed open.** The page had a `HasRequiredExports()` check
already. It was worthless, because it began:

[code example removed; the text around it says what it showed]

AMF loads as `ApocryphaMenuFramework.dll`, so that handle is always null and the function always
returned true. **A capability check that assumes success when it cannot look is not a check.**
Resolve through the same path the wrappers use - `GetMenuFrameworkFunction<void*>(name)` - and
refuse to register the page when anything is missing, so an old framework costs the player a
missing page and a log line instead of a crash.

**The dumpbin habit that settles it in seconds.** `dumpbin /exports <framework>.dll`, then diff
against every `ImGuiMCP::` call the page makes. Do this against the OLDEST framework the mod claims
to support, not the newest one on the development machine - the newest hides the whole class of bug.

### The same build's second bug: trusting an accessor whose numbers were impossible

`TESDataHandler`'s `GetLoadedMods()` / `GetLoadedLightMods()` reported **202 full and 3,438 light
plugins** for a profile with ten, and the catalogue duly stored thousands of junk `TESFile` pointers.
Those accessors go through version-dependent offsets and one of the two branches is `[value removed]`.

The fix was to stop asking for the list at all: **every form knows the file that defined it
(`TESForm::GetFile(0)`), so building the plugin list FROM THE FORMS needs no offsets and is right on
every runtime.** It also drops plugins that provide nothing, which is what the page wanted anyway.
Afterwards: 482 plugins and 35,424 items, in load order, with recognisable names.

**The check that would have caught it instantly:** a count that cannot be true is a bug in the
reader, not a surprising fact about the data. Sanity-bound anything read through relocated offsets
and log it - 3,438 light plugins against a ten-plugin profile should have stopped the build there.

## 50. When the game dies during plugin load, skse64.log NAMES the plugin - read it before bisecting (2026-09-08)

The Apostasy `Test Build` profile stopped booting. The game started, every SKSE plugin wrote its
log, and then the process ended about ten seconds in with **no crash log at all**. Roughly eight
launches went into it: disabling our own two new mods (cleared them), disabling the three mods named
in the one crash log that did exist (no change), and switching off the framework's watchdog and fast
exit on the theory that they were killing the process before Crash Logger could write (they were
not - the watchdog fires at 120 seconds and the death was at ten). The conclusion at that point was
"nothing cheaper has worked, next is a bisect of the profile's SKSE plugins".

**The answer was one grep away the whole time.** `skse64.log` ends with:

[code example removed; the text around it says what it showed]

and earlier in the same file says:

[code example removed; the text around it says what it showed]

**SKSE records a plugin that fails to load, WITH ITS HANDLE, and the handle is the same number the
dispatch stops at.** The plugin was `dmenu.dll`, bundled inside Risa's All In One Menu 5.0, which
fatals on 1.5.97; disabling that one mod fixed the profile immediately - 95 plugins, no fatal error,
boots every time.

**The routine, and it costs seconds:** when a game dies during startup, before touching the load
order at all, read `skse64.log` for

* the LAST `sending message type 0 to plugin N` - where the dispatch stopped, and
* any line containing `fatal error occurred while loading plugin` - which names the file and gives
  its handle.

If the two numbers agree you have the culprit by name. Only bisect when they do not.

**Why the wrong path looked reasonable.** A missing crash log reads as "the crash logger never got
to run", which sends you hunting for something that kills the process abruptly - a watchdog, a fast
exit, a hard fault. But a plugin SKSE has already disabled after a fatal load error is not a crash
at all, so nothing writes a crash log, and the one stale crash log lying in the folder from an
earlier failure actively misleads: it named three mods that had nothing to do with it, and turning
them off "not fixing it" was taken as evidence about the load order rather than as evidence that the
crash log was irrelevant. **Check the timestamp of a crash log against the run you are diagnosing
before believing a word of it.**

## 51. `[NoDelete]` in an MO2 folder name is a WILDCARD, so a path check on it silently answers about nothing (2026-09-08)

**Symptom.** A check on a mod folder returns a confident, wrong answer with no error: a directory
listing comes back empty for a folder that plainly has files in it, or "is this mod enabled?"
reports *off* for a mod that is enabled and loaded.

**Why.** This project prefixes its installed mods `[NoDelete] 0403 Compass Navigation Overhaul
1.1.2`. Square brackets are a character class in both of the languages used here:

* **PowerShell** treats `-Path` as a wildcard pattern. `Get-ChildItem $dst` where `$dst` contains
  `[NoDelete]` matches a folder whose name has ONE character from the set `NoDelet` at that
  position - i.e. nothing - and returns empty **without erroring**.
* **grep / ripgrep** treat the pattern the same way: `grep -c "^+[NoDelete] 0403 ..."` matches a
  single character from that set, so an enabled mod reads as disabled.

**It bit three separate checks in one evening**, each time producing a plausible answer that sent
the reasoning somewhere else: an "empty" mod folder right after a successful 8-file extraction, and
a CNO-vs-MiniMap-Menu crash where all three candidate mods were reported *off* while the crash log
listed one of them as loaded. The tell is a check that disagrees with something you have direct
evidence for - a crash log naming a module, an archive that just reported "Files: 8".

**The fix, both languages:**

* PowerShell: `-LiteralPath` on every `Get-ChildItem` / `Get-Content` / `Test-Path` / `Remove-Item`
  touching a mod folder. `-Path` is the wildcard form and there is no reason to use it here.
* grep: `grep -F -- "<name>"` for a fixed string, or compare in a real parser rather than a regex
  (`$line.Substring(1) -eq $name`).

**Already recorded once in a narrower form:** `PROGRESS.md` notes `pre-finalize-check.ps1` resolving
the install paths "through PowerShell wildcards" so `[NoDelete]` never matched, which was written
off as a to-do. It is the same bug, and it is worth fixing there too - a gate that cannot see an
installed mod reports a FAIL that a human then has to overrule by hand, which is how a real failure
would eventually get overruled along with it.

---

## 52. The markers on screen belonged to a different mod, and both halves of the before/after were its work (2026-09-09)

**Symptom.** A new feature is measured working on the C++ side - counts, timings, the right forms
by name - and draws nothing. A before/after screenshot pair looks *identical*, which reads as "my
change does nothing", so the investigation turns to the rendering layer and stays there.

**What was actually true.** The test profile still had **MiniMap Menu** enabled, installed an hour
earlier for an unrelated FPS investigation and never removed. It was doing two things at once:

* **drawing the markers being looked at** - every icon in both screenshots was its own object
  marker, so the pair could not possibly differ no matter what the new code did; and
* **breaking the mechanism under test** - it hooks the same Scaleform map objects, which is why
  `_markerList` came back as an empty array and the extension's replacement loop never ran.

Disabling it made the numbers causal on the first try: replaceable markers matched the contributed
count exactly, in both the on and off arms, and forty markers appeared on the map.

**The wrong turn.** Three build-and-test cycles went into the rendering layer - a handle-validity
probe (refuted: handles were valid), an empty-array guard fix in the ActionScript (no effect), and
a written-up hypothesis about Scaleform timing that was simply false. Each was a reasonable next
step *given the environment*, and the environment was the thing that was wrong.

**The check that would have caught it, and it costs one command:** before believing any visual
comparison, **list what is enabled and ask what else draws on that surface.** `LOGIC-LIBRARY 48`
already says a before/after proves nothing unless the thing you changed was on screen. This is its
sharper sibling: *something else may own everything on screen*, and then both frames are evidence
about that other mod.

**The generalisation worth keeping:** a profile carrying a leftover from the previous investigation
is not a test environment. When an investigation ends, put the profile back - the mod installed for
the last question becomes an uncontrolled variable in the next one, and it will not announce itself.

---

## A driving op nested inside another op's branch is unreachable - and it looks exactly like "the feature was never tested" (2026-09-09)

**Symptom.** A shipped feature - Item Explorer 1.0.3's 3D item preview - had never once been seen
to draw, and its own source said so in a comment: *"a click is exactly what a headless test cannot
do, which is how the 3D preview reached a release without anyone having seen it draw."* The
conclusion drawn from that was that the feature simply had not been tested yet.

**What was actually true.** It *could not* be tested. The DevBench tool's `preview:` and `place:`
ops - the two ops that exist precisely so a test does not need a mouse click - had been written
INSIDE the [code removed] branch, between that branch's local variables and
its search call. The code compiles, reads correctly at a glance, and the ops are only reachable
when the arguments *also* contain `find:`. Every attempt to drive the preview would have fallen
through to the tool's default reply, which is a settings dump that looks like a working answer.

**Why it was convincing.** Rule 64 says every interactive surface ships a driving tool, and one
existed: registered, documented in the descriptor, listed in the changelog. The gap was not a
missing tool but a tool whose branch structure quietly excluded two of its own ops - and nothing
about a JSON reply from the fallback path says "your op was never matched".

**The check, and it is cheap:** after adding an op to a dispatch handler, **read outward from the
new `if` to the enclosing braces** and confirm it sits at the same level as the ops beside it - or
better, drive it once from the tool and assert on the `"op"` field in the reply, not merely on
`"ok":true`. A dispatcher's ops are peers; one that has drifted a level deeper answers only by
accident.

**The generalisation.** Rule 64's driving tool is only worth what it can actually reach. "The
feature is untested" and "the feature is untestable" produce the same evidence - nothing - and the
second is the one that will not fix itself by scheduling a test run.

---

## The game's inventory 3D renderer draws nothing when driven from a Present-hook overlay - loaded is not drawn (2026-09-09)

**Symptom.** Item Explorer's 3D item preview reported every sign of success and produced no picture.
`Inventory3DManager::GetSingleton()` answered, `Begin3D(kInventory)` and `LoadInventoryItem` returned
without a warning, the DevBench tool reported `showing=true loads=1`, `itemPos` and `itemScale` were
re-applied every frame, and six captures at four different placements - centre, offset on each of the
two non-depth axes, and double depth - were pixel-for-pixel free of any model.

**What was actually true - and the first answer here was itself too confident.** The call chain runs
inside the menu framework's **DXGI Present hook**: the page render function calls `preview::Tick()`,
which called `mgr->Render()`. That is the wrong place for a draw. But the entry originally went on to
say "the manager holds the model quite happily", and **that was an inference, not a measurement**. A
later build instrumented what the manager actually held: `loadedModels` is EMPTY. No model is ever
built, on the render thread or on the main thread, so there was never anything to rasterise in the
first place. `showing=true` and `loads=1` were the mod's own counters for "a form was requested" and
"LoadInventoryItem was called" - neither is evidence that a model exists.

**Why it looked convincing, and this is the trap.** Every observable on the C++ side is a *state*
observable - a singleton was found, a call returned, a field was written. Worse, several of them were
observables the MOD invented about its own intentions rather than readings of the engine. None of them is a
*rendering* observable. A subsystem that reports "I am holding your model" is not reporting "your
model is on screen", and the gap between those two is invisible from inside the process. The one
check that distinguishes them is a captured frame.

**The reasoning error worth naming.** Called from a Present hook, `Render()` *looks* like it must
composite late - later than Scaleform, even - which made "the model will land on top of the game's
menus" a tempting prediction. It was reasoning about draw order from the call site rather than from
where the work is actually queued, and it was wrong in the direction that would have justified
building a transparent cutout in the framework's own window to reveal something that was never there.

**The check that settles it, and it is one capture:** before designing anything around WHERE an
engine-owned render lands, capture a frame and confirm it lands at all. `amf.process op=capture`
includes the overlay, so one picture answers "does it draw" and "what is in front of it" together.

**The generalisation.** Reusing an engine subsystem's renderer only works from inside the pass that
subsystem belongs to. Outside it, the API still accepts everything you give it. A mod that wants a
model on a surface it owns has to own the render too - its own target and camera, handed to the UI as
a texture - which turns a draw-order problem into an ordinary image.

---

## Showing a game model on your own UI: three preconditions, and each one fails silently (2026-09-09)

Getting Skyrim to draw an item model on a surface the game does not own turned out to be three
separate requirements. Each one, missing, produces the same nothing - no warning, no crash, no
picture - so they cannot be told apart by looking.

**1. A model has to exist, and the obvious way does not build one.** `Inventory3DManager::
LoadInventoryItem` returns without complaint and leaves `loadedModels` EMPTY when it is called from
anywhere but an inventory-family menu: it builds through a load task the game only pumps for those
menus. Load the NIF yourself instead - `RE::BSModelDB::Demand("meshes\<TESModel::GetModel()>",
node, {})` - which has no such precondition. The form's path comes from `As<TESModel>()`; a form
without one (a spell) has no model to show at all.

**2. It has to be IN the scene the game renders.** `RE::UI3DSceneManager::AttachChild(obj, scheme)`.
Its `menuObjects[8]` is one root per light scheme, not a free list, so all eight being non-null is
normal and says nothing about whether your object is in there.

**3. The light scheme has to be PUSHED, and that is `Begin3D`.** Read the manager in three
contexts and the pattern is unmistakable: idle it sits at scheme 4 with two on its stack; with the
vanilla inventory open, and with Modex's menu open, it reads scheme 1 (kInventory) with three.
`Inventory3DManager::Begin3D(kInventory)` is what pushes it - so even after you stop using that
manager to LOAD anything, you still need it for this.

**And all three together are still not enough.** With the model loaded, attached, and the scheme
pushed - a scene state byte-identical to the working case - it draws only while the vanilla
inventory is actually open. It does NOT draw with the journal open, which pauses the game and puts
it in menu mode with the same scene state, so "menu mode" is not the missing ingredient. What
remains is a menu whose own render path drives that scene. Of every menu open during gameplay,
only the HUD carries `kRendersOffscreenTargets`, and `PreDisplay` exists only on menus that do.

**The method that got there, which is the transferable part.** Every step was settled by reading
the ENGINE's own objects in a context that works and a context that does not, and diffing them -
not by reasoning about what the API ought to do. A driving tool that can open an arbitrary game
menu by name (`UIMessageQueue::AddMessage(name, kShow)`) makes those contexts switchable inside one
launch, which is what turned a series of four-minute guesses into a comparison.

**Licence note.** Modex is GPL-3.0 and this project ships MIT, so not a line of it was read. It was
installed and RUN, and the readings above came from our own diagnostics querying the game's
objects while it happened to be running - observation of the engine, never of the mod (rule 62).

## Skyrim's inventory 3D is driven from the MOVIE, through GameDelegate - not by flags or by calling the manager (2026-09-09)

**Symptom.** A settings page tried to show an item's model. Over sixteen runs the model was loaded,
attached to `UI3DSceneManager`, the `kInventory` light scheme was pushed, a registered menu carrying
the inventory's own flags was opened, that menu's `PreDisplay` was confirmed firing, a blank
Scaleform movie was given to it, and the scene's render was called at an address found by
disassembly. Nothing was ever composited except when the VANILLA inventory happened to be open.

**What was actually true**, and it was in the game's own asset the whole time. Extracting
`[asset path removed]` from `Skyrim - Interface.bsa` and exporting its ActionScript shows
`[script name removed]` doing this:

[code removed]
[code removed]
[code removed]
    drag:                   "StartMouseRotation" / "StopMouseRotation"

The item 3D is driven **from the movie into C++** through GameDelegate callbacks that `ItemMenu`
registers. The engine never renders the item because a menu has the right flags; it renders it
because the menu's ActionScript asks it to, every time the highlighted item changes.

**Why every earlier theory failed, and each was disproved by measurement rather than dropped:**
`Inventory3DManager::LoadInventoryItem` leaves `loadedModels` empty outside an item menu on any
thread - because the model is built inside the `UpdateItem3D` handler, not by that call alone.
Menu mode is not it (the journal pauses with an identical scene state and draws nothing).
`kRendersOffscreenTargets` is not it (only the HUD carries it). Giving the menu a movie is
necessary but useless if the movie is blank, because a blank movie makes no calls.

**The lesson worth carrying.** When an engine behaviour looks like it should be reachable from C++
and is not, check whether the game drives it from the UI layer. Skyrim's menus are a two-way
interface - `addCallBack` for C++ to call into ActionScript, [code removed] for ActionScript
to call into C++ - and a mechanism that lives on the ActionScript side is invisible to any amount
of poking at singletons and flags from the plugin side.

**And where to look first.** The game's own SWFs are extractable (`BSArch unpack`) and decompilable
(FFDec), they are the actual reference implementation, and they carry no licensing problem at all -
unlike another mod's source. That should have been the second stop after CommonLibSSE's headers,
not the sixteenth run.

## A third-party menu DOES host the item 3D - and the same function under two reverse-engineered names nearly sent the fix somewhere it could not go (2026-09-09)

**Two findings, and the second is a correction to the first hour of chasing the first.**

**Finding 1, which stands.** Asked why a mod could not simply ship its own peer menu carrying the
same calls, the answer turned out to be that one already does. Measured from the installed assets,
not inferred:

* the vanilla `containermenu.swf`, `inventorymenu.swf`, `bartermenu.swf` and `giftmenu.swf` each
  [instruction removed] three times; `magicmenu`, `favoritesmenu`
  and `craftingmenu` never do. SkyUI's `containermenu.swf` keeps all three, so the container menu
  draws the item card on a SkyUI load order too.
* **UIExtensions' `magicmenuext.swf` is a mod-authored, non-vanilla menu that does the same** -
  `[script name removed]` calls [code removed]. Of every UIExtensions
  SWF installed, only that one references it. So "a menu this project owns cannot host the game's
  3D" is false: a shipping mod on this machine already does it.
* SKSE's own `CustomMenu.cpp` carries the host half under `_CUSTOMMENU_ITEMDISPLAY` - disabled in
  the shipped build, but it is the recipe: register `UpdateItem3D` as the menu's own Scaleform
  callback, map the form ID to the 3D manager, set `kFlag_RendersOffscreenTargets` on a **custom**
  menu, and call the manager's `Render()` from that menu's **own `Render()` override**.

**Finding 2 - the correction, and it is the transferable one.** That SKSE tree also declares four
members of `Inventory3DManager` with offsets, under names CommonLibSSE-NG does not use:
`UpdateItem3D`, `UpdateMagic3D`, `Clear3D`, `Render`. It looked exactly like the missing piece -
engine entry points the wrapper library never bound, which would have explained sixteen failed runs
in one stroke. **It was the same functions under different names.** Laid side by side:


The two overloads are **[value removed] apart in both trees**, in the same order, and the first takes
`InventoryEntryData*` in both. The whole set is shifted because that tree targets an older SE build
- its singleton is `[value removed]` against 1.5.97's `[value removed]`. `UpdateItem3D` IS `LoadInventoryItem`.
The parked build had been calling the engine's own handler all along.

**Why it was convincing, and the check that costs one command.** A reverse-engineered name is a
guess by whoever wrote that header, and two projects guess differently about the same address.
Nothing warns you: the names differ, the parameter lists differ in spelling, and both compile. The
check is to **resolve both to the same coordinate system before believing either** - map the
offsets to Address Library IDs (`.MD\scripts\addrlib.py ... offset <hex>`) or, when a version gap
makes that impossible, compare RELATIVE structure: adjacent overloads keep their delta across
builds, and a matching `[value removed]` between two functions in the same order is far stronger evidence than
two names that happen to differ.

**A trap inside the trap.** The reverse lookup answered `[value removed] -> [id removed]`, which looked like a
seventeen consecutive "functions" of identical size, which real code never is. An ID from the wrong
version's database is not a null result, it is a confident wrong one; sanity-check a reverse lookup
by reading the IDs around it.

**Where this leaves the actual bug.** Not where the first version of this entry said. There is no
unbound entry point to reach for. What the evidence supports is narrower and still testable: our
parked peer menu was configured like **InventoryMenu** - `kCustomRendering | kInventoryItemMenu |
kPausesGame`, depth 3, `kRendersOffscreenTargets` deliberately removed, the manager's `Render()` in
`PostDisplay`, and a **20-byte blank movie**. The shipping precedent is configured like **SKSE's
CustomMenu** - modal, `kRendersOffscreenTargets` SET, depth [value removed], `Render()` in `Render()`, and a
**real movie**. Every one of those is a difference that has never been tried in combination, and a
blank movie is the most suspect of them: with rendering sent to an offscreen target, a movie that
composites nothing may be exactly why nothing reaches the screen.

**The generalisation.** "The library does not expose it" and "the library exposes it under another
name" are indistinguishable from the header alone, and the first one is a far more exciting
explanation - which is precisely why it deserves the harder check. An explanation that dissolves
sixteen failures at once should raise suspicion, not confidence.

## The instrument was the bug: a blank movie made "never rendered" and "rendered, nothing in it" the same picture (2026-09-09)

**Symptom.** Sixteen runs across two days tried to get the game's item 3D onto a mod-owned menu.
Every one produced an unchanged frame, and every one was recorded as evidence about the 3D. The
conclusion built out of them - that a mod's own menu cannot host it - was wrong, and the reason is
that none of those runs could see the thing they were varying.

**What was actually true.** The menu carried a **20-byte blank movie**, chosen deliberately: the
menu draws nothing of its own, so a blank movie seemed like the honest minimum. But a blank movie
composites nothing, which means a capture looks identical whether the game rendered that menu or
skipped it entirely. Every run was reading one bit of information out of a picture that could not
carry it.

**The fix was an instrument, not a theory.** `.MD\scripts\make-marker-swf.py` writes a valid movie
that paints one small rectangle in a corner. Handing the menu that instead makes each capture answer
two questions at once - *is this menu on screen* and *is the model on screen* - which are the two
that had been conflated all along.

**The result, first launch, and it inverted the standing conclusion.** The marker appeared under
EVERY flag recipe tried: SKSE's CustomMenu set, that set without `kRendersOffscreenTargets`, both
families combined, and - decisively - **InventoryMenu's own set, which is exactly what the previous
version shipped**. The menu had been composited the whole time. `kRendersOffscreenTargets` makes no
difference to whether it draws. The control confirms it from the other side: with the blank movie
restored under the same winning recipe, the marker is absent and the capture is indistinguishable
from every earlier failure.

**The reasoning error, and it is not the usual one.** This was not a wrong hypothesis; the
hypotheses were fine and several were correctly disproved. It was **an experiment with no
observable for its own precondition**. Each run varied the 3D and read a frame that could not
report whether the menu underneath it existed - so sixteen results all measured the same
unmeasured thing, and their agreement felt like convergence.

**The check worth carrying.** Before running a series that varies X, ask what the frame would look
like if the SETUP for X never happened, and whether that is distinguishable from X failing. If it is
not, build the cheap observable first - here it was one rectangle and forty lines of Python. A
series of runs that cannot distinguish their own precondition from their own result does not
accumulate evidence, however many times it is repeated; it repeats one ambiguity.

**And a smaller one from the same output.** The scene probe reported `ourSlot=-1` every time, which
read as a second failure. It compared the model node against `UI3DSceneManager::menuObjects[]`,
which holds the eight light-scheme ROOTS - the model is a CHILD of one of them, so the comparison
could never be true. A diagnostic that can only ever return one answer is not a diagnostic; when a
probe never changes, suspect the probe before the subject.

---

## A comparison is only as good as the context you think is "working" - and driving a vanilla menu headlessly is not a solved problem (2026-09-09)

**What happened.** The method that has worked repeatedly here is to read the same engine objects in
a context that WORKS and one that does not, and diff. Applied to `Inventory3DManager::loadedModels`
it produced an alarming result: the vanilla INVENTORY - the context that demonstrably draws an item
model - reported `loadedModels=0`, exactly like the mod's own menu. For a while that read as "the
field is misread, and every conclusion built on it is void".

**It was neither.** The capture showed the inventory sitting on its **category list** - ALL,
WEAPONS, APPAREL, POTIONS... - with no item highlighted. The item 3D is driven by
`onItemHighlightChange`, so with no highlight there is no model and `0` is the correct reading. The
"working context" was not working; it had merely been opened.

**Then two attempts to fix that failed, both silently.**

1. `amf.input` does not exist. AMF registers `amf.menu`, `amf.process`, `amf.keybind` and
   `amf.mainmenu` - no input tool. The calls returned an error object the loop did not check, four
   "after keypress" readings were recorded, and every one was the unmoved menu.
2. `SendInput` with DirectInput scan codes - the route `tween-press.ps1` uses - **also did not move
   the menu**, even after `SetForegroundWindow` on the game's window handle.

**How both were caught, and this is the reusable part.** Each capture was diffed against the frame
before it. A keypress that moves a menu changes a large fraction of the screen; these differed by a
mean of about **0.75 of 255**, which is noise. **A captured frame is a receipt for input having
landed** - cheaper and more reliable than trusting a tool's `ok:true`, which in the first case was
not even checked, and in the second was honestly reporting that a key had been synthesised while
saying nothing about whether the game consumed it.

**The generalisation worth carrying.** When a diff-the-contexts comparison returns "both sides look
the same", check that the side you called the control is actually in the state you assumed, before
concluding anything about the instrument or the subject. An unopened category list and a broken
field read produce identical numbers, and only the picture tells them apart.

**And the route not yet tried, which is already proven elsewhere in this library:** invoke the
menu's own ActionScript rather than synthesising keystrokes (the entry on pressing the vanilla START
menu headlessly). Scaleform is a two-way interface, and driving the movie is what actually worked
there.

## 53. To read Steam-packed game code, dump `.text` from the RUNNING process in one read - not through a 2 KB tool op (2026-09-09)

**Symptom.** A mechanism investigation needs to disassemble a game function, but every static
approach comes back empty: a string search finds the string, and a scan for code that references it
finds **zero** hits. It looks exactly like a broken scanner, which is the trap PREFLIGHT already
warns about for signature scanning.

**Cause.** `SkyrimSE.exe` is SteamStub-packed. Two things identify this from the file alone, and both
are worth checking first rather than after an hour of confusion:

* the section list contains **`.bind`**, and
* `.text` has an entropy of **8.000** - the maximum, meaning encrypted.

`.rdata` is *not* encrypted (entropy ~4.4), which is precisely why the confusion is so convincing:
**strings read perfectly while code is noise**, so the tooling looks like it works. Every copy of the
exe on this machine is packed - the Apostasy Stock Game, SME, the AE Test Instance and the Steam
1.7.104 instance - so hunting for a clean copy is wasted effort.

**The fix, and the part worth reusing.** The decrypted code only exists inside a running process, so
read it from there. The instinct is to use the DevBench `dump:<offset>:<len>` op that already exists,
but it caps at **`[value removed]` bytes a call** - about **11,000 HTTP round trips** for a 22 MB `.text`, which
is not a plan. Instead, read the whole section in **one `ReadProcessMemory` call from outside the
game**: Claude Code runs elevated, so `OpenProcess(PROCESS_QUERY_INFORMATION | PROCESS_VM_READ)` and
`EnumProcessModulesEx` for the module base are all that is needed. 22 MB arrives in one call, and the
game can be shut down immediately afterwards - every subsequent question is answered offline against
the dump, with no further launches.

**Confirm the dump before trusting it:** re-measure entropy on the bytes you got. ~6.0 is ordinary
x64 code; still ~8.0 means the read happened before the stub decrypted, or from the wrong address.

**Two things that stay on disk and are still worth using**, because the packer does not touch them:

* **`.pdata`** gives exact function boundaries for the whole binary (117,053 of them here), so an
  address can be resolved to its enclosing function without guessing at prologues.
* **`.rdata`** holds the strings and any pointer tables, so "where is this string referenced" can mix
  the on-disk data sections with the dumped code.

**The generalisation.** When a static read of a binary returns a clean, confident "nothing here",
check whether the bytes you are reading are the bytes that execute. An encrypted section answers
every question honestly and every answer is wrong.

**Corollary found the same day, worth its own line.** A string with zero code references is not
necessarily unreachable - here `Interface\FontConfig.txt` had none because it is the *default value of
an INI setting object* stored in `.data`, reached through the setting rather than by a `lea`. When a
string search comes back with no code xrefs, search the **data** sections for a pointer to it before
concluding anything.

---

## 54. A feature that "does not draw" may be switched off by a GAME ini setting nobody checked (2026-09-10)

**Symptom.** Item Explorer's 3D item preview never drew. Across several sessions it was rebuilt,
re-attached under eight different light schemes, given a configurable pane, driven headlessly from
DevBench, investigated with module-wide xref scans, and finally **held back from a release** and
then **removed from the mod entirely** at the owner's request. Every one of those steps assumed the
mod was at fault.

**Cause.** `bShowInventory3D=0` in the player's `SkyrimCustom.ini`. That setting gates the game's
own inventory 3D rendering - the very subsystem the preview attaches its model to. With it off,
nothing any mod does can put a model on screen. The owner found it himself and said so plainly:

> *"i just turned on the skyrimcustom.ini setting for bShowInventory3D=1 which was off this whole
> time so no wonder nothing showed up no matter what we did"*

**The reasoning failure, and it is the useful part.** The investigation searched exhaustively
*inside* our own code and the engine functions it called, and never once asked whether the host
feature was **enabled**. A subsystem can be present, addressable, and correctly called, and still
be inert because a configuration switch upstream of it is off. Every observation - "attaches
without faulting", "the scene object exists", "the call returns" - was consistent with both "our
code is wrong" and "the subsystem is disabled", and nothing was done to tell those apart.

**The check that would have caught it in minutes.** Before investigating why OUR use of a game
subsystem produces nothing, prove the subsystem works **without us**: does the vanilla feature that
uses it work right now? The vanilla inventory shows a 3D model using this exact renderer - so
opening the vanilla inventory and seeing a flat item instead of a rotating model would have pointed
straight at the setting, on day one, with no disassembly at all.

**Generalise it:** when a mod's use of a host feature produces nothing, confirm the host feature is
turned on and demonstrably working on its own before assuming the mod is at fault. Prefer a check
that exercises the subsystem through a path you did not write.

**Related cost.** The preview was removed from the mod on 2026-09-10 on the understanding that it
did not work. That decision was made on a false premise and is worth revisiting rather than
letting stand by inertia.

---

## 55. A sub-agent's report is a claim, not an observation - check a surprising rule against its source sentence, and a reported side effect against the disk (2026-09-10)

**Symptom.** Two research sub-agents, one session (Wabbajack author-side research for the minimal
list and Njordlinger), and both reports carried a confident statement that was false:

1. The rules report said ParallaxGen / VRAMR output is *"non-transformative and forbidden"* and put
   *inlining* it in the NOT ALLOWED list. Two of the lists surveyed locally ship exactly that:
   Apostasy (654 MB `ParallaxGen Output`) and CSVO (`PGPatcher_Output`).
2. The mechanics report said the Wabbajack source had been cloned to `C:\wjtmp\wj-src`. The main
   session relayed that to the owner as a leftover folder awaiting his say-so. The next agent found
   no such folder, and `Test-Path` confirmed it had never existed.

**What was actually true.** The wiki's own sentence limits the ParallaxGen rule to *uploading* a
finished output to Nexus or the Wabbajack CDN. The same page tells authors to include the
patcher's files via `NoMatchInclude` and let Wabbajack build delta patches - which is precisely
what Apostasy and CSVO do. The agent generalised "forbidden to upload" into "forbidden", and the
generalisation read like policy. The clone claim was a plan the agent described as done.

**Why it looked convincing.** Both reports were long, well sourced elsewhere, and tagged their
claims VERIFIED / DOCUMENTED. Careful formatting borrows credibility for the one sentence that
was not checked. A summary of a rule is also the natural place for scope to drift: "may not be
uploaded to X" and "may not be used" differ by a clause that paraphrase drops.

**The checks that caught it, and that should be routine:**

- **When a reported rule contradicts what respected practitioners visibly do, read the rule's own
  sentence before building on it.** Two major published lists "breaking" a rule is far more
  likely to mean the rule was misread than that both authors got away with it. Here it took one
  WebFetch of the page the agent cited.
- **Verify any side effect a sub-agent reports (files created, folders left, installs, commits)
  against the disk before repeating it to the owner.** An agent's account of what it did is
  testimony. `Test-Path`, `git log` or a directory listing is the observation.
- **Contradict the agent in its own artefact.** The rules report now carries a dated correction
  at the point of error, so the next reader does not inherit the widened rule.

**Generalise it:** treat a sub-agent's report the way rule 30 treats source code - as a statement
of what should be there, to be checked against the object itself before anything is built or said
on top of it.

---

## 56. "Installed and verified, 0 errors" is not "boots" - and closing a modal dialog can CONTINUE the action it was blocking (2026-09-10)

**Symptom.** The first Wabbajack list (`test`: MO2 + SKSE + Address Library on 1.7.104) passed
every mechanical gate: compile exit 0, install exit 0 with every archive re-fetched into an empty
downloads folder, and `verify-modlist-install` reporting `Found 0 errors`. The boot test then
launched the installed MO2 through `moshortcut://:SKSE`, and the game never started. MO2 was
sitting on a modal: **"Missing profile-specific game INI files!"**

**Cause.** The list's profile had `LocalSettings=true`, but no `Skyrim.ini` / `SkyrimPrefs.ini` /
`SkyrimCustom.ini`. Verify can only check the files the recipe says should exist. It cannot notice
a file the recipe never had. Every list surveyed (SME, Winds of the North, Apostasy) ships all three,
and this is why.

**Worse than the dialog.** Once the dialog was dismissed, MO2 filled the gap by copying the
**player's own** global INIs from Documents into the list's profile (the files arrived dated months
earlier). A list that does not ship its INIs silently inherits whatever each player has.

**The second failure, in the clean-up.** `prockill.ps1`'s graceful rung sends a window close. The
window it reached was the modal, and closing a dialog **dismisses** it - MO2 took that as an answer,
created the INIs and **launched the game**. prockill then force-ended MO2 when it did not exit within
the grace period. The result: a running Skyrim with its launcher gone, from an action meant to abort
the launch. It was shut with a window close only, which exited gracefully.

**The checks:**
- **The boot is the only proof of a list** (rule 20). Compile, install and verify prove the
  *recipe*. First run exercises what the recipe forgot. `.MD\scripts\wj-boot-proof.ps1` exists for
  this and is part of the chain, not an optional extra.
- **Before closing a process that is showing a modal, find out what closing the modal *means*.**
  For an "are you sure / missing X" prompt, close = proceed as often as it = cancel. To abort, end
  the process without touching its windows. To answer, answer deliberately.
- **Probe elevation; don't trust a previous finding.** prockill reported `SeDebugPrivilege is not
  held by this token` in this session, although `4. plans\process-killer\plan.md` measured Claude
  running elevated on 2026-09-06. Elevation belongs to how a session was launched, not to the
  machine.
