## 57. `'build.bat' is not recognized` from a `cmd /c` started IN the repo folder: the session sets NoDefaultCurrentDirectoryInExePath=1, so cmd never searches the current directory for a program - call scripts by full path (2026-09-11)

**Symptom.** Character Progression Control's `build.bat`, run as `cmd /c "cd /d <repo> && build.bat"` and
again through `Start-Process cmd -ArgumentList '/c','build.bat' -WorkingDirectory <repo>`, failed at once
with "'build.bat' is not recognized as an internal or external command" - twice, both build lines -
while `cmd /c "cd & dir /b *.bat"` with the same working directory printed the repo path and listed the
file. No `Command Processor\AutoRun`, `PATHEXT` normal.

**Cause.** `$env:NoDefaultCurrentDirectoryInExePath` is `1` in this session's shells. With it set,
cmd.exe does not look in the current directory for an unqualified program name - only on `PATH`.
Built-ins (`cd`, `dir`) are unaffected, which is exactly what makes it read as a working-directory
problem: every probe of the working directory says it is right.

**Why the wrong explanation survived.** The 2026-09-11 handoff said "call by FULL PATH; `cmd /c` does
not inherit PowerShell's `Push-Location`". The fix was right and the mechanism was wrong, so the next
attempt repaired the working directory - and failed the same way twice.

**Check / fix.** `$env:NoDefaultCurrentDirectoryInExePath` first. Invoke the script by its absolute
path (`cmd /c "D:\...\build.bat"`); a name with a directory part (`.\build.bat`) is not subject to the
current-directory search either. And check a build's exit code in a file, never through a pipe
(entry at line 2004). Same session, a second trap of the same family: a `.cmd` wrapper written LF-only
(the Write tool's output) stopped executing after its first `call` - cmd seeks by byte offset in a
batch file and loses its place on LF endings. Write batch files CRLF.

## 58. A test that answers a confirm box "by index 0" answers whatever question is first - read the buttons, or four runs measure "No" (2026-09-11)

**Symptom.** Character Progression Control's legendary reset hook fired and wrote 40, yet the skill stayed
at 100, run after run - which read exactly like "the reset happens outside Run, the hook restores too
early" (falsification episode 18's listed rival).

**Cause.** The harness answered the game's "Making a skill Legendary will set it to 15... Are you sure?"
box with `accept index 0`, and the buttons are `["No","Yes"]` - so every "test" declined the legendary.
Then the box that followed a Yes (a SECOND confirm, "Are you sure you want to make this skill
Legendary?") was never answered at all, and the leftover box confused the next attempt's reading. The
hook was right the whole time; the reset lands inside Run on the second Yes.

**Why it looked convincing.** The hook's own log line ("Run(message 0)") was faithfully reporting the
button index, and a skill that does not change is exactly what a wrong mechanism would also produce.

**Checks.** `menu describe` a box and pick the button by its TEXT, every time. Loop until no box is open -
a game action can ask twice. Read the result from the value the game uses (Papyrus
`Actor.GetBaseActorValue`), not from a console capture: `console read` returned a stale
`GetBaseActorValue >> 100` long after the hook had seen 40. And one more thing the run taught: a
threshold check can have a TWIN inside the action it gates - Skyrim compares the skill with 100 again
inside the legendary answer and skips the reset below it, so lowering the eligibility check alone
produced "legendary, but the level stays".

## 59. Porting a hook to Skyrim 1.7: the AE offsets were already right, and one dump of the running game proved it in minutes (2026-09-11)

**Situation.** Infinity UI (alexsylex, MIT) has no 1.7 build, and three of our mods draw through it. It
hooks two calls INSIDE `BSScaleformManager::LoadMovie` at hardcoded in-function offsets -
`IMenu*` at both. Hardcoded offsets and a register assumption are exactly the expensive kind of port
(rule 44), so the estimate hung on whether 1.7 moved them.

**What it actually took.** One launch. Every `SkyrimSE.exe` here is SteamStub-packed, so `.text` was read
out of the RUNNING 1.7.104 process in one `ReadProcessMemory` (entry 53), the game was closed, and every
later question was answered offline. The answer: 1.7.104's `LoadMovie` is instruction-for-instruction the
same around both calls as AE's, at the SAME offsets ([value removed], [value removed]), and `rdi` is reloaded from the
`IMenu*` argument's home slot in both builds. The port was a recompile against CommonLibSSE-NG 7.2 with
NO address changed - confirmed live afterwards on 1.7.104 and SE 1.5.97.

**The three things worth reusing.**

* **Verify, do not assume, that a new runtime moved anything.** "1.7 changed the Address Library format"
  is true and says nothing about whether a given function moved. All 27 of this plugin's ID pairs resolve
  on 1.5.97, 1.6.1170 and 1.7.104, and the AE ids are the ones 1.7 uses.
* **A dump taken while the mod is INSTALLED shows already-patched sites.** The 2026-09-09 1.5.97 dump had
  `jmp` where the two calls belong, because Infinity UI was loaded in that instance. That confirmed the SE
  offsets for free, but the ORIGINAL instructions were unrecoverable from it - so a reference dump that
  needs the untouched bytes must be taken with the mod disabled.
* **Byte-check a hardcoded site before writing to it.** The port now reads the site first and requires
  copy of the same plugin, fails the check, and the mod patches nothing and says why in the log instead of
  writing a jump into the middle of another instruction. It caught nothing this time - that is the point:
  it is what makes the next game update a "no patches" log line rather than a crash report.

**Tooling this left behind.** `.MD\scripts\gamecode.py` resolves an Address Library id to an offset on any
of the three runtimes (formats 1, 2 and the 1.7 dense format 5) and disassembles the function from the
dumps in `.tools\dumps\` (1.5.97 and 1.7.104 kept). The Local Map Upgrade and Dragon's Eye Minimap 1.7
ports need exactly this, and need no further launches to start.

## Gotcha: a command refused as touching a "system path" may be naming a string that only APPEARS in its text - and the whole command is rejected before anything runs (2026-09-11)

> **Caveat added 2026-10-08 (archive sweep):** the mechanism this entry gives - a word-split at the space in the
> project root - was never demonstrated. On 2026-09-12 a save meant to record that explanation was refused the same way,
> which falsified it, and the precise trigger was never isolated. Read the mechanism below as a hypothesis; the
> lesson that holds is the entry "When a tool refusal's error text is mangled, isolate the operation" near the end of
> this file.

**Symptom.** A cleanup script was refused with `... on system path ''D:\Claude' is blocked. This path
is protected from removal.` - while its actual targets were `<MO2>\Apostasy\mods\...` and
`<MO2>\Steam 1.7.104 Test\mods\...`. Neither is a system path, and neither is what the message
named.

**Cause.** The guard scans the command TEXT rather than the resolved target, and split an unrelated
string literal in the same script - the repo path, assigned twenty lines earlier - at the space in
`<ROOT>`, leaving `D:\Claude` as what it believed was being removed.

**It is not limited to commands that delete anything.** Writing THIS library entry tripped it twice:
a script whose only operations were an append, a version bump and a commit was refused, because the
entry's own text quoted the deletion cmdlet's name next to that path. Anything carrying both tokens
in its text is a candidate, documentation about the trap included.

**The expensive half: nothing in the command runs.** The first time it fired, the script's earlier
steps - a `set-version.ps1` call and a health gate - had not executed either, and it would have been
easy to carry on believing the version had been stamped. After a block like this, re-check state
instead of assuming the statements above the refused one took effect.

**Fix.** Keep unrelated paths, and the names of destructive cmdlets, out of the command text: name
the target with `-LiteralPath` and let the script contain nothing else that looks like a path. The
identical cleanup, with the same targets, succeeded once the unrelated literal was gone. When the
text itself must contain those tokens (a note like this one), write it to a file with the editing
tool and have the shell command only reference that file.

**Related, same session:** folder names carrying `[NoDelete]` need `-LiteralPath` for a different
reason - brackets are a wildcard character class, so a `Get-Item` without it matched nothing and
reported a freshly installed DLL's version as blank, which read as a broken install rather than a
broken query.

## Licence: the LICENSE file inside a mod ARCHIVE may be the UPSTREAM's, not the mod's - check the source repo at the RELEASED TAG (2026-09-11)

**Symptom.** Wheeler Refined's installed package ships `LICENSE` = BSD 3-Clause (dTry, 2024) and a
`NOTICE.md` saying "Unless a file says otherwise, Wheeler Refined modifications are distributed
under the same BSD 3-Clause License as the original Wheeler project." Read together those look
decisive, and a standing project record saying "GPL-3-only, never read the source" was CORRECTED on
the strength of them. The repo's own `LICENSE` says: "Wheeler Refined is licensed under the GNU
General Public License version 3 only."

**What was actually true.** GPL-3.0-only, including at the released version. Checked properly: the
`LICENSE` at tag **v1.3.3** is GPL-3, and the commit that introduced it is an **ancestor** of that
tag - so it was not a later relicence that left the shipped archive innocently stale. The BSD-3 file
in the archive is the **inherited** notice for the code the mod derives from; the same package's
`THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md` lists BSD-3 under the heading "Original Wheeler", which is the tell.

**Why the wrong reading was convincing.** Everything about it looked like primary evidence: a real
licence file, in the mod's own folder, naming the mod in a NOTICE clause. A derivative work must
carry its parent's notice, so the presence of a permissive LICENSE in an archive says nothing about
the derivative's own terms - and a NOTICE written by the fork author can simply contradict the
repo, as it does here.

**The checks.**

* Read the licence from the **source repository at the tag matching the installed version**, not
  from the archive. the GitHub API.
* When an archive's NOTICE and the repo's LICENSE disagree, that is **unresolved, not a verdict** -
  the stricter of the two governs what may be read until the author clarifies.
* A `THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES`/`LICENSES/` folder naming a licence under an "Original <upstream>" heading
  means that licence is inherited. Look there before concluding.
* GitHub's own detection is not evidence: this repo reports `NOASSERTION` while carrying plain GPL-3
  text.

**What it cost, and the second-order lesson.** A false correction was written into the project's
queue - the record that gates whether a codebase may be read at all - and the fork's public API
header was read on the strength of it, creating a contamination note for a clean-room rebuild that
did not need to exist. This is the SECOND licence-reading failure of the same family in one day; the
first was concluding permissions from a Nexus page while the repository said otherwise. Both share
one shape: **one artefact was treated as the whole licence position.** Licence facts come from the
repository, at the version in question, corroborated - and a correction to a licence record is the
last place to be quick.

## 60. `auo.input`'s BSInputEventQueue press CRASHES SE 1.5.97 - drive input with `bench.input`'s PollInputDevices splice instead (2026-09-12)

**Symptom.** Driving the Wheeler settings page headlessly in Apostasy (SE 1.5.97), an `auo.input`
`op=press device=keyboard code=87 hold=6` returned `{"queued":true}` and the game died within a
second. `EXCEPTION_ACCESS_VIOLATION` - *"Tried to execute memory at [value removed]"*: a call through
a **null function pointer**, not a bad data read.

**What the stack actually said.** The PROBABLE CALL STACK resolved nothing useful - `CrashLogger.dll`
x3, `KERNELBASE`, `ntdll` x5, i.e. the handler's own frames. The attribution is in the STACK dump
instead: `TrueHotkeys.dll` x8, `ApocryphaUIOverhaul.dll` x4 (including its own `source\Input.cpp` and
its vendored `g_devBenchInterface`), `STB_Widgets.dll` x1, `InputBench.dll` x1. `RSI` and four stack
slots all held the same `ButtonEvent*`, and `[RSP+180]` held `[value removed]` = 87 - the injected code. The mod
under test, `wheeler.dll`, appeared **twice and only in inventory sections** (module base, version
list) with **zero stack frames**.

**Why it was predictable, and why it was not predicted.** The gotcha at line 2070 already recorded
that `RE::BSInputEventQueue::GetSingleton()` returns garbage on SE 1.5.97 in this CommonLibSSE-NG
build, and that the fix was to stop touching that singleton and instead SPLICE a `ButtonEvent` into
the dispatch list inside the input hook. `auo.input` is the BSInputEventQueue route. `bench.input`
(InputBench) is the splice route - the one that targets `PollInputDevices`, where mods' own input
hooks live. Entry 39 records the two mechanisms differing in REACH; this records them differing in
SAFETY on SE. The library had the answer before the press was sent; it was read afterwards.

**The checks.**

* **On SE 1.5.97, drive synthetic input with `bench.input`, never `auo.input`.**
* A crash whose PROBABLE CALL STACK contains only CrashLogger/KERNELBASE/ntdll has resolved **no**
  frames - that is not "no culprit", it is "read the REGISTERS and the STACK dump", where the
  module-attributed slots are.
* Changing two variables at once - a new mod present AND a synthetic press never used on this list
  before - makes timing correlation worthless. Module attribution in the stack dump is the evidence;
  "it crashed right after my change" is not.
* A synthetic event is a **test instrument**, and an instrument that crashes the target is a fault in
  the instrument until the target is on the stack.

**The recipe that then worked**, end to end, nobody at the keyboard (Apostasy, SE 1.5.97):

1. Launch with `Start-Process ModOrganizer.exe -ArgumentList '-p', '"Test Build"', 'moshortcut://:Play'`
   - literal quotes INSIDE the single-quoted element (entry at line 2262), and `:Play`, never a
   shortcut label invented from the executable list.
2. `game action=loadLast`, then wait for `inspect kind=state` -> `playerLoaded: true`, and confirm
   with `menu action=list` that `Main Menu` is NOT in `openMenus`. **A key press before this proves
   nothing**: Wheeler's `ShouldBypassWheelerInputInterception()` returns true while MainMenu is open,
   so `Input::ProcessAndFilter` returns before any mod logic runs. A press tested at the main menu
   looks exactly like a broken splice.
3. Drive the mod's own tool for state and writes; use `bench.input op=press device=keyboard code=N
   hold=3` for real presses.
4. Read the verdict from the mod's OWN observable, never from the absence of an error. Here
   `wheeler.page status` reports `open` / `wheelOpen`, cross-checked against Wheeler's own log line
   `action=Toggle raw=N mapped=N ... decision=OpenRequested`.

**A measured gotcha in the instrument.** `bench.input`'s `hold` is not a frame count you can reason
about: a `hold=3` press logged `heldMs=32495.0` at its release, because the splice leaves the key
down until some later dispatch releases it. The DOWN edge is reliable; anything depending on hold
DURATION is not - Wheeler's `ToggleHoldThreshold` is 0.2s, so every driven press trips
`decision=DeniedHoldThreshold` on release. Test down-edge behaviour this way and treat held-key
behaviour as needing a real device, which is where entry 39 arrived from the other direction.

**What it proved, which is the point of having the recipe at all.** A keymap rebind driven entirely
through the tool took effect LIVE: `InputBindings.MKB/toggleWheel` 34 -> 36, pressing 36 opened the
wheel, and pressing the old 34 afterwards did nothing. Both halves matter - the new binding works AND
the old one is gone - so `Controls::BindAllInputsFromConfig()` plus the lightweight apply sequence is
sufficient for a keybind change, and the heavy close/reopen cycle is not needed for that case.

# A null result from an injected keypress is meaningless until the binding's EFFECT SCOPE is verified

**Symptom.** A key is injected through a working input path with the target mod loaded, logging on
and every known gate open. Nothing happens and nothing is logged. This looks exactly like the defect
under investigation, and is about to be recorded as a reproduction.

**What it actually was (2026-09-12, AMF report 2 / Gear Toggle SKSE).** The mod's config bound the
key correctly - `"toggleKey": 35` - but scoped its effect to nobody:

```json
{ "name": "Helmet and hood", "toggleKey": 35, "toggleKeyAffects": "none" }
```

`[source reference removed]`: [code removed]
with `kNone = 0` matching no actor. The press was received and discarded by design. The mod's own
settings page draws a warning for this state - "The key is bound but reaches nobody" - so the author
expected people to hit it.

**Why the usual checks did not catch it.** Everything that was verified was verified correctly and
none of it was sufficient: the key code matched the config, the input path was proven live by a
control injection (F1 opened the framework menu through the same transport), the game was loaded and
responsive, every early-return gate in the handler was measured false, and logging was confirmed on.
A binding has TWO halves - which key, and what it reaches - and only the first was checked.

**The second trap in the same failure.** There was also no readout even in principle: every log line
on the press path sat AFTER the scope check, so a discarded press writes nothing. "No new log line"
therefore could not distinguish "press never arrived" from "press arrived and was correctly ignored".

**The rule.** Before treating a null result from an injected input as evidence of anything:

1. Read the binding's full configuration, not just the key code - scope, target, enable flag,
   and any "affects/applies to" field.
2. Find the first log statement on the press path IN THE SOURCE and confirm it sits BEFORE every
   early return, or accept that silence is uninformative and find another readout.
3. Keep the control injection (a key with a known, independently observable effect through the same
   transport). It is what separates a dead transport from a real null - it is necessary, and it is
   not sufficient.

**Cost when skipped:** a false "the bug reproduces" written into a bug report, and a fourth theory
chased against a rig where the stimulus was inert.


# Get-ChildItem -Include is silently ignored unless the path ends in \* (or -Recurse is paired with it correctly)

**Symptom.** A filtered listing returns files that plainly do not match the filter, and the output
reads like a finding. On 2026-09-12, checking whether a mod shipped an ESP:

```powershell
Get-ChildItem -LiteralPath $root -Recurse -File -Include '*.esp','*.esl','*.esm'
```

printed `meta.ini`, `GearToggle.dll` and `GearToggle.json` under a "PLUGIN:" label - none of which is
a plugin. The real answer (SKSE-only, no plugin, so `plugins.txt` needs no sync) was the opposite of
what the output appeared to say, and it was one careless read away from being recorded as "this mod
ships a plugin".

**Cause.** `-Include` filters the PATH argument, not the results. It applies only when the path ends
in a wildcard (`$root\*`) or when `-Recurse` is present AND the provider applies it to leaf names -
which is exactly the case that behaves inconsistently in Windows PowerShell 5.1. With a `-LiteralPath`
that has no trailing wildcard, the filter is dropped and everything is returned.

**Use instead**, in order of preference:

* `Get-ChildItem -LiteralPath $root -Recurse -File | Where-Object { $_.Extension -in '.esp','.esl' }`
  - explicit, works everywhere, and reads as what it does.
* `Get-ChildItem -Path "$root\*" -Recurse -Include '*.esp'` - if `-Include` is wanted, the path must
  carry the wildcard. Note this cannot be combined with `-LiteralPath`.
* `-Filter` for a SINGLE pattern - it is applied by the provider and is much faster, but takes only
  one pattern.

**It came back inside a gate (2026-10-06).** `version-gate.ps1`'s `Package-Dlls` used exactly the line above with
`'*.dll','*.asi'`, so every package "had DLLs" (an asset-only Witcher 3 package of an input.xml, a script and string
tables counted 22). The finalize stage's asset-only branch (no DLL -> hash a shipped asset) could therefore never run,
and the hash check matched against every file. Fixed with the `Where-Object { $_.Extension -in ... }` form. Same
session, the companion PowerShell trap: `@($null).Count` is 1, so a function returning nothing counted as one item -
write `@(F | Where-Object { $_ }).Count`.

**Related trap, same family (same session).** `Test-Path`/`Join-Path` against a directory whose name
contains `[` or `]` - MO2 mod folders like `[NoDelete] 0817 Gear Toggle SKSE 1` - treat the brackets
as a wildcard character class and report the file missing when it exists. Always `-LiteralPath` for
these paths. A `Test-Path` on such a folder returned "(no GearToggle.json)" for a file that the Read
tool had already opened successfully.

**The general rule:** when a filtered command returns something that contradicts a filter, suspect
the command before recording the result. Both traps here produced confident, wrong-looking output
rather than an error.

# Skyrim's main menu is reported as "Main Menu" (with a space) - testing for "MainMenu" silently reads False

**Symptom.** A readiness poll waits for the main menu to disappear, reports it is already gone, and
then times out waiting for `playerLoaded` that never becomes true. The game is in fact sitting at
the main menu the whole time, doing exactly what it should.

**Cause (2026-09-12).** `menu action=list` returns the engine's menu names verbatim, and several
carry a space that the CommonLibSSE constant/class name does not:

| in `openMenus` | often mistyped as |
| --- | --- |
| `Main Menu` | `MainMenu` |
| `Fader Menu` | `FaderMenu` |
| `Cursor Menu` | `CursorMenu` |
| `Journal Menu` | `JournalMenu` |

`$m.openMenus -contains 'MainMenu'` returned `False` while `Main Menu` sat plainly in the same list
next to `Fader Menu` and `Cursor Menu`. A `-contains` miss is indistinguishable from a genuine
absence - no error, no warning, just a confident wrong answer that cost a six-minute poll.

**The rule.** Never hand-type an engine menu name into a comparison. Either

* print `openMenus` and read it, or
* match loosely: `$m.openMenus -match 'Main\s*Menu'`, or
* test on the tool's own answer (`inspect kind=state` -> `playerLoaded`) rather than on a menu name,
  which is what actually indicates "in world" and cannot be misspelled.

**Generalises to:** any string-keyed liveness check against a list supplied by another system -
menu names, mod names, registry keys. When a `-contains` / `in` test drives a wait loop, a typo
converts into "the condition is already satisfied" or "it never happens", and both look like
findings about the game rather than bugs in the check.

**Related, same session:** the game's own `game action=list` is authoritative for saves, not a
directory read of the saves folder - under MO2's VFS `sLocalSavePath` may resolve somewhere other
than the obvious `Documents\My Games\...\Saves`.


## A rule enforced by several tools, each holding its own copy, is not enforced - it drifts; ONE tool that REFUSES is the shape that holds (2026-09-12)

**Symptom:** version numbers kept going wrong for weeks after "strict enforcement" was asked for
(rule 48, 2026-08-27) and after three scripts, a hook and two gate checks existed for it: duplicate
ledger identities (`AutoDraw` beside `AutoDraw-SMF`, `DragonsEyeMinimap` beside
`DragonsEyeMinimap-SMF`), three mods finalized at 0.1.0 with no ledger line, a fork recorded under
its upstream's 1.3.3, and a hardcoded `"v1.3.3"` in a `Plugin.h.in` that no tool knew about.

**Why it looked enforced:** every piece of the rule WAS implemented somewhere - `version-ledger.ps1`
computed next, `set-version.ps1` wrote locations, `check-version.ps1` compared them,
`package-mod.ps1` checked the DLL resource, `pre-finalize-check.ps1` re-checked five locations,
`docs-pipeline.ps1` and `rules-version.ps1` each had their own rollover arithmetic. Reading any one
of them, the rule was there.

**The mechanism:** none of them was a gate on the others. The number was a free-typed `-Version`
parameter at every step, the ledger's `-Mod` was whatever string the caller chose, `next` fell back
to guessing from CHANGELOG headings when the ledger was silent, and `working` needed no hash - so a
number could be minted, written, packaged and recorded without any tool ever refusing. Seven
implementations of a rule are seven places for it to be applied by care, and care is what fails at
2am.

**The fix (the owner's shape, 2026-09-12):** one file, `version-gate.ps1`, owns identity, arithmetic,
writing, checking, recording and the gate; every consumer calls it and stops on a non-zero exit; a
number is never typed (`bump` issues it, `current` hands it to the packager); `working` requires the
binary's hash and the finalize gate compares it to the packaged DLL; a version literal in a file the
tool was not told about is itself a failure. The retired scripts were deleted rather than kept as
shims, because a shim is a second location.

**The transferable check:** when a rule "keeps being broken despite being enforced", count the
places that implement it. More than one means none of them is the gate. Collapse to one tool whose
exit code the others obey, and make the thing being protected (here, the number) impossible to
supply by hand.


## A hook that consumes EVERY event must write the empty head back - the engine hands the same list pointer back on idle frames, so a consumed node is re-processed every frame until new input arrives (2026-09-12)

**Symptom:** AMF's search box stopped taking input after the player erased what they had typed;
earlier, its menu-reorder fields "stopped responding". Both reports said the same thing: nothing
typed appears, nothing clicked reacts.

**Mechanism:** AMF's input hook unlinks consumed nodes from the engine's event list. If ANY node
survives it writes the pruned head back and dispatches it; if NONE survive it dispatches a static
dummy list and left `*a_events` untouched - still pointing at the node it had just consumed. The
engine does not reset that variable when it has no new events, so on every idle dispatch the hook
received the stale node again: a released Backspace read as held and deleted each character on
arrival, a CharEvent replayed sixty times, modifiers latched, and every later press was swallowed.

**Why it looked like something else:** the reorder field's id/index drift (fixed in 1.7.4 by
deferring the move) was real but secondary - the deferral narrowed the symptom and the report came
back on the next text field. Three headless runs found nothing because the driving ops entered at
the record queue, AFTER the hook; only events spliced ahead of the hook reproduced it, and on the
first such run the instrument itself looked broken (three characters became sixty-three). The
instrument was right; it had exposed the stale pointer.

**The check:** any hook that edits a dispatch list must leave `*a_events` valid on EVERY path,
including "all consumed" (write nullptr, then hand the callee whatever idiom it needs). When an
input hook "goes dead after the last key", suspect a stale head before suspecting the widget.
Wheeler's own filter does this right: it prunes in place and passes the pointer through.


## A runtime debug switch is only as durable as the next config reload - and the driving tool's own ops trigger reloads (2026-09-12)

**Symptom:** Wheeler's input spy, switched on through a new `wheeler.page spy` op (the tool echoed
`inputSpy:true`), logged nothing for events spliced directly in front of the filter. Three runs.
The one entry-trace line that did appear showed an empty list, written before the injections.

**Mechanism:** every page `rebind` and `set` calls `ApplyChangedSettings()`, which re-reads the
config; `ReadWheelBehaviorConfigFromIni` reads `[Debug] inputSpy` and overwrote the runtime flag
with the INI's `false`. The proof script switched the spy on and THEN rebound the toggle - so the
spy was off for every injection, and the silence read as "events never reach the filter".

**Two lessons.** (1) A runtime override of a config-backed value must be re-asserted after any
operation that reloads config, or the tool must set it after those operations; the honest fix
here was ordering the script, since the reload is correct behaviour. (2) "No output" from an
instrument is not a negative result until the instrument is shown to be on at the moment of the
event (LOGIC-LIBRARY 18, again): the entry trace that finally printed `0 event(s)` was the first
line that proved the flag's state at a known instant.

## Same-site hooks: the plugin that installs LAST runs FIRST, so a splicer that loads earlier never feeds a filter that loads later (2026-09-12)

InputBench, AMF and Wheeler all hook `[id removed] + [value removed]` (the PollInputDevices ->
DispatchInputEvent call). `write_call<5>` chains: each installer wraps the previous. Load order is
alphabetical by DLL name, so `wheeler.dll` (last) is the OUTERMOST wrapper: its filter runs on the
raw engine list and only THEN calls InputBench's thunk, which prepends its synthetic presses for
the original. An InputBench press therefore reaches the game and AMF (which loaded first, so it is
innermost) but never Wheeler. The measurement that settled it: InputBench logged every splice;
Wheeler's spy never saw one. The cure is a splicer inside the target itself (`wheeler.page inject`),
which puts the event ahead of that filter and everything downstream - exactly a hardware press from
that point on. Check the hook order before trusting any cross-plugin injection.

## A menu that never opens from ANY synthetic press is not an observable - prove delivery with a control the profile does answer (2026-09-13)

Wheeler 1.0.6's "tap replays the D-pad press to the game" was first judged by whether the Favorites
menu opened after the replayed D-pad-down (its user event is `Favorites`). It did not, and the
first reading was "the replay is not delivered". The killing test was to bypass Wheeler entirely:
InputBench's splice (inside Wheeler's hook, never filtered) of the same D-pad-down, of D-pad-up,
and of keyboard Q - all `Favorites` - opened nothing either, while a gamepad Start from EITHER
splicer opened the Journal at once. So synthetic gamepad events reach the engine; the Favorites
menu is simply blocked in the Test Build profile (True Hotkeys or another favorites mod holds it),
for hardware-equivalent presses too. The replay's delivery therefore rests on the Journal result
plus the logged untouched pass-through, and Favorites is struck off the list of observables in
that profile. Rule: before reading "menu did not open" as a defect in the path under test, open
the same menu with a press that skips the path; if that fails too, the menu is not a witness.

## A shipped default that points at an asset pack nobody has draws NOTHING, and every proof by state passes anyway - take one picture before calling a surface working (2026-09-13)

Wheeler 1.0.1 through 1.0.6 were each recorded WORKING on state proofs (`wheelOpen=true`, slots
counted, keys refused, pages toggled) and none of them ever drew a wheel. The fork's shipped
`Styles.defaults.ini` carried `UseGeometricPrimitiveForBackgroundTexture = false`, which tells the
wheel to draw its slots from `slot_background.svg` and `wheel_background.svg` - files that no
release of Wheeler or Wheeler Refined ships (checked: the original 1.2 zip, Refined 1.3.3.0's
main file, and the repository). With the files absent the draw calls run against null textures
and the frame stays empty, with no warning at info level. The descriptor's own default is true and
its help text says not to turn it off without a texture pack; the original mod ships true. Two
lessons. First, when a setting selects between primitives and an external asset, the shipped
default is the one that needs nothing installed. Second, the state proofs were all true and all
blind: a surface that draws is proven by a capture, so the first proof of any visual feature
includes one picture, read by eye, before the ledger says working.

## A DPI-unaware screenshot process captures the top-left fraction of a high-DPI screen - the "wheel at 0.75" was the capture, not the wheel (2026-09-13)

Screen captures taken from PowerShell (System.Drawing `CopyFromScreen` over
`Screen.PrimaryScreen.Bounds`) came back 2133x1200 on a high-resolution display at 150% scaling, and
every element sat at 0.75 of the picture: the wheel, the compass, the game's own crosshair. Two
builds were spent moving the wheel before the crosshair gave it away - the game's centre cannot be
off-centre. A DPI-unaware process reads logical bounds (2133x1200) but copies physical pixels from
(0,0), so it gets the top-left two thirds. The fix is one line before the capture:
`SetProcessDPIAware()` through user32 (see `scratchpad\wheeler-shots7.ps1`), after which Bounds is
its native resolution and the capture is the whole screen. Rule: before diagnosing an element's POSITION from
a capture, find something whose position is known (the crosshair, the compass) in the same
picture; if that is off too, the capture is wrong, not the element.

## A proof rig must satisfy the feature's own validity predicate, or the feature quietly takes its default and the proof reads as a pass (2026-09-13)

AMF 1.7.8 clamps the key-opened window to the screen. The first proof set the stored size to
1.5 x 1.5 and expected 1.0 x 1.0 back; the window came back 0.55 x 0.7 - the DEFAULT - and the
capture looked fine. The stored size was never read: the profile's `IsSet()` needs x and y >= 0,
and 1.7.7's scaling had left them negative in the owner's INI, so the whole profile counted as
unset and the clamp was never exercised. Two things saved it. The write-back debug line
(`window profile (hotkey) saved: ... w=0.550 h=0.700`) did not match the rig, and the rule from
part 05 - verify what actually ran, not what was set up - made that mismatch a stop rather than a
footnote. The second launch, with x/y set to 0, returned exactly 1.0 x 1.0. Lessons: when rigging
a stored value to drive a code path, read the predicate that gates the read (`IsSet`, a version
check, a non-empty string) and satisfy all of it; and a proof of a clamp asserts the CLAMPED value
came back, not that the surface looked right - the default looks right too. Incidentally proven:
a profile left invalid by an older build self-heals to the default and is rewritten sane.

## Driving an AMF consumer's tab bar from DevBench: `nav right` needs keyboard nav ON a tab, a recorded click does not switch tabs, and `inject` cannot send a left click (2026-09-13)

**Symptom:** photographing Unbind Vanilla Controls' Gameplay tab, three routes all left the page on its
first tab (General) while every tool call answered ok: four `amf.menu op=nav dir=right`; `op=click` at the
Gameplay tab's pixel (the tab visibly hovered, never selected); `op=inject device=mouse code=0` (refused:
"inject needs a code" - the guard is `code <= 0`, and 0 IS the left mouse button). The state JSON gave
no help either: AMF 1.8.1's `state` carries `tab=mods` but not the tabName/tabIndex the source publishes.

**Mechanism (Renderer.cpp, the consumer tab bar):** a nav step switches tabs only when
`contentHasNav && g_tabBarHasNav`, and `g_tabBarHasNav` is `ImGui::IsItemFocused()` on a TAB ITEM. After
`op=focus pane=options` plus an arrow key, ImGui's nav cursor lands on the tab-LIST BUTTON at the left of
the bar, which is not a tab item, so every `nav right` is ignored.

**What works:** `op=focus pane=options`, `op=key code=208` (Down), `op=key code=205` (Right - moves nav
from the list button onto the first tab), then `op=nav dir=right` steps one tab per call. A long table
then scrolls with `op=cursor` over the pane and `op=inject device=mouse code=9` (the engine's wheel-down
button), about six per page. Check each step by an in-process capture (`amf.process op=capture`), read by
eye - the tool's ok and the empty tab fields proved nothing. Script: `4. plans\unbind-vanilla-controls\`
is the page, the driving sequence is in the session scratchpad `uvc-shots*.ps1` and the 8a/8e captures.

## Driving the game's own Controls menu with spliced keys REMAPS a control: selection moves invisibly, Enter starts a remap, and the result is written to ControlMap_Custom.txt in the game root (2026-09-13)

**What happened:** photographing Unbind Vanilla Controls' result in Journal > System > Controls, the list was
opened with Enter, then `bench.input` Down presses were sent to scroll it. The captures showed the list NOT
moving, so the presses looked ignored. They were not: the selection moved down the rows invisibly. A second
Enter, meant to focus the list, started the game's "press a key" remap on the selected row (System Tab =
Pause), and the next Down press became its key. Live map afterwards: `Pause=[value removed]` instead of `[value removed]`.

**Where it went:** the game wrote `<MO2>\Apostasy\Stock Game\ControlMap_Custom.txt` immediately
(329 bytes, 18:24:17), including the six controls the mod had unbound as [value removed]. Root Builder deploys MO2's
`overwrite\Root\ControlMap_Custom.txt` into that root at every launch of every profile, so a changed copy left
there is a cross-profile hazard (see the Root Builder entry above). After quitting, `overwrite\Root` still
held the original (304 bytes, 2026-09-10, sha [id removed]...); the Stock Game copy was put back from a backup
taken BEFORE quitting, and both hashes were verified equal.

**The checks:** (1) in any game menu that can rebind, a key press that seems to do nothing may still be
moving an invisible selection - never follow it with Enter or a click; (2) scroll such a list with the mouse
wheel over it, or not at all; (3) before driving the Controls menu, back up every ControlMap_Custom.txt
(game root, `overwrite\Root`, My Games) with hashes, and compare after; (4) after any input-driving run,
dump the live map (`uvc.control op=dump`) for keys that moved - that is how this was caught.

## A GPL library linked into ONE build line makes the whole mod GPL - Nexus took Lock Interaction Overhaul's page down for shipping MIT beside CommonLibSSE-NG 7.2 (2026-09-13)

**What happened.** Nexus staff put Lock Interaction Overhaul (191014) under moderation: "Your mod is currently in
violation of the GNU GPL v3 license ... due to usage of CommonLibSSE-NG". Conditions to restore it: permissions
GPL-compliant (re-upload, modification, conversion, asset use, Donation Points and monetisation ALL allowed); the
GPL v3 licence and a copyright notice included; the erroneous MIT licence removed from the source.

**Why the MIT label was wrong.** The FOMOD's Skyrim 1.7 build links CommonLibSSE-NG 7.2.0 (alandtse `ng`, commit
7a60f4de), which is GPL-3.0-or-later WITH a Modding Exception and a Linking Exception - and its README says outright
that the exceptions cover Skyrim and proprietary SDKs, NOT plugin code: a plugin that statically links it "must itself
be licensed under the GPL-3.0-or-later". The 1.0.2 package tried to scope GPL to the Line-17 folder (a NOTICE saying
"our own source remains MIT") while the repo, the DLL version resource and the page all said MIT. One work, one
licence: the moderator reads the page and the repo, not the folder split. Two more facts found the same day: the
SE/AE line's CommonLib (alandtse/CommonLibVR at e617713) is still MIT, and the vendored SKSE Menu Framework consumer
header comes from QTR-Modding/SKSE-Menu-Framework-3 - LGPL-2.1 until 2026-08-29, GPL-3.0 after ("Updated the license
file to comply with the commonlib license"). Our copies descend from one taken 2026-08-24, so they are LGPL-2.1-era:
judge a vendored file by the licence on the date it was copied, not by today's upstream.

**The fix (1.0.3).** LICENSE = GPL-3.0 text verbatim (gnu.org); NOTICE.md = copyright + the GPL's own 'how to apply'
notice + why; THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md = the notices MIT components REQUIRE (the SE CommonLib, the DevBench consumer
API, Remember Lockpick Angle's mechanism) - removing MIT means removing the false claim about OUR work, not deleting
notices the MIT licence obliges us to keep. Version resource LegalCopyright, vcpkg manifests, source header, README,
FOMOD texts and the Nexus page all say GPL-3.0-or-later. Permissions on the Nexus page are the owner's click - no API.

**The check.** Before labelling any mod's licence, list what each shipped binary LINKS (every build line, every
vendored header) and read those licences at the pinned commit. If any is GPL, the mod is GPL everywhere: repo LICENSE,
version resource, README, package and page - and the Nexus permissions must allow everything. The same scan found
about twenty of our repos still labelled MIT with a CommonLibSSE-NG 7.2 line or the SMF3 header (to-do list).

**Audit result (2026-09-13, the owner: "double check all of them").** Read from the zips in `11. Nexus distro`. SAME problem as Lock
Interaction Overhaul (a Line-17 build on CommonLibSSE-NG 7.2 while the mod says MIT): Apocrypha Menu Framework 1.8.1
(+ the Custom Menu Art Preview file), Auto Draw 1.0.7, Carryweight on Level Up 1.0.4, Character Progression Control
1.1.6, Custom Difficulty UI 1.0.6, Infinity UI 2.1.1, Item Explorer 1.0.4, Potion of Clarity 1.0.9, SkyHUD Settings
Menu 1.0.4, Souls to Perks 1.0.3. NOT affected by the GPL problem (no 1.7 line, MIT CommonLib): Dragon's Eye Minimap,
Local Map Upgrade, Local Map Item Markers, Compass Navigation Overhaul, Unbind Vanilla Controls; the first four carry the
LGPL-2.1-era SMF header (a notice question, not the moderation issue). Wheeler - Refined is already GPL.

## A boot that "times out" with the game Responding and its window titled `<plugin>.dll` is a CommonLibSSE-NG fatal dialog waiting for OK - read the dialog text before theorising about a hang (2026-09-13)

**Symptom.** The Auto Audio Input Switch 1.7 boot check on the Steam 1.7.104 Test instance never reached the main
menu; after five minutes SkyrimSE was alive, `Responding=True`, 0.2 s of CPU, and no DevBench answer. The plugin under
test had logged its load and its hooks and then nothing - which looks exactly like that plugin hanging startup.

**What it was.** `Get-Process SkyrimSE` showed `MainWindowTitle = wheeler.dll`. Enumerating the process's windows
(EnumWindows + EnumChildWindows + GetWindowText, read-only, no click) gave a `#32770` dialog with the static text
`CommonLibSSE-NG/include/REL/ID.h(219): failed to open address library file` and an OK button. `skse64.log` ended at
`loading plugin "wheeler"`, and `wheeler.log` showed an old v1.3.3 build (built Sep 12) in the instance's
`WHEELER - Refined 1.7test` folder - a build that cannot read the 1.7 Address Library. CommonLibSSE-NG's
`report_and_fail` shows a modal box titled with the module name and terminates the process when OK is pressed, so
startup waits forever for a click nobody makes. The plugin under test had nothing to do with it.

**The check, in order, before any theory:** (1) the game's `MainWindowTitle` - a `*.dll` title is a plugin's fatal
dialog; (2) the dialog's text through the window enumeration above; (3) the last `loading plugin` line in
`skse64.log` and that plugin's own log. It takes seconds and names the culprit. Close the game with
`.MD\scripts\prockill.ps1 -Name SkyrimSE` (the graceful rung closed it here). Boot scripts now stop waiting and report
the dialog text when the title ends in `.dll`.

**Second blocker of the same shape (2026-09-14):** on Skyrim 1.7.x, SKSE 2.3.1 itself refuses an old plugin ("plugin
X.dll ... must be recompiled for new address library" in skse64.log) and shows a small window titled
`SKSE Plugin Loader (2.3.1)` that holds startup until OK is pressed - the game window's title is that, not a
`*.dll` name, so a boot check that only watches for `*.dll` titles times out. Watch for both titles, and read
skse64.log's "must be recompiled" lines. Seen with Auto Resolution 1.1.0 (PreSSEDisplayTweaks.dll, CommonLibSSE-NG
built 2024, old address-library flag) on 1.7.104.

**Standing state found:** the Steam 1.7.104 Test instance's `WHEELER - Refined 1.7test` copy is NOT a 1.7 build, so
that instance cannot reach the main menu until it is replaced or disabled. It sits outside that instance's test mods
area, so it was left untouched.

## XAudio2 2.7: removing the active audio device invalidates the WHOLE engine - a new mastering voice cannot be created on it, and calling into it again crashed the game (2026-09-13)

**Context.** Auto Audio Input Switch gives Skyrim a stand-in submix voice as its mastering voice, so that switching
devices only means destroying and recreating the real mastering voice underneath. The open question in its plan was
whether XAudio2 2.7 survives device REMOVAL that way. It was measured live on 1.5.97 with a Bluetooth neckband and a
monitor connected.

**Result.** When the active device (the neckband) was disconnected, the engine's OnCriticalError fired; the old mastering
voice was destroyed and `CreateMasteringVoice` on the remaining device returned **[value removed] XAUDIO2_E_DEVICE_INVALID**.
When the neckband came back, a second attempt on the same engine returned the same error, and at that same second the
game crashed with an access violation in AUDIOSES.DLL[offset removed] on an XAudio2_7.dll worker thread (no frame in our module;
attributed to our call by timing). So in 2.7 the engine itself is dead after its device goes away; only a NEW engine
can play again, which means rebuilding every voice the game owns.

**What to do with it.**
* An engine that reported a critical error, or returned [value removed], is never called again (the mod's hotfix).
* Switching while the current device is still PRESENT (a default change, a preferred device appearing) is the case a
  mastering-voice swap can serve.
* Recovery from removal needs the game to rebuild its audio: BSXAudio2Audio Shutdown + Init (SE [id removed]/66705) on
  the audio thread with live sounds stopped first - reverse-engineering work, not a variation on the swap.
* Measure device behaviour with real hardware before building a recovery path on assumptions; the standalone probe
  (`xa27probe`, modes `list`, `swap`, `hold`, `setdefault`) can drive default changes without hands.

**Resolved the same night (2026-09-13):** Auto Audio Input Switch now rebuilds the game's own audio engine on the
audio thread (detach every sound's voice, clear freed voices from the game's two voice lists, the game's own
BSXAudio2Audio shutdown + init, the game's own per-sound voice setup) - the procedure of Live Audio Output Switching
SE (MIT). A simulated unplug recovers in ~70 ms with every live sound revived on SE 1.5.97 and 1.7.104. A second
lesson from the dead ends before it: swapping a mastering voice under a RUNNING XAudio2 2.7 engine crashes the mix
thread; stop the engine first. Search for an existing open-source solution before reverse-engineering one - the
search took minutes and replaced several sessions of work.

## Calling an ActionScript function by a path that runs THROUGH a function object crashes the game - [code removed] access-violated the moment it ran (2026-09-14)

**What happened.** Unbind Vanilla Controls 1.0.2 (first build) had to blank unbound rows in the game's Controls list
(Journal > System > Controls). AMF's System row had already recorded that `GetVariable`/`GetMember` return no
ActionScript functions, so the original `SetEntry` could not be read out and wrapped. The workaround tried: replace
`SetEntry` on the list instance with a native `GFxFunctionHandler`, and forward each row to the class's own function
with [code removed]. A "safe probe"
made that same call once with no clip and no entry before replacing anything. The probe itself crashed the game the
instant the journal opened: `EXCEPTION_ACCESS_VIOLATION` at [offset removed] (`[instruction removed]`, RAX 0) in
[id chain removed] <- our TryAttach (ControlsList.cpp, the probe line). SE
1.5.97, crash-2026-09-14-08-52-56.log; the path string sat on the stack.

**What it means.** `GFxMovie::Invoke(path)` resolves the path's last segment as a method of the object before it, and
its caller dereferences an object interface it does not have when that "object" is a function (`SetEntry`) - it does
not fail cleanly with `false`. So a probe call is NOT a safe test for this shape: the failure mode is a crash, not a
return value. Invoke by path is safe for methods of real objects/clips (`<list>.InvalidateData`, `.addEventListener`,
`_root.MenuHolder.Menu_mc.FadeOutAndCall` all work).

**What worked instead.** Do not call the journal's code at all. Wrap the menu's `AdvanceMovie` (IMenu [vfunc removed],
`[vtable removed]`) and, after the original, read the list's visible row clips (`Entry0`.. up to
`iMaxItemsShown`, each clip's `itemIndex` into `EntriesA`) and change only visibility (`GetDisplayInfo` /
`SetDisplayInfo`). Every redraw path (scroll, selection, InvalidateData) has finished by then, and the frame has not
been drawn yet.

**The check.** Before invoking an ActionScript path, every segment but the last must be an object or display object,
never a function; `.call`/`.apply` on a method cannot be reached this way. To change what a Scaleform list draws
without its source, post-process its row clips after AdvanceMovie rather than wrapping its row function.
