## Rebuilding Skyrim's XAudio2 engine: the game's output-mixer table still points at destroyed voices, and a send with no output voice crashes XAudio2_7[value removed] seconds later (2026-09-14)

**What happened.** Auto Audio Output Switch passed simulated unplugs (an endpoint disabled through IPolicyConfig) on
SE 1.5.97 and 1.7.104. The first REAL Bluetooth headset unplugs on SE did not: run 1 left the switch untaken for 10 s
(no sound on either device afterwards, no crash); run 2 switched in 39 ms with 51 sounds revived and then crashed
nine seconds later - EXCEPTION_ACCESS_VIOLATION at [offset removed] (`[instruction removed]`, RSI 0) under
[id chain removed] (the game's per-sound voice setup) <- [id chain removed] (audio thread). In run 2 the old
engine's OnCriticalError ([value removed]) arrived ~50 ms BEFORE the rebuild ran; in the simulated tests it never did.

**Falsified first (rule 56).** Live Audio Output Switching's source says vanilla BSXAudio2Audio "reacts to
OnCriticalError by permanently disabling sound creation" and proxies the game's callback. On SE 1.5.97 that is not
so: the game registers the static object [id removed] (vtable [value removed]) and its OnCriticalError ([id removed]) is a bare
`ret 0`. The shield is not what was missing.

**What it was.** 66708 builds each new source voice's send list as {mastering voice [bs[value removed]], reverb submix
(global 523604), then one send per output-mixer slot the sound's output uses: list A 511864 entry {effect object,
submix voice}}. An empty slot is still emitted, as a send with pOutputVoice NULL, and XAudio2 2.7's CreateSendList
reads pOutputVoice[value removed] with no check. The game's shutdown (66706) walks lists A and B (the spare pool, 511867),
DestroyVoice()s each voice and deletes each effect object, but never clears the entries or B's count, and init
(66705) never refills them (it only recreates the reverb submix, unconditionally). 66712 makes a mixer (reusing a B
entry, or a new submix) into the first empty A slot; 66713 moves a slot back to B and clears it. Live Audio Output
Switching documents the same crash address and drops NULL sends in its CreateSourceVoice / SetOutputVoices hooks.

**The fix that held (in game, real headset, 2026-09-14 06:28):** hook IXAudio2::CreateSourceVoice, CreateSubmixVoice
and every voice class's SetOutputVoices (patched on first creation of each class) and drop sends whose
pOutputVoice is NULL; after the game's shutdown, empty every A slot and set B's count to 0 so nothing is left
pointing at freed voices or effect objects. Unplug switched in 30 ms (50 sounds), re-plug back in 49 ms (53 sounds),
five NULL sends dropped over the following seconds, clean exit, no crash log. Run 1's untaken switch did not recur;
the build logs the audio thread's stack and state after 2 s and at 10 s if it ever does.

**The checks.** A device-switch test is not done until a REAL device is removed: an endpoint disabled in software
does not deliver the engine's critical error before the rebuild. When rebuilding an engine that a game owns, list
every voice pointer the game keeps OUTSIDE the object you rebuild (globals, pools, tables) and what its own shutdown
and init do to each - read both functions, do not assume shutdown and init are inverses. A delayed crash in the
middleware seconds after a switch is a stale or null pointer the game fed it, not the switch itself.


## Unbinding a gameplay control also empties every MENU action the control map LINKS to it - the Favorite button showed [???] because Toggle POV was unbound, not Favorites (2026-09-14)

**Symptom.** A Nexus user of Unbind Vanilla Controls 1.0.2 reported favorites unreachable: the Favorite key showed `[???]`
in the Magic menu and nothing could be favorited. The shipped list unbound Favorites, so the 1.0.3 hotfix put Favorites back.
The owner then gave Favorites Q again in the Controls menu - and the inventory STILL showed `[???]` as the favorite key.

**What was actually true.** `controlmap.txt` defines many menu actions by LINKING them to a gameplay control with
`!0,<control>` instead of a key of their own:

| Context | Action | Linked to (keyboard / mouse / gamepad) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Item Menus | YButton (the Favorite button in inventory and magic) | Toggle POV / Toggle POV / Jump |
| Item Menus | Item Zoom | [value removed] / - / Toggle POV |
| Stats | YButton | Toggle POV / Toggle POV / Jump |
| Inventory | ChargeItem | Wait / Wait / Shout |
| Menu Mode | Toggle Always Run | Toggle Always Run |

The engine keeps the links (CommonLibSSE-NG: `UserEventMapping::linked`, `ControlMap::linkedMappings` of `LinkedMapping`
{linkedMappingName, linkedMappingContext, device, linkFromContext, linkFromName}). Once the gameplay control's key is [value removed]
and the links are resolved again (a saved ControlMap_Custom.txt loaded at startup, or a Controls-menu remap), the linked menu
action gets [value removed] too. DevBench dump in Njordlinger after the saved map loaded: Item Menus YButton keyboard/mouse = [value removed],
Inventory ChargeItem keyboard/mouse = [value removed] - while the unbind list held Toggle POV and Wait, not Favorites.

**Why the wrong diagnosis looked convincing.** The broken thing was CALLED "favorite", and Favorites was on the unbind list,
so the name matched the cause perfectly. The label text `[???]` is SkyUI failing to name a key, and it named no control, so
nothing pointed at Toggle POV. Only reading the Item Menus context of controlmap.txt showed that the Favorite button borrows
Toggle POV's key.

**The check.** Before unbinding (or remapping) any gameplay control, grep controlmap.txt for `!0,<control name>` in every
context: each hit is a menu action that loses its key along with the control. Verify live with a dump of those contexts, not
only Gameplay. A mod that empties a control's key owns the side effects on everything linked to it.

## A gamepad mapping created at runtime never fires: the engine's button lookup matches key AND modifier exactly, and "no modifier" is 0, not [value removed] (2026-09-14)

**Symptom.** Unbind Vanilla Controls 1.0.5 appended a Gameplay/gamepad mapping for "Pause" on Start ([value removed]). The log said
"created one on Start ([value removed])" and a DevBench dump showed Pause = [value removed], yet every Start press logged `code [value removed] userEvent ""`
and nothing opened. Keyboard Esc, controller A and B resolved normally in the same session.

**Cause.** The created mapping carried modifier [value removed] (the value the mod uses for "unmapped" keys). The engine's button -> user
event lookup (SE [id removed]) binary-searches the context's device array with comparator [id removed], which orders and matches on
inputKey AND modifier; a press builds its search key with modifier 0. A ([value removed], [value removed]) entry is never found, so the event gets no
user event. The game's own mappings all carry modifier 0 (dump: Journal/Wait modifier=[value removed]). With modifier 0 the same press
logged `userEvent "Pause"` and the journal opened.

**Why it looked like something else.** CommonLibSSE-NG's `ControlMap::GetUserEventName` mirrors the lookup with equal_range on
inputKey ONLY, so reading it suggests the modifier is irrelevant. My first explanation of the disassembly (a "held modifier"
scan) was also wrong - the adversarial sceptic showed that scan only runs after an exact (key, 0) match. Two corollaries: sort a
device array key-then-modifier after editing it, and never store [value removed] in `modifier`.

**The check.** Before appending or rewriting a UserEventMapping: copy modifier from an existing engine mapping (0), re-sort by
(inputKey, modifier), and prove it with an input listener that logs `QUserEvent()` for the real press - a dump that shows the key
is not proof the lookup uses it.

## A controller "Pause" press opens the journal on the SAVED tab; only keyboard Esc gets System (2026-09-14)

**Symptom.** With System Tab (Pause) bound to a controller button, the journal opened on whatever tab was used last (Quests after
a reload); visiting System > Controls "fixed" it until the next time Quests was the last tab. Keyboard Esc always opened System.

**What was established.** MenuOpenHandler::ProcessButton ([id removed]) passes the same flag to the journal-open call (52428) for
Pause from any device; JournalMenu::ProcessMessage (52418) hands RestoreSavedSettings the saved-tab global (520167); the journal
SWF (vanilla, SkyUI, Quest Journal Overhaul Redesigned) opens on the tab it is given. Owner test: after a reload, Esc -> System,
controller Back (Pause) -> Quests (falsification episode 35 killed "same for every Pause event"). Where the engine forces System
for keyboard Esc was not traced.

**Fix that works without an address.** Note a controller ButtonEvent whose user event is Pause (input sink, journal closed); when
that press opens the journal (< 1 s), call `<menu>.RestoreSavedSettings(lastTab, bTabsDisabled)` on the journal movie in the
first frames (JournalMenu::AdvanceMovie hook) until iCurrentTab shows the last tab. Logged "the journal shows the System tab
(2 of 3)" on every controller press.

## A hang whose stack runs through YOUR call is not necessarily yours - two unplug hangs were blamed on AAOS's DestroyVoice, and a dump with Microsoft's public symbols showed an XAudio2 2.7 internal deadlock with AAOS nowhere in it (2026-09-15)

**What happened.** Auto Audio Output Switch hung on real headset unplugs (1.0.0 and 1.0.1, 2026-09-14). AAOS's own audio
thread watch logged the game's audio thread inside AAOS's rebuild, in `IXAudio2Voice::DestroyVoice` on the old engine,
plus two XAudio2 threads waiting (XAudio2_7[offset removed] under AUDIOSES, XAudio2_7[offset removed]). Episode 46 concluded "the rebuild races
XAudio2's device-removal handling"; episode 48 "fixed" it by waiting up to 3 s for the engine's critical error before
switching, and four clean unplugs followed, so it was closed resolved. Then 1.0.2 hung on an unplug with the audio thread
NOT in AAOS at all (switch step 0), stuck in the game's own `IXAudio2SourceVoice::GetState`.

**What was actually true.** The owner's Task Manager dump, read with cdb, `.sympath srv*C:\symbols*https://msdl.microsoft.com/download/symbols`
(XAudio2_7 9.29.1962 HAS public symbols) and `!locks`: one locked critical section, owned by the AudioSes session-disconnect
thread. That thread was in `LEAPCORE::CLeapSystem::OnCriticalError` -> `StopGraph`, waiting (INFINITE) for the graph thread
to exit, while holding the CLeapSystem critical section. The graph thread had detected the lost device itself and was
blocked entering the SAME section in `OnCriticalError` ([value removed]) - its last act before exiting. XAudio2_7[offset removed] = StopGraph[value removed]
and [offset removed] = OnCriticalError[value removed]: the earlier "DestroyVoice deadlock" was this race, with AAOS's thread merely another waiter.
The 3 s wait avoided it only by timing.

**Why the wrong diagnosis looked convincing.** The stack of the thread that could not proceed ran through our own call,
and removing our call from the timing (waiting first) made the next few tries pass. Neither says who holds the lock.

**The checks.** For a hang, ask the lock, not the stack: capture a dump (Task Manager "Create memory dump file" works) and run
`!locks` with symbols - the owning thread is the answer. Try Microsoft's symbol server even for old DirectX DLLs before
assuming "no symbols". A fix that turns a race into "4 passes" is not evidence; count the failure rate before and after.
Offsets reported by our own stack walker can be symbolized later against the PDB - keep them in the log.

## A step that repoints a mod's meta.ini installationFile changes what "not installed yet" means for every later step - an installer run after the SE swaps reinstalled the replaced AE archives (2026-09-15)

Njordlinger rebuild, 2026-09-15. `nj-se-swaps.py` replaced 42 AE-only SKSE plugins with SE builds; for the seven taken from a
different Nexus file it rewrote `installationFile=` to the new archive. `nj-install-downloads.py` ran straight after it in
the same command and decided "not installed" by exactly that field - "no mod's meta.ini names this archive". The replaced
AE archives were now unnamed, so it installed six AE-only duplicates (Archery Rebalance 2.2.0, HelpExtender AE, Scrambled
Bugs AE, Simple Item Spawner Boost AE, SkyPatcher AE, the DynDOLOD 1.6.1170 plugin whose SE folder had just been dropped).
The same test also installed two OLDER versions of mods already present (Paarthurnax Quest Expansion 1.12 beside 1.13,
Producers of Skyrim 1.16 beside 1.18): an archive nobody names is not the same as a mod nobody has.

**The rule.** Compute an installer's "already installed" set BEFORE any step that rewrites installation records, or run the
installer first. And "unreferenced archive" is only a candidate: drop it when a mod with the same Nexus mod id is already
installed (a different file of the same mod is an update or an alternative, not a missing mod) unless it is a known
add-on file. The duplicates were caught by reading the install report line by line - folder names with a "(fileid)"
suffix meant the destination already existed - and moved to quarantine before any modlist line pointed at them.

## pefile.PE(path) keeps the DLL mapped until pe.close() - moving its folder later fails with WinError 32 halfway, leaving a copy in both places (2026-09-15)

`nj-se-swaps.py` read each plugin's exports with `pefile.PE(path, fast_load=True)` and never closed it. pefile memory-maps
the file, so the handle lived until garbage collection. When the script then `shutil.move`d the mod folder to quarantine,
`os.rename` failed on the still-mapped DLL, `shutil.move` fell back to copytree + rmtree, and rmtree failed on the same
file: "Sandbox When Idle" ended up fully in quarantine AND still in mods. Forty other moves in the same run succeeded,
which is what made it look random - it depended on when the collector had released earlier PE objects.

**The rule.** Close every `pefile.PE` in a `finally` (`pe.close()`), or read the bytes first and use `pefile.PE(data=...)`.
After any failed move, check both ends before retrying - a retry that moves INTO the existing quarantine folder nests the
copy instead of replacing it.

Related, same session: folder names containing `[NoDelete]` passed to `glob.glob(os.path.join(folder, "**", "*"))` match
nothing, because `[...]` is a glob character class - the FOMOD evidence reader silently found zero files for
"[NoDelete] 0199 New Armory Series". Wrap a literal path in `glob.escape()` before adding wildcards. And "the file Apostasy
runs" is not evidence a plugin loads on SE 1.5.97 - Apostasy runs on AE, and two of its files (Leveled List Crash Fix 1.1.0,
Mute On Focus Loss 4) were AE-only; the DLL's exports (SKSEPlugin_Query present) are the evidence.

## MO2's mod list ignores a style sheet's view/viewport background for plain rows; only ::item rules reach rows, and they replace separator colours (2026-09-15)

Njordlinger, the owner: separators black, mod rows dark grey. A theme copy (`stylesheets\Njordlinger.qss`) set
`QTreeView#modList { background-color; alternate-background-color }` and the owner saw "only every other mod is grey".
Adding `QTreeView#modList > QWidget#qt_scrollarea_viewport` / `> .QWidget` changed nothing. The owner's own method (select
the row, Select color) does not work for mods either.

**What MO2 2.5.2 actually does** (`src/modlist.cpp`, `src/modlistview.cpp` at tag v2.5.2): the model returns a mod's
`meta.ini` colour as `Qt::BackgroundRole` only for the Notes column - a full-row colour is a separator-only feature. The
delegate (`ModListStyledItemDelegate::paint`) puts that colour into `opt.backgroundBrush`. With the skyrim theme, plain rows
come out #000000 regardless of the view's or viewport's `background-color`; alternate rows take
`alternate-background-color`.

**How it was settled without guessing:** one MO2 launch per hypothesis, each candidate rule given a DIFFERENT colour
(#110000 view, #001100 viewport; then #000022 `::item:!alternate`, #002200 `::item:alternate`, #220000
`::item:has-children`), a `PrintWindow(hwnd, hdc, PW_RENDERFULLCONTENT=2)` capture (captures the window even when another
app is in front - `CopyFromScreen` had captured the Claude window), and pixel samples across each row. Result: only
`::item` rules paint rows, and an `::item` background REPLACES the separator's colour brush.

**The rule that works:** [code removed] plus the theme's `:hover`
and `:selected` colours repeated at the same specificity. With collapsible separators on, a separator that contains mods
has children and keeps its own black; the limit is that EMPTY separators match `:!has-children` and turn grey too.

**Transferable:** to find which paint layer wins in a Qt app you cannot debug, colour every candidate differently in one
run and sample pixels - one launch answers what several single-rule tries could not. Capture a specific window with
PrintWindow, not a screen copy. Note also: the list's scroll position can differ between launches, so read the capture
before trusting row positions from an earlier one.

**Corrected later the same day - the ::item rule hid MO2's conflict colours, and the real blocker was the border-image.** The
owner: *"its hard to tell which mods overwrite others bc the row doesnt change colors anymore"*. MO2's delegate
(`ModListStyledItemDelegate::paint`) sets `opt.backgroundBrush = markerColor(index)` for rows that overwrite / are
overwritten by the selected mod, and an `::item` background is drawn INSTEAD of that brush - so the grey rule erased every
conflict highlight. The earlier view/viewport attempts failed because the skyrim theme gives `ModListView#modList` a
`border-image` whose centre fill covers the view background. A distinct-colour capture (list #3a0000, alternate #003a00,
viewport #00003a) proved it: with `border-image: none`, `QTreeView#modList { background-color; alternate-background-color }`
paints plain and alternate rows, separators keep their own colour (empty ones too), and the viewport rule only reaches the
header. The working rule is that one block, with no ::item background; the owner confirmed the highlight shows again.
Tool: `scripts/mo2-modlist-capture.ps1` (launch, click a row by name, PrintWindow capture, row pixel samples, graceful close).

## A DLL that exports both SKSEPlugin_Query and SKSEPlugin_Version can still be AE-only: it refuses SE at query time (Currency Swapper, Container Distribution Framework, 2026-09-15)

Njordlinger (SE 1.5.97). The AE->SE swap pass (`nj-se-swaps.py`) classified plugins by their exports: Version without Query =
AE-only, Query + Version = "NG, loads on SE". On launch a dialog from `CurrencySwapper.dll` said `REL/ID.h(252): Failed to
locate an appropriate address library with the path: Data/SKSE/Plugins/versionlib-1-5-97-0.bin`, and skse64.log showed
`CurrencySwapper.dll ... reported as incompatible during query` and the same for `ContainerDistributionFramework.dll`.

**Not an Address Library problem.** The installed Address Library All in One v13 (the latest) has `version-1-5-97-0.bin`,
which is the correct SE file. `versionlib-*.bin` is the AE (1.6+) naming; a plugin asking for `versionlib-1-5-97-0.bin` was
built for AE only and its CommonLibSSE-NG query path does not have SE offsets. Both Nexus pages say so plainly: "Skyrim SE
version 1.6.1130+" (Currency Swapper 2.2.0) and "requires Skyrim SE version 1.6.1130+ ... Please do not ask me to support older
versions" (Container Distribution Framework 3.1.0).

**The rule.** Exports only prove the plugin CAN be asked on SE; they do not prove it supports SE. For an SE-only list, confirm
each SKSE plugin's supported runtimes from its Nexus page (or, after a launch, from `skse64.log` lines "reported as
incompatible during query") before calling it SE-capable. A `versionlib-1-5-97-0.bin` error on 1.5.97 means "this plugin is
AE-only", not "update Address Library".

## An AE-only mod's SE build can be a SEPARATE Nexus page - search by name before porting or writing 'no SE build exists' (Currency Swapper, Container Distribution Framework, 2026-09-15)

**What happened.** The owner's SE 1.5.97 launch popped an Address Library dialog for `CurrencySwapper.dll`; skse64.log showed
Currency Swapper 2.2.0 and Container Distribution Framework 3.1.0 refused at query (both AE-only). The Njordlinger TODO then said
"no SE build exists for Container Distribution Framework 3.x", and the owner asked for SE ports. The CDF port got as far as a
GitHub fork, every Address Library id mapped to SE and the build converted to CommonLibSSE-NG before the owner said: *"theres
already a currency swapper 1.5.97 version on nexus"* ... *"and the same for container distrobution framework"*.

**The miss.** Only the main mod pages' files were checked. The author ships the SE builds as separate mod pages - "Currency
Swapper for Skyrim 1.5" (127689) and "Container Distribution Framework for Skyrim 1.5" (120386) - DLL-only add-ons that sit
above the main mod and override its DLL (the main mod still supplies the INI). The owner had installed both 15 minutes after the
failing launch, so the instance was already fixed while the port was being built.

**Tell the builds apart from the DLL, not the page:** an SE CommonLib build names the Address Library file `version-{}.bin`, an
AE build `versionlib-{}.bin` (search the DLL's strings for both).

**Do instead.** Before a port, or before writing that no SE build exists: search Nexus BY NAME for pages titled "for Skyrim 1.5",
"SE", "1.5.97" or "No Version Lock"; check the main page's optional files; and check the instance's own `mods` folder for one
already installed (compare folder install times with the failing launch). Porting is the fallback when that comes back empty.

## An SE list's AE-only plugins cannot be found by DLL strings or mod names - the skse64.log refusals plus each mod's Nexus page are the evidence (Njordlinger, 2026-09-15)

**What happened.** After the Apostasy layout rebuild and the AE-to-SE swap pass, the owner's SE 1.5.97 launch still stopped on
popups (IFrame Generator RE AE Support: "failed to open address library file"; Widescreen Scale Removed: "not required for
version 1-5-97-0") and skse64.log showed four more refusals: Honed Metal, LeveledList Crash Fix, Magic Tweaks ("reported as
incompatible during query") and CoMAP ("does not appear to be an SKSE plugin").

**Why the swap pass missed them.**
- CommonLibSSE-NG builds contain BOTH Address Library file names (`version-{}.bin` and `versionlib-{}.bin`) even when the author
  only supports AE, so a string scan cannot separate an AE-only NG build from a dual-runtime one.
- A FOMOD install can pick the wrong runtime: Honed Metal's installed DLL was byte-identical to the installer's `VR_1.4.15` build.
- A mod can be AE-specific with no DLL at all: "Modern Toggle Walk-Run Fix 1.6.1130 and newer" ships an AE `controlmap.txt`,
  the only control map in the list - the leading suspect for the owner's controller faults.
- SE ports are often separate pages by a porter ("... for Skyrim 1.5" by Fuzzlesz: Magic Fixes and Tweaks 148821, LeveledList
  Crash Fix 129152), and an AE port of an old SE mod hides the SE original (Regular Quicksave for 1.6.1170 vs maxsu's 90343).

**Do instead.** After any launch on an SE list, read every non-"loaded correctly" plugin line in skse64.log and every popup; SKSE
loads alphabetically and a popup halts the rest, so run `scripts/nj-ae-only-sweep.py` for the plugins not yet reached. For each
suspect read the Nexus page's compatibility text and file descriptions, compare a FOMOD-installed DLL's hash against each runtime
variant in the archive, and search Nexus by name (v2 GraphQL `mods(filter: name WILDCARD)`) for a separate SE port page.

## A mod folder named after the parent can hold only one of that page's PATCH files - check installationFile against the page's MAIN file before trusting the folder name (Njordlinger, 2026-09-15)

**What happened.** After MO2 reported "Missing Masters", 80 ticked Njordlinger plugins had masters that existed nowhere in the
instance. About twenty folders carried the parent mod's own name - "Apothecary - An Alchemy Overhaul", "Artificer - An Artifact
Overhaul", "Gourmet - A Cooking Overhaul", "Unmarked Locations Pack - All In One", "Beyond Skyrim - Bruma" - but their meta.ini
`installationFile` was a patch or optional archive from that page ("Apothecary - Wyrmstooth Patch", "Artificer - Dragon Priest
Staves", "Beyond Skyrim - DLC Integration Patch"). The main file had never been downloaded; the folder name made it look installed.
Patch collections and FOMOD patch hubs brought the rest (patches for Lux, Enhanced Landscapes, Spaghetti's Cities...).

**Also learned in the fix.**
- The owner suspected masters "load later than their requirement"; the files showed no inversion at all - read loadorder.txt and the
  TES4 MAST records before assuming order.
- A FOMOD's newest MAIN is not always the right one: Holds' newest MAIN is the Modular edition with no `Holds.esp`; Lawless's newest
  MAIN is its Simonrim addon. Check that the chosen archive contains the master the patch needs.
- A FOMOD destination of "." means the mod root; treating it as a subfolder silently dropped Saints & Seducers' plugin from the plan.
- Inserting plugins one at a time cannot keep masters ahead of patches that arrive in the same batch - finish with a fix-up pass that
  moves any plugin after its last master, keep generated outputs (PGPatcher/Synthesis/DynDOLOD) last, and audit the plan before writing.

**Do instead.** For "missing master" reports, classify first (`nj-masters-audit.py`: order / hidden / absent), and for each absent
master compare the would-be parent folder's `installationFile` with that page's MAIN files (`files.json`). Resolve FOMODs against the
FINAL plugin set (`nj-fomod-resolve.py`, two passes) and run the install as a dry run with an audit of the resulting plan.

## "Before the generated outputs" must mean the TRAILING block - MO2 sorts ESM-flagged PGPatcher.esp into the master block, so min(index) of output names clamps everything to the top (Njordlinger, 2026-09-15)

**What happened.** The missing-masters install placed each new plugin "never later than the first generated output", computed as
the lowest index of any plugin named PGPatcher.esp / PG_*.esp. PGPatcher.esp is ESM-flagged, so MO2 keeps it in the master block
(load position ~65), while PG_1.esp sits last. Every placement was clamped to position 65: about 95 of 135 new plugins landed at
50-150 instead of their Apostasy positions. The masters audit still said 0 problems, because it only checks that masters are
present and earlier - it cannot see "wrong area". Found only because the next script's dry run proposed putting a plugin at 66.

**Do instead.** Find the outputs as the contiguous block at the END of the load order (walk back from the last line while the
name is an output), never by name anywhere in the list. After any bulk placement, print the new plugins' distribution by band
and a few anchor positions against the reference list - the audit of masters is necessary but is not a placement check.
Repair tool: `scripts/nj-masters-replace.py` (takes the added plugins out and re-inserts them).

## Attributing a crash to a mod: compare every stack value against the MODULE BASES, and know that DevBench tools register at DATA LOAD (2026-09-15)

**What happened.** A test launch verifying Apocrypha Menu Framework 1.8.4 crashed
(crash-2026-09-15-23-17-36.log, SE 1.5.97) roughly one second after the journal opened - and AMF had injected its
System row into that journal 3 ms earlier. The temporal correlation looked damning, and 1.8.4 was the newest thing
in the load order.

**The check that settled it.** CrashLoggerSSE's log carries a MODULES section listing every loaded DLL with its base
address, and a STACK section dumping the raw stack. Parsing both and testing every hex value in the stack against
`[base, base + module size)` for our own DLLs answers "is our code anywhere in this call path" mechanically, without
symbols and without trusting the PROBABLE CALL STACK's symbolication. Here: no value fell inside
`!ApocryphaMenuFramework.dll` ([value removed]), `ApocryphaUnbindControls.dll` ([value removed]) or `wheeler.dll`
([value removed]). The only non-game frames were CommunityShaders.dll's `MenuManagerDrawInterfaceStart::thunk` and
hdtsmp64.dll's `UnkEngine::onFrame`, and the stack carried `BSShaderAccumulator*` and `BSGeometryListCullingProcess*`
- a RENDER-path access violation during menu draw, not a Scaleform list fault.

**The falsifying evidence that mattered more than the correlation.** The SAME journal open had happened 3 minutes
earlier (19:14:47), with AMF injecting the row at the same index and Unbind Vanilla Controls hiding the same System
row 3 ms later, and the journal then stayed open and was browsed for 9 seconds with no crash. Identical mod actions,
opposite outcomes: the injection cannot be the differentiator. Log the pair of opens before blaming the new build.

**A second lesson from the same session: a 404 from DevBench is not a wrong tool name.** Three calls to `amf.menu`
returned HTTP 404 and looked like a naming error; AMF registers its DevBench tools at DATA LOAD, and the same calls
worked once `[info] ... registered` appeared a minute later. Ask `/api/tools` for the registered list rather than
inferring a name from a 404. (Wheeler's tool is `wheeler.page`, not `wheeler.settings`.)

**The check.** Before attributing a crash to our mod: (1) parse MODULES for our bases and test every STACK value
against those ranges; (2) find an earlier occurrence of the same mod action that did NOT crash; (3) only then look at
what differed. A mod being newest in the load order is not evidence.

## A proof that cannot tell success from failure proves nothing: the driven rebind "passed" on a row that already held the target value (2026-09-15)

**What happened.** Wheeler 1.2.1 added a device-match guard to keymap capture. It was verified through DevBench by
driving `wheeler.page op=rebind` on `InputBindings.GamePad/toggleWheel`: code 256 (mouse) returned `wrongDevice`, and
code 267 (D-pad down) returned `bound` with the row reading 267. That was recorded as proof and the version was marked
working. The owner then reported that rebinding still failed - and he was right.

**Why the proof was vacuous.** The row ALREADY held 267 when the test ran (it had been restored by hand in the INI
minutes earlier). A rebind that writes the value the row already has produces an identical before and after, so
`outcome:bound` and "the write never reached this row" are indistinguishable. The only case that could falsify the
claim - a row at 0 being given a value - was never exercised. The owner hit exactly that case: rebinding from unbound
left it unbound, while "rebinding to the key it was already on" appeared to work, for the same reason the test did.

**The real bug the vacuous proof hid.** Capture was keyed by INI key alone (`g_capturingKey = a_entry.iniKey`), and the
key is NOT unique: `toggleWheel`, `nextItem`, `prevItem`, `activatePrimary` and most others exist in BOTH
`InputBindings.MKB` and `InputBindings.GamePad`. Arming the gamepad row also armed the keyboard row; whichever drew
first consumed the captured code. The keyboard row took the D-pad press and refused it ("code 267 is a controller
button, but this row binds a key or mouse button"), so the gamepad row never received anything. Fixed in 1.2.2 by
keying capture and row notices on `section + "/" + key`. Note the source comment asserting the key was unique across
the catalogue - it was wrong, and nothing checked it.

**The check.** Before calling a driven test a proof, ask: what STATE would make this test pass even if the feature were
broken? If the assertion is "X was written", start from a state where X is NOT already present - a write test whose
expected result equals the starting value cannot fail. Prefer round trips that change the value and change it back,
each half asserted (the unbind test on a different row did exactly this: 35 -> 0 -> 35, and it was sound).

## A control must come from the SAME toolchain, or it proves nothing - "Pandora didn't patch the dodge" was wrong twice over (2026-09-15)

**What happened.** The owner reported the dodge had stopped working. TK Dodge AIO's DLL was loading, its key listener was
registered (`uDodgeKey = 42`), and the log showed input arriving and stamina being charged
(`Sprint key tapped - dodge input` -> `Dodge Cost after is 15` -> `step dodge active`) with NO dodge animation event.
I grepped Njordlinger's `Pandora [asset path removed]` for "TKDodge", got 0, grepped
Apostasy's equivalent, got 5, and concluded Pandora had failed to apply the `tkds` patch.

**Both halves were wrong.** (1) The control came from `Apostasy - Nemesis Output` - a DIFFERENT behaviour engine.
Pandora and Nemesis do not place the same nodes in the same files, so the comparison was meaningless. (2) The file was
wrong: scanning ALL 18 character behaviour files showed the patch present in Njordlinger after all -
`[asset name removed]` (4 hits) and `[asset name removed]` (2 hits).

**What was actually true.** TK Dodge's behaviour patch covers the ONE-HANDED and MAGIC states only. With the weapon
sheathed the player is in MT locomotion, which has no dodge node - so the plugin fires, spends stamina and logs
`step dodge active` while nothing can animate. The owner worked it out himself: *"I think I forgot to have my weapon
drawn while trying to dodge too"*. The identical thing was diagnosed the same morning ("TK behaviour is 1hm/magic only")
and I did not connect it.

**The checks.** (1) A control must come from the same tool, version and pipeline as the thing under test - comparing
Pandora output to Nemesis output, or a patched build to a differently-built one, measures the toolchain, not the
feature. (2) Before concluding "X is absent", search the whole set, not the one file where X was expected; a single-file
grep answers "not here", never "not anywhere". (3) When a plugin logs that it FIRED and the effect is missing, the gap
is between the request and the animation/graph state - check which states the patch actually covers before blaming the
build step.


## Four tool misuses in a row, each null read as a fact - and a verification harness that passed having compared nothing (2026-09-16)

**What happened.** The owner asked for every Lux interior light beam to be set to its dimmest variant. The work needed
two lookups: which vanilla `_Dim` meshes exist, and which records to change. Both were straightforward. Getting them
took four wrong tool invocations in a row, and then the verification of the result was wrong three more times.

**The four misuses, all the same shape.** (1) I wrote a hand-rolled Python BSA parser while `BSArch.exe` sat in
`<HOME>\tools\bsarch` - it returned nothing and I briefly treated that as evidence. (2) I called
`BSArch.exe list <archive>`; there is no `list` subcommand, and the empty output read as "no matches". (3) I filtered
its output with an escaped grep that could not match. (4) I re-ran the same wrong form. The correct call -
`BSArch.exe <archive> -list` - was in the tool's own help text, which I had truncated at 25 lines and never read
through. Earlier in the same task I had also announced "xEdit isn't installed" after listing only the top level of
`tools\`; both SSEEdit and Synthesis were there and registered in MO2.

**Then the verification failed three ways.** (1) A bash loop reported "ALL NINE MESHES EXIST" having compared zero
entries, because `miss=0` survived a `while read` over an empty file - a check that cannot distinguish success from
failure, the exact defect already recorded in this library. (2) The next attempt reported nine MISSING against an
archive that demonstrably contained all nine, because one side of the comparison carried `\r` line endings and
`grep -qxF` can never match across that. (3) A Python cross-check crashed because Git Bash's `/tmp` and native Windows
Python resolve to different directories.

**The rule that would have prevented all of it.** *A null result from a tool you have just misused is evidence about
your command, not about the world.* Every one of these was an empty or negative result accepted as a finding. The
discriminator is cheap: before believing "X is absent", prove the harness can see something you KNOW is present. When
the BSA list was finally correct, `grep -i fxambbeam` returned 115 filenames immediately.

**The checks.** (1) Read a tool's full help before its first use, not the first screen. (2) Prefer the installed
purpose-built tool over anything hand-rolled, and confirm what is installed by searching for it rather than by
eyeballing one directory listing. (3) Every verification harness must fail loudly on empty input - assert the expected
count before comparing (`[ "$checked" -eq 9 ]`, [code removed]), or a harness that runs nothing will report
success. (4) Normalise both sides of a string comparison, including line endings, and print them through `cat -A` when
two visually identical strings refuse to match. (5) Verify a generated artifact with a DIFFERENT reader than the one
that wrote it; self-verification by the authoring code proves nothing.

**What went right, and why.** The owner's question - *"can you mitigate the consequences of automating it?"* - turned a
refusal into an engineering problem. Running xEdit against a seven-plugin sandbox (`-D:` at a scratch `Data` folder,
hardlinked masters but real copies of the two files that could be written, everything backed up first) made the whole
risk vanish: the automation then failed harmlessly (xEdit's `-script:` opens its script editor, it does not apply a
script to a load order) and cost nothing. The fallback - hand-authoring the patch plugin in Python - was only safe
BECAUSE the sandbox existed: it was built and fully verified there, and copied into the live instance only after every
record, master, FormID, flag and mesh path had been checked. `Lux.esp` was byte-identical to its backup throughout.

## A Python SyntaxWarning printed on three consecutive runs, ignored each time - and \f silently wrote a form feed into eleven meta.ini files (2026-09-16)

Installing mods into Njordlinger, three separate scripts built each mod's `meta.ini` from a NON-RAW
Python string containing `1\modid=` and `1\fileid=`.

`\m` is not a Python escape, so it survived as a literal backslash and `1\modid=` came out correct.
`\f` **is** a Python escape - form feed, [value removed] - so `1\fileid=` was written as `1<FF>ileid=`. One key
survived and the key beside it was silently corrupted, which is exactly what made it invisible: a glance
at the file showed `1\modid=70868` and looked fine.

**Python warned every single time.** Each run printed `SyntaxWarning: invalid escape sequence` before any
output. It was read past three times, because the warning appeared above a wall of successful-looking
install output and nothing downstream failed - the mods installed correctly, only the metadata was wrong.

**Then the repair failed and its verification hid the failure.** The first repair script wrote with
`io.open(p, "wb").write(new)` - no context manager, no flush - then immediately re-read the file to check.
It reported `repaired: 0, still bad: 11`, and the proof it printed was the file's TEXT, which rendered as
`1ileid=798744` and looks repaired. It was not: **a form feed is invisible in terminal output**, so
printing a file's text to prove a control character is gone proves nothing.

**And then it happened a fourth time, writing this entry.** The script appending this very text used a
non-raw triple-quoted string, so its `\n` sequences became real newlines and its `\f` became another
form feed - shredding the code sample and putting a control character into the index row. Python warned
again. That warning was read past too.

## The rules

1. **A `SyntaxWarning` is a defect report, not noise.** Read what a tool prints *before* the part you
   were waiting for. Four runs announced the exact cause of the bug above their own success output.
2. **Never prove the absence of a control character by printing text.** Use `repr()`, `od -c`, or a byte
   count - something in which the character cannot render as nothing.
3. **Build byte patterns from explicit values when escaping is what is in doubt.** The repair only worked
   once the patterns were `bytes([[value removed]]) + bytes([[value removed]]) + b"fileid"`, with no escape sequence involved.
4. **Write, flush, fsync, close - then re-read.** Verifying through a handle that may not have flushed
   returns the old bytes and reads as a failed repair.
5. **Author file content as raw strings** (`r"..."`) whenever it contains backslashes, especially when
   the content is itself about backslashes.

A size check settles it instantly in both directions: the corrupt run `1` + FF + `ileid` is 7 bytes and
the correct `1` + backslash + `fileid` is 8, so every repaired file grew by exactly one byte.

## A field you WRITE may be a field something else READS to decide - prefixing a modifier onto a Controls row would have flipped the list's device-family detection (2026-09-16)

Unbind Vanilla Controls 1.0.8 shows a bind's modifier on the game's own Controls page by writing the
list entry's `buttonName` from `360_Y` to `LT + 360_Y`. That field looked like display text.

It is not. `ListShowsGamepad` decides whether the page is showing the keyboard or the controller by
taking the FIRST entry with a non-empty `buttonName` and testing it with
`starts_with("360_"/"PS3_"/"PS4_"/"PS5_")`. It reads that field precisely because it must not trust the
input manager's gamepad flag - an earlier 1.0.2 build did and blanked Start and Back while the
controller was on screen.

`"LT + 360_Y"` starts with none of those prefixes. So the composed string would have been read as a
keyboard name, the whole list taken for the keyboard, and the blanking logic applied to the wrong
device family. Not on the first frame - detection runs before the row loop - but on every frame after,
because the prefix PERSISTS on the entry.

**Fix:** keep the game's original string on the entry as `_uvcBaseName` when prefixing, and have the
detector prefer it. The detector's own logic is untouched; it simply never sees a name this mod composed.

## The rule

**Before writing into a field you do not own, find every reader of that field.** A field is not "display
text" because it looks like display text - it is whatever the code around it treats it as. Here one
consumer used it as a *classifier*, and the tell was in a comment explaining why it read that field
rather than a more obvious one.

Three things make this shape easy to miss:

1. The write is correct in isolation, and looks correct in the frame you test.
2. The damage is delayed - frame one is fine, because the decision is made before the write.
3. The consumer is somewhere else in the file, reading a field, not calling your code.

**What found it:** reading the consumer, not running the game. The question that surfaced it was "what
else looks at `buttonName`?", asked because the value being written was no longer the value the game
put there. When mutating shared state, grep for readers of that exact member before the build, not
after a test behaves oddly.

A near-miss, not a shipped bug: the commit that introduced it (59b0e38) was followed by the fix before
the build was ever installed or launched.

## A mod with two build lines will happily package the WRONG one, and only the strictest mod complains (2026-09-16)

**Symptom.** The owner, after a test launch: *"wrong amf version warning"*. Apocrypha Menu Framework 1.8.7 refused
to start on the Njordlinger instance and said so on screen. Nothing in the mod's own code had changed in a way that
could explain it - the version had only just been bumped for a curtain fix.

**Cause.** AMF is built from one source in TWO lines, selected by a CMake cache variable per build directory:
`AMF_RUNTIME_LINE=1` is SE 1.5.97 / AE 1.6.x on CommonLibSSE-NG 3.7, and `AMF_RUNTIME_LINE=17` is Skyrim 1.7.x on
CommonLibSSE-NG 7.2, whose address-library format the older runtimes cannot read. AMF checks this at startup and
REFUSES the wrong runtime by design. I had run `build17.bat`, so `package-mod.ps1` was handed a tree with two
candidate DLLs, and it picked - as its own warning says it does - *"the newest one with a PDB beside it"*. That was
the 1.7 build. Njordlinger runs 1.5.97.

**Why it was not obvious.** The packager does warn (`2 candidate DLLs in this tree; chose the newest one ... Pass
-Target / -BuildDir if that is the wrong one`), but it is a warning in a long successful run, and the version gate
PASSES either way - the gate binds a number to a DLL hash, and it has no opinion about which runtime that DLL is
for. Worse, the same mistake had already been made on Unbind Vanilla Controls in the same session and produced NO
symptom at all: UVC hooks by vtable and reads singletons rather than the address library, so its 1.7-line build ran
correctly on 1.5.97 - it applied binds, injected rows and wrote its INI. Only AMF, which refuses on purpose, made
the mistake visible. A mod that does not check is not a mod that is safe; it is a mod that fails later.

**The check.** When a mod has more than one build directory, the build line is chosen twice and both must agree:
once when BUILDING (`build.bat` = line 1, `build17.bat` = line 17) and once when PACKAGING. Pass `-BuildDir`
explicitly to `package-mod.ps1` for any such mod rather than letting it choose, and match the line to the runtime
of the instance being installed into - Njordlinger and Apostasy are both SE 1.5.97, so both want line 1. Confirm by
size or by reading `RUNTIME_LINE` / `AMF_RUNTIME_LINE` out of that directory's `CMakeCache.txt`; the DLL gives no
other outward sign of which line it is.

## TESQuest::IsRunning() does not mean the quest is running - it is true for a quest that never ran (2026-09-16)

**Symptom.** Alternate Perspective - Civil War Starts was tested by loading an ordinary save. Without anyone
choosing a start, the mod teleported the player to Windhelm, handed them a Stormcloak uniform and started the
civil war questline. The same predicate was also used to decide whether the vanilla recruitment quest needed
starting, so that half was silently skipping Start() and relying on SetStage to do the work.

**Cause.** CommonLibSSE-NG's `TESQuest::IsRunning()` is not a flag test:

[code example removed; the text around it says what it showed]

A quest that has never run is not stopping and has no promote task, so it answers **true**. The name reads as
"is this quest currently going", and it is not that. The neighbours differ too: `IsStopped()` tests
`none(kEnabled, kStageWait)`, and `IsStarting()` needs `IsEnabled()` first. The one that means what it sounds
like is **`IsEnabled()`** - `data.flags.all(QuestFlag::kEnabled)` - which the engine sets when a quest is
genuinely running.

**Why it was convincing.** The mod's own watchdog read as obviously correct prose: "if our quest is running but
the event never reached us, run the start". Every word of that is right; only the function was wrong. And it
was not visible in a normal launch, because a quest that has never run and a quest that is running look the
same to the predicate - it fires on the first game load and looks like the feature working.

**The check.** For a CommonLibSSE predicate whose name is a plain English question, read its body before
trusting it - several of them are derived rather than a flag test, and the derived ones have different
edge-case answers at the exact moment you care about (before anything has happened). `IsEnabled()` for "is
this quest running"; `IsCompleted()` for "is it done". A predicate used to decide whether to ACT on the
player's game deserves that reading even when it costs a minute.

## Two lookups that read alike: LookupByID<T> walks the hierarchy, TESDataHandler::LookupForm<T> demands an exact type (2026-09-16)

**Symptom.** A kit that pulls six items out of another mod's plugin reported every one of them missing -
`kit: Windhelm Heavy Armor ([id removed]) is not in the game; skipped`, six times - in a game where that
plugin was plainly loaded, and where the mod's own check had just logged `Sons of Skyrim is installed`.
The plugin was found; not one of its forms was.

**Cause.** The two lookups CommonLibSSE offers are not the same function with different inputs:

[code example removed; the text around it says what it showed]

Asking the second one for a **base class** - `TESBoundObject`, which every armour and weapon derives from
but which nothing actually *is* - can never match, because an ARMO's form type is `Armor` and a WEAP's is
`Weapon`. It compiles, and it returns null for every form in the game.

**Why it was convincing.** The same kit also contained vanilla items, and those were resolved with
`TESForm::LookupByID<TESBoundObject>` - which uses `As<T>()` and works perfectly. So half the code proved
the type was right, the plugin check proved the mod was loaded, and the failure looked like a load-order
or FormID-masking problem in the cross-plugin half. It is neither: it is the type test.

**The check.** When a templated lookup returns null for something you can see exists, read the template's
body before touching the FormID arithmetic. In CommonLibSSE specifically: `As<T>()` for anything abstract
(`TESBoundObject`, `TESObjectREFR` subtrees, `MagicItem`), and reserve the `<T>` overload of
`TESDataHandler::LookupForm` for concrete form classes that really do have their own `FORMTYPE`. The safe
form for a base class is the untemplated lookup followed by `As<T>()`:

## A clean boot proves nothing about a plugin that never loaded - check the LIVE load order, not the profile files (2026-09-16)

**Symptom.** A newly built ESP was installed into Njordlinger with MO2 closed: the mod folder copied in,
`modlist.txt` given a `+` entry inside the test-mods block, `plugins.txt` given a `*` entry, `loadorder.txt`
kept in step. All three files verified by grep afterwards. The game was launched, reached the main menu,
ran three minutes and wrote no crash log - which was reported as evidence that the plugin's records parsed
in-engine, because data files load before the menu.

Then a console command against the mod's quest failed with `self form 'ACWFBE_EquipmentQuest' not found`,
and `inspect kind=mods` showed the truth: **the plugin was not in the load order at all.** 704 plugins
loaded, and ours was not one of them. The owner enabled it by hand in MO2 and it appeared.

**Cause.** Writing a mod's lines into a profile's `modlist.txt` and `plugins.txt` while MO2 is closed is
not the same as MO2 knowing about the mod. For a folder MO2 has never seen - or has seen under a previous
name, which was the case here, since the mod had been installed earlier as `test Civil War Champion 1.0.0`
and then renamed - MO2 can start, read the profile, and still not carry the new plugin through to the
game. The profile files kept their exact 12:42:15 timestamps across the whole MO2 session, so MO2 never
rewrote them and never reconciled them either.

**Why it was convincing.** Every check that was run passed. The folder was on disk with the right file
count, the ESP's hash matched the package, all three profile files grepped clean, the game booted, and no
crash log appeared. The reasoning was "the records must be fine, because a malformed plugin would have
crashed during data-file load" - which is true, and completely worthless when the plugin was never opened.
**A negative result from a test that did not run the thing under test reads exactly like a pass.**

**The check.** Before drawing ANY conclusion from an in-game run, confirm the plugin is actually loaded:

    inspect kind=mods   ->   search .plugins[] and .lightPlugins[] for the file name

One call, in the running game, and it distinguishes "it works" from "it was never there". The same applies
to any mod installed by editing profile files rather than through MO2's own UI - the edit is the intent,
the live load order is the fact. When they disagree, the load order wins and MO2 needs the mod enabled by
hand (or re-added) before the run means anything.

## A FormID slot the merge schema did not name is a dangling pointer the game follows to a crash - "DATA" means different things per record type, and VMAD is not 4-byte aligned (2026-09-16)

**Symptom.** Njordlinger Test crashed before the main menu inside `ArcheryRebalance.dll`, reading
`[operand removed]` with rax = 0. Crash Logger named the object: `TESAmmo` "Iron Arrow" `[value removed]` from
`Civil War Guard Armor Replacer.esp` - our merged ESPFE. The ammo's projectile pointer was null.

**Cause.** `merge-to-espfe.py` rewrote FormIDs only in the subrecords its SCHEMA listed, and the
schema was keyed by subrecord NAME. `DATA` carries no FormID in most records, so it was left out -
but in an AMMO record `DATA` starts with the projectile's FormID, and in a PROJ record `DATA` holds
nine of them. Sons of Skyrim's `0_IronArrow` still pointed at `[value removed]`, its own pre-merge number
for its own projectile; the game resolved it to nothing, and the first SKSE plugin to ask an arrow
for its projectile dereferenced null. The same pass found a second one: New Legion's siege quest
script property (`QUST VMAD`) held one of that mod's own forms, and script properties are packed
behind counted strings, so a 4-byte-aligned scan never sees them.

**What was wrong in the method.** The stale-reference sweep was on the to-do list ("still to do:
the stale-reference sweep over the merged plugin") and the plugin was installed for an in-game test
without it. A merge that translates *some* references is worse than one that translates none: the
plugin loads, the catalogue looks right, and the null sits there until something reads it.

**Fix (in the tool, not by hand).** `TYPED` = FormID slots keyed by `(record type, subrecord)`:
`("AMMO","DATA") -> [0]`, `("PROJ","DATA") -> [16,20,36,40,56,60,64,84,88]`, `("WEAP","CRDT") -> [16]`.
`VMAD` is scanned at EVERY byte offset against the source's own new-record numbers and rewritten on
an exact hit. And the tool now re-reads its own output before writing: any dword (byte-stride for
VMAD) equal to a source's own number for one of its records fails the run and names the record,
subrecord and offset. It refuses rather than warns, because this is the class of error that
"loads fine and does nothing" until it crashes.

**Rule.** A merge or renumber tool is not finished when it writes a file; it is finished when it
has proven that no source-local number survives in the output. Build that proof before the first
in-game test, not after the first crash log.

## A lesson that stays in the library is not a gate: the same defect shipped again the same evening, and the answer is a rules file the pipeline evaluates (2026-09-16)

**Symptom.** Unbind Vanilla Controls 1.0.9 sat in the Nexus distro with `ApocryphaUnbindControls.dll`,
a prefixed INI and prefixed translation files, plus a doubled `Interface\Interface` folder in its
zip - hours after the unprefix pass had been declared done for every mod and written up. The same
evening: four FOMOD packages flattened to a bare DLL, and a distro 7z with no plugin inside it.
Each class was already known. The owner: *"YOU SAID YOU DID THESE ALREADY BUT AGAIN YOU MISSED IT,
I WANT YOU TO COME UP WITH A WAY TO DYNAMICALLY ADD LOGIC GATES TO CLOSE LOGIC LOOPS AS NEEDED
WHEN POSSIBLE INSTEAD OF JUST ADDING TO THE LOGIC LIBRARY."*

**Why it kept happening.** The only thing between the lesson and the next package was recall. A
library entry is read when a symptom is recognised; a package with the wrong file names has no
symptom until a user installs it.

**The mechanism.** `.MD\scripts\gate-rules.json` - one JSON row per class of defect (id, kind,
pattern or parameters, the date, and the incident) - evaluated by `.MD\scripts\package-gate.ps1`
against a package folder, its Nexus distro folder and its previous release, exiting non-zero on any
hit. `pre-finalize-check.ps1` calls it, so finalize fails. Kinds so far: forbidden path pattern
(prefixed names), forbidden extension (`.esl`), `.esp` without the light flag or with the ESM bit,
doubled path segment, a file class the previous release shipped and this one lost (INI, plugin,
translations, either build line, SWF, JSON), distro archive not equal to the finalized folder, page
text naming a stale file, page missing a linked Credit section, page version mismatch. Proven on
the bad 1.0.9 package (hits) and clean on the twelve staged releases.

**Rule.** Finding a mistake has two outputs: the library entry (why) and a gate-rules row (never
again, mechanically). If no rule kind fits, add one to package-gate.ps1 - it is small on purpose.
"Done across mods" is the gate's output, not a recollection.

## An enable parent has a whole lifecycle - a reference a quest switches ON may be switched OFF again minutes later (2026-09-17)

**Symptom.** Ysgramor's Armor addon's quest gate hung the sarcophagus lid (opposite) and the body
(normal) off `C06KodlaksGhostREF`, "initially disabled, enabled when his soul is freed". Found by
listing the tomb's disabled references and reading the quest's aliases - and never tested, because
the gate stayed off for testing. Flipping it on would have shipped a tomb that opened for the
ghost's farewell and RESEALED itself the moment the quest completed: `c06questscript`'s `OnUpdate`
runs `gk.Disable(True)` then `SetStage(200)`.

**Why it looked right.** The enable event was real and verified. The check stopped at the moment
the parent turned on; nobody asked what happened to it afterwards. A parent whose state goes
off -> on -> off is, to an enable-parented child, the same as never having changed.

**How it was caught.** Before flipping the flag, the vanilla quest scripts were decompiled
(Champollion over `Skyrim - Misc.bsa`, now installed at `%USERPROFILE%\tools\champollion`) and
every `Enable`/`Disable` in C06 listed. No vanilla reference flips permanently at completion:
each is early (funeral, statue activator, Kodlak's journal) or undone (the ghost). The gate is now
the mod's OWN marker with a script that enables it when the quest reports complete.

**Rule.** Before using any reference as an enable parent, trace its ENTIRE lifecycle in the
scripts that touch it - every Enable and Disable, not just the one you want. A parent that returns
to its starting state is useless as a gate. And an untested gate that ships behind a flag is not a
gate; it is a guess with a delay.

## A hand-built record header with form version 0 loads, runs, and is still wrong - the gate now reads every header (2026-09-17)

**Symptom.** MO2's plugin check on the owner's screen: "YsgramorsArmor.esp (form 0)". The
generator's `record()` helper packed `formVersion = 0` into every record it authored and into the
rebuilt TES4 header, for seven days and two releases, while the body, recipes and armatures all
worked in game.

**Why it looked right.** The engine parses most subrecords by tag, so a wrong form version shows
nothing until it hits one it parses by version (BODT vs BOD2 in ARMO/ARMA - the Dragonbone
generator's crash of 2026-09-16 was the same field from the other direction: 44 stamped onto a
record that carried a BODT).

**Fix.** Authored records are 44; a record CLONED from a master passes the master's own form
version through (`clone_vanilla_npc` returns it; TreasCorpseDraugrMale is 40, XMarker 35). Gate
rule `esp-header-is-form-44-and-no-record-is-form-0` (kind `esp-form-version`) walks every record
header in every packaged `.esp`: the TES4 header must be 44 and no record may be 0. It was
deliberately NOT written as "every record is 44" - that would fail every plugin that correctly
carries copied records, and the Dragonbone changelog says exactly why.

**Rule.** When a check is added for a defect, write the invariant that is actually true of correct
output, not the one that matches the bad sample. Then run it on a known-good package with copied
records before trusting it.

## An ARMO's addon list is one MODL subrecord PER addon - packed into one, the engine keeps none, and the piece is invisible (2026-09-17)

**Symptom.** Nordic Skyforged 1.0.0: the cuirass, boots, gauntlets and shield rendered on the
player; the helmet did not, leaving a bare head with the hair partly hidden (the owner: "the
skyforged made the head look wierd"). Legacy of Ysgramor's own Wolf Helmet - the same mesh, the
same slots, the same addon records - rendered in the same spot seconds later.

**Cause.** The generator copies each ARMO from a vanilla template. The wolf helmet template carries
FOUR `MODL` subrecords (one armour addon per race family); the generator wrote our four addon
FormIDs as ONE 16-byte `MODL`, "as one array". The engine reads `MODL` in an ARMO as a single
4-byte FormID; a 16-byte one is not an addon link at all, so the record had no addons and nothing
was drawn. Single-addon pieces were unaffected because one FormID IS four bytes.

**How it was found.** Not by staring at the mesh: a side-by-side in game (LoY's helmet vs ours on
the same character) proved the mesh and slots innocent, and a subrecord-by-subrecord dump of the
two ARMO records showed the one difference.

**Fix and gate.** One `MODL` per addon, in addon order, at the template's first `MODL`; gate rule
`armo-addon-links-are-one-subrecord-each` (kind `esp-armo-modl-4-bytes`) fails any packaged `.esp`
whose ARMO carries a `MODL` that is not 4 bytes.

**Rule.** A subrecord that repeats in the template repeats in the output. "Written once, as one
array" is a shape the format does not have, and the engine's answer to an unknown shape is silence.

## A task handed to the game thread that captures locals BY REFERENCE outlives its caller's timeout - and writes into a dead stack frame (2026-09-17)

**Symptom.** Loading Menu Overhaul - Model Sync run 9: three model swaps accepted, then an access
violation INSIDE our DLL in `std::string`'s move-assignment, called from `std::function`, called
from `skse64_1_5_97.dll` - the SKSE task queue, on the game thread.

**Cause.** The DevBench tool's `state` op did `std::string state; RunOnMainThread([&]{ state =
StateJson(); }, 2000);`. During a cell load the game thread does not service SKSE tasks; the wait
timed out, the op returned, `state` died; seconds later the game thread ran the task and assigned
into the dead frame. The same shape sits in every `RunOnMainThread([&]...)` copied from Civil War
Starts' DevBench tool: harmless while the game thread is prompt, fatal the first time it is not.

**Fix.** Results travel in a `std::shared_ptr` captured by value (or an atomic the lambda owns),
never a reference to the caller's locals; anything that does not need the game thread is read on
the caller's thread with its own locking. The `apply` op was rewritten that way; `state` no longer
touches the game thread at all.

**Rule.** A lambda queued to another thread may run after you have given up waiting for it. It
must own everything it touches. This applies to every `RunOnMainThread` in the DevBench tools
(Civil War Starts still carries the pattern - fix it when that mod is next touched).

**Amendment 2026-09-28 - it shipped again, so it is a gate.** Unbind Vanilla Controls 1.1.1's first boot crashed
inside its own DLL ([value removed], `std::string` move-assignment) two seconds after data load: a DevBench `dump` sent while
the game was still loading timed out and the queued `RunOnMainThread([&]{ out = DumpJson(); })` ran into the dead frame
later. The fix moved into the helper itself - the task runs the function under the lock the caller takes on timeout and
skips it once a `cancelled` flag is set - so every `[&]` caller is safe at once. Gate rule
`queued-task-never-outlives-its-caller` (`main-thread-task-gate.py`) now fails any package whose repo calls a timed-wait
helper with no such flag, or queues a `[&]` lambda straight to the task interface. At the time it was added it also
flags AutoDraw-SMF, CivilWarStarts, HomeownerStarts and LocalizedDamage; each is fixed when that mod is next packaged.

## A font atlas picked by a case-sensitive name check holds the wrong script - build the ranges from the language in play and the text itself (2026-09-17)

**Symptom.** littlefot on the Wheeler - Refined page, 1.2.6: `font = japanese` in FontConfig.ini,
the Japanese face loaded, the log read *"Language 'japanese' - using GlyphPreset 3 (Latin Full)"*,
and every kana and kanji on the wheel drew as `?`.

**Cause.** The folder name was compared with `==` against `"Japanese"`; Windows opened the
lower-case folder just the same, so the face loaded but the range table fell through to the Latin
presets. A second gap of the same class in the menu framework: its atlas was built from the
translation files only, so an item name a Japanese GAME supplies (Item Explorer lists them) was in
no text the builder had read.

**Fix.** Ranges are BUILT, not picked: `ImFontGlyphRangesBuilder` with the preset, the folder
script's built-in ranges matched without regard to case, the built-in ranges of the game's own
`sLanguage`, and every character of the loaded translation; a Windows face that has the script
(Meiryo/Yu Gothic, Malgun Gothic, YaHei/SimSun, Leelawadee) is merged for what the chosen face
lacks; the atlas is rebuilt after translations load and on every language switch, outside a
frame. Both mods' driving tools gained `op=font`: one probe glyph per script
(`FindGlyphNoFallback` of U+3042, U[offset removed], U[offset removed], U+0416) read from a state the build records,
so the fix is proved by reading the atlas, not a capture. Wheeler 1.2.7, AMF 1.8.8.

**Rule.** A user-typed name is matched case-insensitively, always. An atlas covers three sources
- the UI's own strings, the game's language, and whatever the game hands the page - or one of
them draws as `?`. No package-level gate rule fits this class (it is a code property); the gate is
the `op=font` probe in each atlas-owning mod's driving tool, run at every in-game proof. Only
three mods own an atlas: Wheeler, AMF and the postponed UI Overhaul.

## `ImFontAtlas::GetTexDataAsRGBA32` writes through its pixel pointer unconditionally - a null there is a crash at boot (2026-09-17)

**Symptom.** AMF 1.8.8 first proof: the game vanished ~30 s after launch, before the main menu,
with no crash log in the usual place; the loop timed out on "boot".

**Cause.** The new atlas probe called `GetTexDataAsRGBA32(nullptr, &w, &h)` to get only the size.
Dear ImGui dereferences `out_pixels` without a null check, so the first atlas build (D3D init)
faulted.

**Fix.** Pass a real `unsigned char*` and ignore it. **Rule.** Read the ImGui function body before
passing a null for an "unwanted" out-parameter; the atlas API has no optional outs.

## "failed to open the address library file" names nothing - check the file CommonLib will open BEFORE resolving anything, and say so (2026-09-17)

**Symptom.** oproso on the Wheeler page, Fluorine on SteamOS (Proton): `wheeler.dll -
CommonLibSSE-NG/include/REL/ID(219): failed to open the address library file`, and the same from
our CNO patch, on a 16-mod list where the rest ran. Two replies of "install Address Library" got
nowhere because the message carries no file name, folder or runtime.

**Cause.** The text is `stl::report_and_fail` inside `REL::IDDatabase::load()`, which opens
`Data/SKSE/Plugins/versionlib-<v>.bin` (AE) or `version-<v>.bin` (SE) RELATIVE TO THE WORKING
DIRECTORY, with `<v>` read from the executable's version resource. Under Proton any of the three
can be wrong, and nothing of ours has logged by then.

**Fix.** `src/bin/AddressLibraryGuard.h` (Wheeler 1.2.9, self-contained, to be carried by every mod
on CommonLibSSE-NG): in `SKSEPlugin_Load`, before any `REL::ID` resolves, make the same decision
CommonLib will make, log runtime / edition / exe path / file / cwd / present-or-missing (and whether
the file is beside the exe instead), and on missing show a MessageBox with all of it and return
true without registering anything - inert, game continues. Proved with the
`WHEELER_SIMULATE_MISSING_ADDRESS_LIBRARY=1` switch: the dialog, the log line, and the main menu
after dismissing it.

**Two things learned on the way.** (1) You cannot prove this by removing the file in the test
instance: Engine Fixes is loaded by the d3dx9_42 preloader BEFORE SKSE, hits the same failure, and
the game never reaches our plugin - hence the simulation switch. (2) `REL::Module::filePath()` can
be the bare file name; use `GetModuleFileNameW(nullptr)` for the executable's folder.

**Rule.** Every mod of ours on CommonLibSSE-NG carries the guard (gate rule
`skse-plugin-carries-address-library-guard`). A support reply to that error asks for the
`[AddressLibrary]` line, not for "which version do you have".

## "The bottom slot" was the top slot - read the draw code's coordinate convention before building a feature on a position (2026-09-17)

**Symptom.** Perfected Wheeler 1.3.0's shouts-and-powers slot, meant for the BOTTOM of the wheel,
appeared at the TOP in the owner's test ("the powers ended up at the top instead of the bottom").
Every comment, default table, descriptor text and changelog line had said "clockwise from the top,
slot n/2 is the bottom".

**Cause.** I named positions from an assumption. `Wheel.cpp` centres entry i at
`arcSpan * i + pi/2`, and ImGui's screen y grows DOWNWARD, so angle pi/2 is the bottom of the
screen: slot index 0 is the bottom-most slot and the indices run clockwise from there (index 1 is
lower-left). The one grep I had done on the angle math (line 390) was read as "starts at the top"
because that is how a compass reads, not how a y-down screen reads.

**Fix.** Powers locked at index 0 (bottom), Shouts at index n/2 (top), every text corrected to "slot
1 is the bottom of the wheel, numbered clockwise", and the owner's own reading of the screen used as
the check (he liked the accident and turned it into the design).

**Rule.** A feature that depends on WHERE something is drawn starts by evaluating the draw code's
convention with real numbers (which angle is 0, which way y grows, which index lands where) - or by
one capture with a known index filled - before any name like "bottom" or "top" goes into code, text
or defaults. Coordinate conventions are verified, not inferred from words.

## A gate that checks the wrong instance passes forever - rule 29 kept looking in Apostasy after the test instance moved (2026-09-17)

**Symptom.** `pre-finalize-check.ps1` rule 29 ("installed at the version being finalized") FAILED
for Perfected Wheeler 1.3.0 only because the mod was renamed - and in failing it showed that it had
been PASSING every finalize since 2026-09-14 on stale `[NoDelete] 08xx WHEELER - Refined ... 1.0.x`
folders in `<MO2>\Apostasy\mods`, while every build actually ran in Njordlinger (the test
instance since 09-14, memory `njordlinger-is-the-test-instance`) as `test <name> <version>`.

**Cause.** The instance list inside the rule was never updated when the test instance moved; the
SME retirement had been written into it on 09-10, the Njordlinger move had not. A check that finds
an old artefact reports PASS with the same green as a real one.

**Fix.** The rule now looks in `<MO2>\<test instance>\mods`, accepts the `test ` prefix and the
registry's aliases (so a renamed mod still installed under its old name is found). Rule 15 wanted a
compatibility record under the new name - written, with the earlier verdict carried inside it.

**Rule.** When an instance, folder or naming convention moves (memory or rules say so), grep the
gate scripts for the old path or pattern the same day; a rename is a good moment to notice, because
it is the only time a stale check fails instead of passing. And: a gate hit caused by a rename is not
"noise to bypass" - the two hits here found a real defect and a missing record.

## A running MO2 instance does not mount a mod folder made after it started - the game loaded the old copy (2026-09-17)

**Symptom.** Perfected Wheeler 1.3.1 was installed into a NEW folder (`test Perfected Wheeler - ... 1.3.1`),
the profile's modlist.txt said `+` for it, the game launched through the owner's running MO2 - and
wheeler.log showed `Wheeler - Refined v1.1.9`, the working copy further down the order.

**Cause.** MO2 builds the virtual file system from its in-memory mod list, which it read at start (and on
its own refresh). A folder that appears in `mods\` afterwards is not in that list, so the modlist line
names a mod MO2 does not have and the VFS skips it; the next enabled copy of the same files wins. Earlier
swaps in this session worked only because they reused a folder name MO2 already knew.

**Fix.** While MO2 runs and must not be restarted, install a test build INTO A FOLDER MO2 ALREADY KNOWS
(replace its contents), and rename later. The forwarded `moshortcut://` launch can also leave the
instance on a modal "failed to receive data from secondary process" dialog; nothing launches until it is
closed (WM_CLOSE to that window worked; check `EnumWindows` for the process before blaming the game).

**Rule.** Before a launch through a running MO2, confirm the build actually loaded (the log banner's
version) before reading any result; a test that passes on the wrong binary is the worst kind of pass.

## Menus draw the character - a wheel picture without the body is taken in gameplay, first person, HUD off (2026-09-17)

**Symptom.** The owner: "the characters body shouldn't be visible in the wheel pictures so retake them in
first person". Set to first person, the pictures still showed the body: the inventory AND the magic menu
render the player model while open, and every earlier capture was of the wheel in edit mode inside them.

**Fix.** A DevBench op that opens the wheel itself in gameplay (`wheeler.page op=wheel sub=open`), camera
`setPov first`, `player.unequipall` (a held torch fills the left third of a first-person frame), `tm` to
drop the Scaleform HUD (the ImGui wheel stays), capture, `tm` again. Edit-mode-only features (the pick-up
ring) cannot be pictured without the body; say so rather than pretend.

**Rule.** A capture request that names what must NOT be in the frame is checked against the frame before
the banner is built - view the capture, not the tool's `ok`.

## Defender's AMSI blocks a PowerShell screen-grab loop as "malicious content" - write screen recorders in Python (2026-09-17)

**Symptom.** A GameWatch recorder in PowerShell (System.Drawing CopyFromScreen in a timed loop, hidden window)
died silently when launched detached; run in the foreground it printed `This script contains malicious content
and has been blocked by your antivirus software` (ParserError ScriptContainedMaliciousContent).

**Cause.** The shape - periodic full-screen capture from a hidden PowerShell process - matches Defender's
screen-spyware heuristics, and AMSI refuses the script at parse time regardless of intent or signing.

**Fix.** The same grab in Python (Pillow ImageGrab.grab, the same GDI BitBlt) runs untouched; the PowerShell
front end only launches it. Frames verified real (mean brightness 102, 2 fps).

**Rule.** Screen capture, input injection and similar "spyware-shaped" loops are not written in PowerShell on
this machine; a detached script that leaves no frames and no error is run in the foreground once to read the
refusal instead of guessing.

## An SKSE C-ABI is addressed by PLUGIN NAME - a renamed host silently loses every consumer (2026-09-17)

**Symptom.** TestBench 1.0.0 (DevBench 1.18.2 forked into the one private test mod, DLL renamed
`TestBench.dll`, plugin declared as "TestBench") came up with its own three bench tools, but the
tool list held NO consumer tool - no `wheeler.page`, no `amf.menu`, no DEM tool - and nothing was
logged about it anywhere; every consumer simply reported "DevBench not detected".

**Cause.** The C-ABI glue every consumer vendors (`DevBenchAPI.cpp`) obtains the interface with
[code removed] - the RECEIVER is the
SKSE plugin NAME from the plugin declaration, and SKSE routes a named dispatch only to the plugin
declared with that exact name. Renaming the declaration renames the mailbox; the consumers keep
writing to the old address, and SKSE drops undeliverable mail without a word.

**Fix.** The plugin declaration keeps the name `devbench` (xmake `commonlibsse-ng.plugin` rule);
the DLL file, version line, author and log file (`TestBench.log`, set explicitly in `InitLogging`
instead of deriving it from the plugin name) are ours.

**Rule.** When forking or renaming a plugin that other plugins TALK TO over SKSE messaging, the
declared plugin name is part of its ABI and stays; only the file name and metadata are free. The
check is the live tool list after data load: a host whose consumers are installed but absent from
`GET /api/tools` has lost its name. No package gate fits (the mod is private and never packaged);
the in-game proof is the gate.

## A spliced key press carries a user event from the GAMEPLAY context by default - inside a menu it is a press with no name, and menus ignore it (2026-09-17)

**Symptom.** The player bot's `talk` order read the Dialogue Menu perfectly (Andurs' greeting, his three
options) but its spliced Down arrow never moved the highlight, and earlier in the day a spliced R did nothing
in RaceMenu while the same splice drives gameplay keys, the wheel and AutoCombat's F10 without trouble.

**Cause.** `bench.input`'s splice named each ButtonEvent with `ControlMap::GetUserEventName(code, device)`,
whose context parameter defaults to kGameplay. The arrow keys have no gameplay mapping, so the event went
out with an empty user event; the menus dispatch on the user event ("Up", "Down", "Accept", "Cancel"), not on
the scan code, so the press was invisible to them. Gameplay-mapped keys worked because their gameplay name
happened to be right.

**Fix.** The splice looks the name up in the ACTIVE context - the top of the control map's
`contextPriorityStack` (runtime data) - and falls back to gameplay only when that context has no name for the
key. Menu mode gives Up/Down/Accept/Cancel for 200/208/28/15.

**Rule.** A synthesized input event is only as real as its user event, and the user event depends on which
input context is on top when the press is delivered. Any input-injection code names its events from the
current context, never from a fixed one. The check is a driven arrow key in an open menu: the highlight must
move.

## An installer gated on a per-character setting at data load can never attach - settings from a co-save arrive after the patches (2026-09-18)

**Symptom.** Character Progression Control 1.1.7: Raosing set the perk-points rows, pressed Save, levelled and got
the vanilla one point; the Patches tab said the perk-point patch was not active whatever the toggle did.

**Cause.** `Patches::InstallAll()` runs at kDataLoaded and seven installers returned false while their "Control
..." toggle was off, telling the player to turn it on and restart. But the character's preset - every toggle - is
applied at kPostLoadGame from the co-save (`Presets::ApplySelection`), thirty seconds later in the live log. At
install time the toggles are always their compiled defaults, so those patches could never attach, and the advice
could not work for anyone. The hooks all read their toggle live; the gate bought nothing.
